items.album: Tegh & Adel Poursamadi ~ Bayal بیل
items.excerpt: Gholam-Hossein Sa’edi’s The Mourners of Bayal (1964) remains one of the defining works of modern Iranian literature. items.body: Gholam-Hossein Sa’edi’s The Mourners of Bayal (1964) remains one of the defining works of modern Iranian literature. Across eight interconnected stories set in the fictional village of Bayal, Sa’edi explores poverty, famine, superstition, grief and death through a world where collective anxiety gradually erodes the distinction between reality and hallucination. Equally striking is his attention to sound. The village first announces itself acoustically: dogs bark across rooftops, a bell drifts through the darkness, voices pass from window to window, footsteps punctuate long stretches of silence. Bayal is heard before it is fully seen. Tegh & Adel Poursamadi respond directly to this sonic imagination, drawing not on the individual plots of the stories but on their atmosphere and, above all, on the way Sa’edi constructs the village through listening as much as through sight. Like Ima and After You Left, Bayal بیل grew out of extended improvisational dialogues between Tegh’s electronics and Adel Poursamadi’s violin, viola and traditional Iranian instruments before being carefully sculpted into finished compositions. Yet this third collaboration feels markedly more concentrated than its predecessors. The earlier records moved through broader dynamic contrasts, opening onto expansive drones. Bayal بیل occupies a narrower emotional register, maintaining an almost continuous state of subdued tension lending the album a quiet claustrophobia entirely in keeping with Sa’edi’s village, where lives unfold beneath the weight of forces that remain largely unseen. The opening “Black Stone” establishes that landscape from the outset. Electronics and bowed strings emerge from a dense greyscale haze where instrumental identities remain deliberately obscured. Sounds appear like distant outlines. “The Cow” deepens this sense of collective but undefined presence. Throughout the piece, faint layers of indistinct voices drift through the mix like fragments of overheard conversation, suggesting the murmur of Bayal’s unseen inhabitants as they move through alleys and courtyards beyond the listener’s field of perception. These ghostly traces repeatedly dissolve into silence before returning once more, punctuated by resonant strikes that resemble a ritual gong, briefly gathering the surrounding sounds before allowing them to disperse again. The effect closely recalls Sa’edi’s opening pages, where barking dogs, distant bells and whispered exchanges establish the village long before individual characters emerge. “Toward the Vast Mountain” broadens the perspective without abandoning the prevailing sense of enclosure. Percussive markers recur throughout the piece, functioning almost like ritual or processional signals that quietly propel the music forward through its suspended atmosphere. The composition advances with measured inevitability, each percussive gesture subtly reorienting the listener while strings dissolve into electronic residue. “Pāpākh” is the shortest track on the album and refers to the village dog in Sa’edi’s stories, whose barking, pacing and sudden silences are interpreted by Bayal’s deeply superstitious inhabitants as signs of looming disaster. The music mirrors that heightened state of alertness without becoming illustrative. “Zanguleh” occupies a distinctive place within the album. Whereas much of Bayal treats the strings as part of a larger electroacoustic fabric, here Adel Poursamadi’s playing comes decisively to the foreground. Long, lyrical violin lines unfold over a restrained electronic backdrop whose role is less to obscure than to sustain the instrument’s resonance. The piece carries the emotional weight of a lament, offering the album’s clearest expression of grief without disturbing its overall restraint. After the denser first half, its relative transparency feels almost startling. The closing “Under the Willow Tree” follows naturally, letting suspended harmonics, slowly decaying resonance and carefully measured silences carry the emotional weight long after the final sounds have disappeared. The artwork by Atoosa Pourhosseini extends this vision with remarkable coherence. Anonymous figures occupy the margins of a blurred architectural landscape whose contours dissolve beneath mist, grain and diffuse light. The image perfectly reflects Tegh’s description in the liner notes of approaching Sa’edi’s village from the crest of a hill, where movements remain visible but faces, conversations and individual lives disappear into distance. Like the music itself, it withholds detail in favour of atmosphere, inviting the viewer to contemplate Bayal from the same remove that shapes the album’s entire aesthetic. The affinity between Sa’edi’s prose and Tegh and Poursamadi’s music extends beyond mood. The Mourners of Bayal rarely explains events directly, allowing rumour, fragments of dialogue and sensory details to shape the reader’s understanding. Bayal follows the same logic. Voices remain indistinct, instrumental identities blur, and meaning accumulates through resonance, silence and suggestion rather than narrative illustration. Slow, and foreboding, the album faithfully captures the psychological climate of Sa’edi’s fictional village, translating one of the great works of Iranian literature into an electroacoustic language of emotional depth. photo by Aram Tahmasebi To find out more we reached out directly to Tegh and Poursamadi. Unfortuantely, due to the current situation in Iran, only Tegh was available to answer. Ima ایما imagined post-human communication through a dialogue between acoustic instruments, Iranian traditional music and electronics, while After You Left revolved around memory and uncertainty. With Bayal, the starting point is much more concrete: Gholam-Hossein Sa’edi’s The Mourners of Bayal. Yet the new album also feels more restrained and claustrophobic than the previous two, remaining within a remarkably narrow emotional and dynamic range. Did the world of Sa’edi’s book lead you towards this concentration, or was this already a direction your musical dialogue was taking after After You Left? TEGH: Yes, exactly. The atmosphere of the book had a very strong influence on the sound of the album. IMA was supposed to be the first chapter of a larger project. The idea was to continue the project by working with other musicians from different backgrounds and bring different worldviews into the kind of world-building I had in mind. Unfortunately, this part of the project has not really worked out so far. But after the first album, both of us wanted to continue working together. We wanted to keep the colours, contrasts and freedom that we found in the making of IMA, but develop them further and make them more mature. We felt that this could give us a lot of potential for different kinds of experiments, both in terms of meaning and technique. This led to After You Left, and I think it will also be present in some of the work we release in the future. But Bayal follows a different path. I see it as a completely different chapter. As you said, the album stays within the space it presents initially, and to me, the pieces have very simple forms of storytelling, and these qualities came from our personal reading of the atmosphere of the book. In The Mourners of Bayal, it was not so much the events themselves that affected us, but the atmosphere of the book. I feel that this atmosphere does not change very much throughout the book and stays with you. The political and social uncertainty in the stories, the way everything is unreal and yet it becomes believable, and the fact that the stories seem to be made up of people who feel isolated from each other, maybe strangers to one another, and sometimes even strangers to themselves, all affected us. This idea of alienation is present throughout the book. Even in that small fictional village, society itself can hurt and oppress people. The village is surrounded by poverty, death, illness and hunger. All of these things pushed us towards creating a more claustrophobic and oppressive atmosphere in the album. Maybe “post-defeat” is the right word for it. That is my own personal way of describing it. What struck me while reading The Mourners of Bayal is how much of the village Sa’edi constructs through sound: barking dogs, bells, footsteps, voices travelling between houses, and long stretches of silence often precede any clear understanding of what is happening. Your description of approaching Bayal “from the top of a hill”, hearing cries and other sounds without being able to make out their details, seems closely related to this. Were you consciously responding to Sa’edi’s use of sound and listening as literary devices, and how did you translate that sense of hearing a community at a distance into pieces such as “The Cow” and “Pāpākh”? TEGH: I think that is exactly spot on. Sa’edi’s use of sounds, and the way he created the atmosphere of the book through them, was one of the reasons we chose this specific work. It was not really a conscious decision to respond to this aspect of the book. We never really sat down and talked about choosing this direction. I think we were simply influenced by it to such an extent that it found its way into the album naturally. For example, there is the sound of the bell attached to the empty carriage, coming from far away in the desert. It is mentioned several times throughout the book, often in connection with moments where there is death. The character of this sound, and the meaning it carries, had a strong effect on us and led us towards making “Zanguleh,” which means “bell” in Farsi. It might sound strange or unrelated, but this carriage and its bell also remind me of the cart in Béla Tarr’s The Turin Horse. It creates a very heavy image like that in my mind. The idea of looking at the events from a distance, as if we were standing on top of a hill looking at the village, came from our wish not to create a direct sonic retelling of the book. This perspective allowed us to stay away from simply recreating the events and focus more on what we personally felt from the atmosphere of the book and do our own thing based on that. We wanted to make music based on the effect the book had on both of us, rather than trying to represent the story itself. That is also why we left quite a lot of time between reading the book and starting to make the music. We wanted to forget as many details of the stories as possible and work only with what had remained in our minds, and of course it helped us avoid using the sounds from the book in a more literal way. For example, Papākh, the village dog, is one of the most important characters in the book for me. He has a strong presence, and in a way he observes everything while remaining silent and the villagers have a strange relationship with him. In general, the villagers have very close relationships with animals. The relationship between Mashdi Hassan and his cow, Islam and his goat, Papākh and the villagers, all stayed in my mind. The fact that this is a village suffering from famine, where some people have to go from one village to another to beg or steal food, but they still do not kill their animals for food, was particularly striking to me. The two tracks came out of this. We were more interested in making music out of the feeling we got from the presence of these characters in the story, rather than directly referring to the sound of Papākh or Mashdi Hassan’s cow. You describe the recording process as a series of improvisational dialogues that were subsequently processed and structured, with responding to the concept taking precedence over conventional musical rules. From your perspective, how does that process work? When Adel produces a sound, are you responding to it electronically in real time, or do the more radical transformations happen later during editing and processing? And at what point, for you, does an improvisation cease to be the documentation of a performance and become a composed piece? TEGH: Naturally, this way of working was not something new for Adel and me. We worked in an almost similar way on the two previous albums as well. We talked a lot about the effect the atmosphere of the book had on us. We both knew what elements of it made us hear things, and what kind of feelings we wanted to communicate. But we never really talked about what the tracks should sound like, what their structure should be, or what we should or should not do. The process usually started with one of us doing something, and the other responding to it. This would continue through different sessions, and then we would listen back to the recordings. Sometimes, from a one-hour recording, only one melody and one beat would come out, like in “Toward the Vast Mountain.” We felt that they were close to the concept we had in mind, and then we developed them into a track at a later stage. “Zanguleh” and “The Black Stone,” for example, both came out of the recording of a single session. A lot of the changes and processing happened afterwards, especially the processing of the sounds and shaping the forms. This was important for bringing the different sounds together and making them feel like they belonged to the same world. One of the main reasons for this is that I am honestly not a very good improviser. In many of the sessions, instead of being able to immediately reach the sound I had in mind, I was more often just leaving some kind of indication of what I wanted to reach later. For example going back to “Toward the Vast Mountain,” I had already written a beat for the melody in the improvisation, but the sounds and the pattern were quite different from what you hear on the final track. As for the last part of your question, it is a little difficult to explain. There is a point during the process when you suddenly think, “Ah, we found it. This is becoming something.” It is a moment when you find each other, everything starts to work together, and you feel that you have reached something. For me, that is the point where I can change the way I look at the material. I can stop thinking only about finding sounds or making the improvisation work, and start looking at what we have from the perspective of storytelling and how the idea can develop, where it can go, and how it can become a composition. artwork by Atoosa Pour Hosseini One of the most affecting moments for me is “Zanguleh”, because Adel’s violin suddenly becomes much more exposed and lyrical after spending much of the record partially submerged within the electroacoustic texture; it almost functions as a lament before “Under the Willow Tree” carries the record towards silence. Across Ima ایما , After You Left and now Bayal بیل, has your understanding of the relationship between strings and electronics changed? Are you increasingly interested in making it difficult to tell where one ends and the other begins, and what made you choose to break that ambiguity so strikingly on “Zanguleh”? TEGH: Absolutely. One of the things I personally question now after several years of working with Adel is exactly this. In IMA, and to some extent in After You Left, there is still quite a clear distance between the sound of the instruments and the electronics. Maybe you could say that the meeting between my world and Adel’s world did not always become a third world, something that was neither completely mine nor completely his. I think this improved in After You Left, and we got even closer to it with Bayal. I would not necessarily say that I am trying to make it difficult to tell the sounds apart. What is more important to me is that, in the composition, sound design and all the different stages of the process, I do not treat the instruments and electronics as separate things. I also try not to let the source of a sound decide how I treat it. I want to reach a point where by the end of the process there is a kind of continuity between the sounds, and they feel like they belong to the same family. It does not matter whether you can recognise where each sound comes from, what matters is that when these different sonic characters are put together, they do not feel like they have been taken from completely different worlds and simply placed next to each other like a collage. As for “Zanguleh,” as I mentioned earlier, the track was influenced by the sound of the bell coming from far away in the story. In my personal interpretation, I connect this sound with death, not as an ending, but as something that has been staying with you. As you said, that section was meant to work almost like a lament. It is actually a mourning. Our idea was for the track to reach a point where it could finally break out and mourn freely, and that is where the track ended up. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: The deluxe box set includes unreleased demos and studio recordings, as well as various non-album cuts The Flaming Lips are reissuing their 2006 album At War With The Mystics to mark its 20th anniversary. Available in 6xCD, 6xLP and digital editions, the deluxe reissue features the full original album, as well as 19 previously unreleased demo tracks, 14 previously unreleased studio recordings, and a further 42 non-album cuts. The audio recordings of 2007 live film U.F.O.s At The Zoo and a concert at The Hollywood Bowl will also be included in the CD release. items.body: “Curandera” opens Bestiaria with a healer giving instructions. “Niña / Escucha cómo tu cuerpo te habla,” sings Ana Karen G. Barajas of Karen y Los Remedios: girl, listen to how your body talks to you. The song comes from Karen’s own illness and from the women in her family who saw her through it with advice, recipes and limpias, the cleansing rituals Mexican grandmothers pass down. The curandera in the lyric hands the work back to the girl, telling her to listen to her body and to how her soul breathes, and warns her that “Cuando callas te guardas / Lo malo / Y lo bueno”: stay silent and you keep the bad in with the good. Karen, guitarist Guillermo Berbeyer and Mexico City producer Jiony set it as a dark cumbia over a low bass and a steady beat. Trombone and cowbell sit around her voice, an organ hangs at the back of the mix, and in the instrumental breaks synth and guitar lines take over. She lives in Hong Kong now, a long way from the Mexico City she was born in and the Guanajuato she grew up in. Bestiaria, the follow-up to 2023’s Silencio, builds its twelve songs around twelve figures, among them the agave goddess Mayahuel and the Fates of “Las Moiras”. “Curandera” is the fourth single from it. Listen to “Curandera” HERE and pre-order Bestiaria, out on 9 October via ZZK Records, following THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: Karen y los Remedios – Curandera appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by yarstruly — TAKEN FROM MY REVIEW ON MY BLOG "SCOTT'S SONG BY SONG SPOTLIGHTS" Which has links for purchasing, and more.Clicked 5, but really a 4.75The prolific UK composer and keyboardist Clive Nolan may be best known as the keyboardist in Pendragon and Arena (see my spotlight on Arena on this blog), but he has really done so much more! He is also part of the bands Shadowland and (formerly) Strangers on a Train. Furthermore, he has a bachelors and masters degree from the London College of Music, and has written, produced and staged musical theater productions with his Caamora Theatre Company. He has also been a part of numerous collaborations, including three albums with Oliver Wakeman. The man is a musical mastermind. His latest solo project "Song of the Winter Throne", due to be released on Friday October 2, is a massive undertaking. It consists of a main CD and a Bonus CD totaling approximately 2 hours in length. The subject of this concept album is H�kon H�konarson, aka Hakon IV, or Hakon the Old. He was a Norwegian King born in 1204, and reigning between 1217-1263, a whopping 46 years! (Interestingly, a Norwegian musician, whose band The Windmill also has been given a Spotlight, Morten L. Clason assisted Clive Nolan in engineering the album.) As H�kon H�konarson ascended to the crown at the age of 13, he was initially King in name only and regent Earl Skule B�rdsson pulled the strings until H�kon reached adulthood. However, B�rdsson would later declare himself king even as H�kon was still on the throne. The true king would have the usurper executed in 1240 and continued his reign. This execution put a close to the long Norwegian Civil War into which H�kon himself was born. His reign is considered to be the zenith of medieval Norwegian civilization.There are a large number of people involved in bringing Clive's musical vision to life. The primary instrumentalists are: Clive Nolan - Keyboards, Orchestration and ProgrammingMirko Sangrigoli - Drums and GuitarsStig Andre' Clason - GuitarsMorten L. Clason - FluteHennie Hagen Johnsen - GuitarsArnfinn Isaksen - BassMeanwhile, the main cast members are:Gemma Ashley - SolveigRyan Morgan - H�kon H�konarsonChristina Booth - TyraClive Nolan - Music & LyricsNatalie Barnett - Freja Ross Andrews - The StorytellerAdditionally, there are 38 members of the chorus, so I will include a picture of that page of the CD booklet, so they get the credit they deserve. (Scroll to the bottom.)Many readers will surely notice the name of Christina Booth, the amazing vocalist of the Band Magenta. Stig Andre' Clason is the son of the aforementioned Morten Clason, who also plays with The Windmill.The album comes courtesy of Anne-Claire of Bad Dog Promotions. As always, I am free to call it as I hear it, and I receive no additional compensation. As per my usual method, this is a cold listen.Obviously, this is a massive production, so let me get on with it and dive into the music!Track 1 - Born in Shadow (3:14)This begins with some sound effects and the narration from Ross Andrews, in dramatic style. Equally dramatic music follows, creating an overture for what is to come. The massive chorus is put to use on this, yet the drums and underlying rhythm keep a rock feel in the music, despite how symphonic it is. A massive opener!Track 2 - The Woman from Varteig (4:34)This begins without a pause from the opener, but the music drops to a drone. Ross Andrews continues the story, discussing the circumstances of H�kon H�konarson's birth. Christina Booth as Tyra sings first, and is joined by both of the other women in their characters. They sing of how they will protect the boy to ensure the safety of the would-be king. Being born "illegitimately" during a civil war was a great danger to the boy. The vocals are flawless and set the tone magnificently. Track 3 - Wolves Gather (3:03)A traditional drum and sound effects accompany Ross Andrews' narration, then foreboding music with chanting enters and then Gemma Ashley and Natalie Barnett sing beautifully in harmony. Power chords from the guitars help to accent the mood of the music.Track 4 - Flight of the Birkebeiners (3:27)The Storyteller continues the saga, then the dramatic music takes over. The string parts are somewhat reminiscent of the piano part on "The Lamb Lies Down on Broadway" (Genesis). The chorus joins in making the scene even more dramatic. Fantastic piece of classical-level music.Track 5 - The Hidden Prince (4:12)The Storyteller continues, then H�kon (Ryan Morgan) joins in for the first time. He sings of the circumstances of his upbringing in the woodlands. A very engaging song!Track 6 - Ritual of Faith (4:29)Ross continues the story, telling of the "Trial by Ordeal" that his mother underwent to prove the boy's lineage and suitableness to become the King. The chorus, along with Tyra and Freja bring the tale to life. A powerful song, fantastically delivered by the amazing cast of musicians Nolan has assembled. Track 7 - The Puppet Crown (4:22)The Storyteller tells us how H�kon was King in Name Only, ruled over by Regents. H�kon sings that it is "The Puppet Crown" along with Solveig. The chorus tells us:This is the puppet Crown,I wear the gold, I wear the gown,But another wields the power,A hand on the hilt of a sword unbound?However, the last line of the song is:"But one day?I'll cut the strings!"The song is probably the catchiest one so far, with lots of power.Track 8 - Fractured Throne (3:40)This song tells of how even after H�kon was King in his own right, his former Regent, Skule B�rdsson, even after being given the title of Duke (the first Duke in Norway), still tried to usurp the Crown and declared himself King?spoilers, It didn't end well for Skule. All of the main characters participate in this song. The song has an air of darkness about it, but H�kon is resolute in saying "I am King, I rule alone!"Track 9 - The Sword and the Fire (6:04)Of course the storyteller starts this one off, and then H�kon and the Chorus perform together on this one. This one describes the civil war battles that finally unified H�kon's power as Skule is executed. Musically there are some odd meters here. Ryan Morgan hits a fantastic sustained high note about halfway through that is fantastic. The resolution portion of the song is so powerful! At the end of this track is the first full stop in the music.Track 10 - A Kingdom Rejoices (3:23)The storyteller describes the full coronation of H�kon as recognized by The Pope, and Norway's rejoicing, and H�kon's successes. There is some joyous music between narrative sections in a quick 6-8. Fun track!Track 11 - Frost Upon the Longships (4:38)Now that H�kon has cemented his position as King, he led Norway to become the most powerful nation in the Northern Seas. The refrains of the song are sung with only H�kon and the male members of the chorus, giving a very masculine sound. The tempo is moderately slow. There are big power chords and heavy drumming along with the orchestrations.Track 12 - Storms and Wrecks (3:51)This one describes the conflict over certain islands that broke out with rival Scotland. Mid-tempo, with some flute-like interludes. This one features Gemma Ashley's beautiful voice as Solveig. Wonderful performance!Track 13 - The King in the Mist (4:52)This is a mid-tempo bittersweet ballad, based on acoustic guitar, with H�kon describing his final days in the Orkney Islands during the Scottish Expedition. "Raise up the King in the mist, I'm ready to go home?"Track 14 - The Winter ThroneAfter the opening from the Storyteller, this one goes into a riff that sounds like a Symphonic Power Metal song. The chorus performs in Norse. It closes out the story harkening us to always remember the great reign of H�kon H�konarson!Bonus CD [Note- I have no real information about these tracks as to how they fit into the saga.]:Track 1 - We Are the Storm and The Iron (6:05)This seems to be an alternate version of "The Sword and the Fire". The lyrics are a bit different. The refrains are in English as opposed to Norse. Track 2 - Back to Varteig (4:40)One of the ladies is speaking in Norse, as opposed to The Storyteller with dramatic music accompanying. She then sings what appears to be a lullaby, in English. The other female leads join in harmony.Track 3 - Strings and Necks (3:20)I think the title refers to the guitar solo in this track. Well actually both electric and acoustic guitar solos. An outstanding (almost) instrumental track that lets the guitarists stretch out and be featured. There is a bit of a chant from one of the ladies near the end of the track. Track 4 - Crowns Across Time (4:31)This seems to be an alternate version of "The Puppet Crown". This one seems to be a little more basic in the arrangement/production; more stripped down.Track 5 - In the Mist (4:51)Once again, one of the ladies is speaking in Norse at the beginning. After that it is an alternate version of "The King in the Mist" in a more basic form, but it's sung from the perspective of one of the female characters. It seems that Clive changed his mind in regards to the point of view on some parts of the story. She speaks in Norse again at the end of the track.Track 6 - The First Prince (4:00)This is an alternate version of "The Hidden Prince" without The Storyteller at the beginning. Also a more stripped down version. I am thinking that many of these are demos/early versions. The harmonies are wonderful, only accompanied by a drumbeat at one point.Track 7 - Ritual of Faith Ceremonial Mix (3:36)No Storyteller at the beginning. There is only a basic drum accompaniment, so the vocals really pop out! The vocals are absolutely pristine!Track 8 - More Wreckage (3:50)It begins in Norse with one of the ladies speaking, as some of the others have. An alternate version of "Storms and Wrecks".Track 9 - Purely Instrumental Flight (3:33)Despite the title, I hear some "throat singing" as this begins. There are gothic choir sounds as well. This is the backing track from "Flight of the Birkebeiners" without the lead vocals. It's an impressive piece of music either way!Track 10 - Puppet Frets (4:32)The guitarists get the spotlight on this version of "The Puppet Crown".Track 11 - Frost Upon the Longships - Backing Track (4:01)The title tells you all you need to know!Track 12 - The Narration Fireside Mix (8:13)This is all of the "Storyteller" narration combined into one track. It recapitulates the opening stanza at the end, to give it a sense of completion.OVERALL IMPRESSIONS:This is begging to be staged! If anyone is capable of doing that, it is certainly Clive Nolan! With his experience in leading Caamora Theatre Company, I would not be surprised if that is already the plan. This is grand musical storytelling at its finest! The arrangements, performances, playing, singing and production are all flawless! If you are a fan of "Jeff Wayne's Musical Version of The War of the Worlds", then this is right up your alley! Three years ago, in September of 2023, I gave that album a 4 out of 5 Stars (80%). I like this one even better than that, but it is not quite one of my absolute favorites of 2026. Don't get me wrong, this is a production on an absolutely epic scale and it is achieved magnificently! Many kudos to Clive Nolan for what he and his massive cast of collaborators have accomplished here! However, I am giving it a near perfect 4.75 out of 5 (95%) as there are a few albums out there that appeal to my tastes a little more in 2026. I am certain that some will unabashedly give it a perfect score, and I certainly wouldn't fault them for it! Again, as I keep saying, 2026 has been an amazing year and prog, and almost on a daily basis, I get offered even more potentially amazing albums to review. This album certainly reinforces my assertion that 2026 will go down as one of the most amazing years in the modern prog era.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — 'Lucro Sucio; Los Ojos del Vacio' is the unexpected, overly mysterious, and definitely dream-likeninth studio album by The Mars Volta, released in April of 2025 through Clouds Hill, serving as thefollow-up to 2022's self-titled LP and its acoustic follow-up from the following year. The reformedband features an interesting lineup that sees masterminds Omar Rodriguez Lopez and Cedric Bixler-Zavala joined by Omar's brother Marcel, who plays some keyboards and is involved in the engineeringof the album, versatile female drummer Philo Tsoungui, keyboardist-saxophonist Leo Genovese, andbass player Josh Moreau, a session player with some serious experiences in well-known rock andalternative bands. As for the album in question, 'Lucro Sucio' is an 18-track labyrinth of hazy andethereal synth soundscapes, indulgent jazzy interludes, and meditative psychedelic melodies,elevated by the iconic voice of Bixler-Zavala, who sounds as solid as ever on this LP.What I really like about this record is how the gently protruding latin rock elements from the twoprevious albums have been preserved on 'Lucro Sucio', but with an artsy, cryptic undercurrent. Thereis also a very generous interpolation of various synths that allows the pristine production to shinethrough, while the tranquil, ambient tones that prevail give the collection a somewhat ominous, hazyfeel. Leaning more towards trippy art rock than prog, 'Lucro Sucio' is not necessarily the mostsubstantial Mars Volta album, especially when compared to some of the band's intimidating andmaximalist early classics. It almost feels as if Omar and Cedric are attempting to capture theopposite of what their early releases had represented, and to be honest, there is something daringand novel in such a risky experiment. The album is innovative yet accessible, with an abundance ofbeautifully composed electronic-laden psychedelic pieces like 'Reina Tormenta/Enlazan lasTinieblas', 'Cue the Sun/Alba del Orate', 'Poseedora de Mi Sombra', 'Vocifer�', and 'Un Disparo alVac�o'.The finale is a little too monotonous for my taste (that would be last five tracks), but the factthat the entire work weaves through like one continuous piece makes it more diverse and immersivethan the band's 2022 self-titled release. Nevertheless, 'Lucro Sucio' is tame and ethereal, whichfor longtime listeners of the band represents just one side of The Mars Volta's expansive studiosound.

items.body: Review by martindavey87 — 'Pulse For a Graveheart' is the second studio album by Italian progressive metal band Mind Key. Released in 2009, the group has shown a significant improvement over the four years that had passed since their debut, with stronger writing and a better-sounding production, a high quality is consistently maintained throughout the album. One major change in the bands line-up is the addition of new vocalist Aurelio Fierro. Former singer Marco Basile had a fantastic range, but at times his voice seemed quite tinny, whereas Fierro's powerful voice fits more comfortably with the music, adapting for soft, melodic sections or heavier, more aggressive parts. As expected with this genre, the musicianship is fantastic as always, featuring plenty of great interplay between all the instruments, with particular praise going to guitarist Emanuele Colella and keyboardist Dario De Cicco. There's also guest appearances by the likes of keyboard maestro Derek Sherinian, Tom Englund (of Everygrey fame), and Winger's Reb Beach.With highlights including 'Sunset Highway', 'Dead Fame Hunter', 'The Seventh Seal', 'Citizen of Greed' and 'Graveheart', this is a solid progressive metal album and sure to please all fans of the genre.

items.body: A Rammstein producer, a string section and a major label: Covenant made their fifth album under different conditions from the four before it. Ka2 Music, a division of Sony Music, released “Northern Light” in Europe on 30 September 2002, and Metropolis Records followed in the United States on 8 October 2002. The Swedish futurepop trio from Helsingborg had spent its previous albums on the independents Memento Materia, Off Beat and Dependent Records. The album turns 24 this year. Jacob Hellner, who had produced Rammstein’s first three albums, produced “Northern Light” after pre-production by the band. Stefan Glaumann mixed “Call the Ships to Port”, “Bullet”, “Invisible & Silent” and “Prometheus”, Ulf Kruckenberg mixed the other seven tracks, and Björn Engelmann mastered. Axwell added programming, Ricard Nettermalm played live drums and Lizzie Zachrisson sang backing vocals on “Bullet”, “Scared” and “Atlas”. The Stockholm Session Orchestra, arranged and conducted by Joakim Milder, played the strings on “Invisible & Silent”, and Ulf Ivarsson played bass on “Atlas”. Joakim Montelius wrote the lyrics for seven tracks and Eskil Simonsson for five. “Rising Sun” carries a co-writing credit for American techno producer Steve Stoll and uses elements of his tracks “Reciproheat” and “Falling Down”. The eleven tracks run 58 minutes and 39 seconds: “Monochrome”, “Call the Ships to Port”, “Bullet”, “Invisible & Silent”, “Prometheus”, “We Stand Alone”, “Rising Sun”, “Winter Comes”, “We Want Revolution”, “Scared” and “Atlas”. Ka2 issued the album as a standard CD, a limited digipak CD and a numbered gatefold double vinyl of 1,000 copies. The vinyl added four tracks not on the CD: club versions of “Bullet” and “Call the Ships to Port”, “Bullet (Funky Indian)” and “Don’t Go”. The Sony CDs carried copy protection and a label reading “Auf PC/Mac nicht abspielbar”, and early copies came with a sticker listing the “Northern Light” tour dates. Metropolis pressed its US edition as an HDCD. Two singles bracketed the release. “Call the Ships to Port” came out on 12 August 2002 as a CD maxi with remixes by Oliver Klitzing, Christian Morgenstern, Kaylab and Thomas P. Heckmann, and reached number 93 on the German singles chart. “Bullet” followed on 9 December 2002 with an Ellen Allien “Flow Mix”, a Le Dust Sucker mix and the otherwise unreleased “Atom Heart”. A “Bullet” DVD with the video and making-of footage appeared in January 2003. About Covenant Eskil Simonsson, Joakim Montelius and Clas Nachmanson, three school friends from Helsingborg in southern Sweden, started making music together in 1986 after seeing Front 242’s first Scandinavian show, and took the name Covenant in 1988. They built a studio in Nachmanson’s bedroom while studying in Lund. Their first released track, “The Replicant”, appeared on a Memento Materia compilation in 1992, and the label issued the debut album “Dreams of a Cryotank” in December 1994. Off Beat signed the trio in 1995 after a German festival appearance. “Sequencer” followed in May 1996, with the “Stalker” single and a tour alongside Haujobb and Steril later that year. San Francisco label 21st Circuitry handled the United States, where the “Theremin” EP appeared in 1997. “Europa” came out in April 1998. When Off Beat closed in 1999, Covenant moved to the newly formed Dependent Records in Germany and SubSpace Communications in Sweden, while Metropolis Records took over the American catalogue. “United States of Mind” appeared in February 2000, with the “Der Leiermann” single, and the live album “Synergy” followed in November 2000. “Northern Light” moved the band to Sony’s Ka2 division in 2002. By then Montelius lived in Barcelona and Simonsson in Berlin, with Nachmanson still in Helsingborg. “Skyshaper” arrived in March 2006, and in March 2007 the band announced that Nachmanson would no longer tour, with Daniel Myer of Haujobb taking his place on stage. The tour film “In Transit” came out on DVD in October 2007 and confirmed Nachmanson’s departure. “Modern Ruin” followed in January 2011, the first album with Myer as a full member, and Daniel Jonasson joined the live line-up that year. Andreas Catjar joined in 2013 on keyboards and guitar, playing on “Leaving Babylon” in September 2013 and on “The Blinding Dark”, released on 4 November 2016 after the “Sound Mirrors” single. Montelius told Side-Line at the time that the line-up had grown to five, and that “Covenant’s basic principle is to always evolve: change is the only constant.” The band handed out the “Fieldworks: Exkursion” EP on its German tour in February 2019 and released a cover of Yazoo’s “Winter Kills” in December 2020. Andreas Catjar-Danielsson died on 29 July 2024 after a long illness, and the charity “Andreas EP”, recorded with Simonsson, came out on Dependent Records on 17 October 2025. Twenty-four years after Ka2 pressed it, “Northern Light” remains the album that brought “Call the Ships to Port” and “Bullet” into the Covenant catalogue.

items.body: The Mission’s tenth studio album, “Another Fall from Grace,” turns 10 this year. The English gothic rock band released the record on 30 September 2016 through Eyes Wide Shut Recordings. Wayne Hussey has described the album as a link between The Sisters of Mercy’s “First and Last and Always” and The Mission’s own debut, “God’s Own Medicine,” citing his return to 12-string guitar as part of that connection. “Another Fall from Grace” runs just over an hour across twelve tracks and was produced by Wayne Hussey and Tim Palmer, with Palmer also mixing at ’62 Studios in Austin, Texas, and mastering by James Bacon. All songs were written by Hussey, except “Another Fall From Grace,” “Can’t See the Ocean for the Rain” and “Valaam,” co-written with Simon Hinkler. The album features a run of guest vocalists: Julianne Regan on the title track and closer “Phantom Pain,” Ville Valo of HIM on “Met-Amor-Phosis,” Gary Numan on “Within the Deepest Darkness (Fearful),” Evi Vine on “Can’t See the Ocean for the Rain” and “Never’s Longer Than Forever,” and Martin Gore of Depeche Mode on backing vocals for “Only You & You Alone.” Duke Garwood contributes alto clarinet and saxophone on “Phantom Pain.” The tracklist runs “Another Fall From Grace,” “Met-Amor-Phosis,” “Within the Deepest Darkness (Fearful),” “Blood on the Road,” “Can’t See the Ocean for the Rain,” “Tyranny of Secrets,” “Never’s Longer Than Forever,” “Bullets & Bayonets,” “Valaam,” “Jade,” “Only You & You Alone” and “Phantom Pain.” The album peaked at number 38 on the UK Albums Chart, number 2 on the UK Rock & Metal Albums Chart and number 49 in Germany. A deluxe edition followed in 2017 under the title “The Complete Another Fall From Grace,” adding a bonus disc and DVD. About The Mission The Mission formed in Leeds, England, in 1986 after Wayne Hussey and Craig Adams left The Sisters of Mercy. The pair recruited guitarist Simon Hinkler and drummer Mick Brown, initially performing as The Sisterhood before settling on The Mission. The band signed to Mercury/Phonogram’s Chapter 22 offshoot and released its debut single, “Serpent’s Kiss,” in 1986, followed by the debut album “God’s Own Medicine” in 1986, which reached the UK top ten. Through the late 1980s and 1990s, The Mission released a run of albums including “Children” (1988), “Carved in Sand” (1990), “Masque” (1992) and “Neverland” (1995), with several lineup changes affecting the rhythm section while Hussey remained the constant frontman. The band went on hiatus multiple times before reconvening for later studio work, including “God Is a Bullet” (2007), “The Brightest Light” (2013) and “Another Fall from Grace” in 2016, the latter recorded with Craig Adams back on bass and Mike Kelly on drums alongside Hussey and Hinkler. “Another Fall from Grace” brought together guest contributions from Gary Numan, Martin Gore, Ville Valo and Julianne Regan, produced by Tim Palmer and released through Eyes Wide Shut Recordings. Ten years on, the album stands as one of the band’s most complete studio statements of its post-2000s period.

items.album: Nitzer Ebb’s ‘Ebbhead’ turns 35 on 30 September
items.excerpt: British EBM group Nitzer Ebb released their fourth studio album, “Ebbhead,” on 30 September 1991 through Mute Records in the UK, with Geffen handling the release in the US. The album turns 35 this year. Nitzer Ebb recorded “Ebbhead” between May and July 1991 at Konk Studios in London, following writing and programming sessions at Sync City earlier that year. Depeche Mode’s Alan Wilder and Flood produced the album together, with Steve Lyon engineering and co-mixing.
items.body: British EBM group Nitzer Ebb released their fourth studio album, “Ebbhead,” on 30 September 1991 through Mute Records in the UK, with Geffen handling the release in the US. The album turns 35 this year. Nitzer Ebb recorded “Ebbhead” between May and July 1991 at Konk Studios in London, following writing and programming sessions at Sync City earlier that year. Depeche Mode’s Alan Wilder and Flood produced the album together, with Steve Lyon engineering and co-mixing. The ten-track record introduced sampled metal guitar to the band’s sound for the first time, most audibly on the single “Godhead,” and brought in a fourteen-piece string and bass section arranged by Andrew Poppy on “I Give to You.” Issued on CD, vinyl LP and cassette, the album runs 44 minutes across “Reasons,” “Lakeside Drive,” “I Give to You,” “Sugar Sweet,” “DJVD,” “Time,” “Ascend,” “Godhead,” “Trigger Happy” and a remix of “Family Man.” Mute lifted three singles from the album: “I Give to You” (27 August 1991), “Godhead” (30 December 1991) and “Ascend” (30 March 1992), while the “As Is” EP, issued in June 1991 ahead of the album, previewed the “Family Man” remix later included on the tracklist. “Ebbhead” streams in full on Spotify. About Nitzer Ebb Nitzer Ebb formed in 1982 in Chelmsford, Essex, England, when school friends Vaughan “Bon” Harris, Douglas McCarthy and David Gooday started the group, first as La Comedie De La Mort before adopting the Nitzer Ebb name. The trio self-released the demo “Basic Pain Procedure” in 1983 and met producer Phil Harding two years later, who produced their 1985 debut single “Isn’t It Funny How Your Body Works?” and helped them launch their own label, Power Of Voice Communications. Three further singles, “Warsaw Ghetto” (1985), “Warsaw Ghetto Remixes” (1986) and “Let Your Body Learn” (1986), followed before the band signed to Mute Records in 1986. “Murderous” (1986) and a re-released “Let Your Body Learn” (1987) built the band’s reputation in the EBM and industrial rock scenes, and “Join in the Chant” (1987) crossed into the emerging Balearic and UK acid house scenes. Nitzer Ebb released their debut album, “That Total Age,” in 1987, and Depeche Mode invited them to open the European leg of the Music for the Masses tour that year. Gooday left after the tour, and McCarthy and Harris completed the duo’s second album, “Belief,” in 1989 as a two-piece with Mark “Flood” Ellis producing. Julian Beeston joined as a touring drummer and became a regular contributor. In 1989 the band also teamed with German EBM act Die Krupps to re-record “Wahre Arbeit – Wahrer Lohn” as “The Machineries of Joy.” The third album, “Showtime” (1990), moved toward a less confrontational sound, and its single “Fun to Be Had” reached the US dance chart in a George Clinton remix. For their fourth album, “Ebbhead,” released on 30 September 1991, Nitzer Ebb brought in Depeche Mode’s Alan Wilder alongside Flood to co-produce, introducing sampled guitars and orchestral arrangement to their sound for the first time. The band promoted the album with a global tour that ran from the southern United States to Barnaul in Siberia. Their fifth album, “Big Hit” (1995), leaned further into live instrumentation, with Jason Payne joining on percussion and John Napier added on guitar for touring, and it remained the band’s final release for close to fifteen years. McCarthy went on to record and tour with Alan Wilder’s Recoil project and later formed Fixmer/McCarthy with French producer Terence Fixmer, while Harris relocated to Los Angeles and produced under the names 13mg and Maven. Nitzer Ebb reconvened in Los Angeles in 2007 and, with Flood back on production, completed “Industrial Complex,” released in 2010 and reissued on double vinyl in 2015 with an Alan Wilder remix. The band toured through the 2010s, including dates opening for Depeche Mode’s Tour of the Universe, and continued to tour with Front 242 on the Join The Forces tour into 2023, with founding members David Gooday and Simon Granger back in the lineup from 2019. McCarthy died in June 2025 at age 58, and Harris has continued Nitzer Ebb with Gooday and Granger, discussing the band’s 2026 European tour and a new album in a recent interview. “Ebbhead,” the album that introduced guitars and orchestration to the band’s EBM sound, turns 35 this year.

items.body: This release is essentially a concept piece comprising a substantial 120-page book and an accompanying Soundtrack. Merciful Nuns needs no introduction by now, and their driving force, Artaud Seth, has found the perfect vehicle here to further flesh out his “Kvltan” universe. The book serves as a guide to the ancient civilization known as Kvltan, which predates known human civilization by a vast margin. It suggests that humanity’s origins lie much further back in space and time than we realize. It is a mythological narrative in which ancient gods, lost knowledge and rituals, portals to other dimensions, dream worlds, and much more converge. Central to this are the ‘Oneironauts’—individuals capable of entering other realms of consciousness through their dreams. The book constantly straddles the boundary between dream and reality, life and death, past and future. It acts as a narrative guide to which Merciful Nuns have composed the accompanying music. The release features a 33-minute-and-33-second track divided into four parts, followed by a second track. The first piece is particularly intriguing, sounding like a genuine film score—a departure from the German band’s usual style. It is entirely Cinematic in nature, defined by an omnipresent ritualistic atmosphere that gradually evolves. Spoken-word elements are incorporated alongside deep, rumbling vocals, while the use of strings further reinforces the Soundtrack aesthetic. To my ears, this piece complements the book perfectly. The second track feels more familiar, offering a blend of Metal guitar and Gothic atmosphere, topped off by Artaud Seth’s deep, charismatic vocals. Beyond the power of the guitars, the track is further enriched by piano passages. Fans of Merciful Nuns may find themselves faced with a somewhat atypical work here, but it fits perfectly within the band’s ritualistic dynamic. Moreover, the book itself is a relatively quick read, making the entire release an intriguing and immersive experience for anyone willing to step into the mysterious world of Kvltan. (Rating:7½). items.body: Daydreaming, lost and found Daydreaming, nowhere bound Falling deeper, falling down, it took me over And I can’t get out The life inside your head has certain advantages: better dialogue, revised endings, people who finally say what you needed to hear. Spend enough time there, though, and the ordinary world begins to feel like an interruption. Somewhere between rehearsing a happier life and forgetting to participate in your own, the imagination acquires a troubling degree of authority. Minsk-based artist Tomorrows Letters traces that retreat on *Daydreaming*, a troubled synthpop lullaby set against a stark, black-and-white DIY video. The solo project of Kiryl Karotki, Tomorrows Letters gives the song an especially compelling frame: music that draws you close as its singer searches for a way out. A deep snare and a looping bassline establish a measured, insistent rhythm, with a low metallic synth figure moving beneath high, resonant chimes. The bells lend the opening a fragile sweetness, soon complicated by Karotki’s voice. Drenched in reverb, his baritone carries regret and despondency with considerable poise, allowing dread to gather beneath the melody. Certain phrases soften toward a tender whisper without losing their weight. There is a strong affinity with Dave Gahan here, particularly the sensual unease of Depeche Mode around Violator and Songs of Faith and Devotion. High harmonies brush the edges of the lead vocal, while a gentle acoustic jangle and deeper string tones add movement beneath it. Karotki gives these familiar pleasures a distinct arrangement: the bass keeps circling, the bells retain their nursery-room delicacy, and the voice seems increasingly conscious of how far it has drifted from safety. “The track was originally titled ‘Maladaptive Daydreaming’, and that’s the core of it,” Karotki explains. “It’s about that state where your inner world becomes so consuming that it starts to replace reality. It’s about how escapism can turn into a trap.” The lyrics trace that loss of control through thoughts taking flight in swirling formations, gathering a momentum their owner cannot arrest. A second voice has apparently dismissed the habit as a way to cope; the singer answers by describing the grip it has taken on him. The chorus keeps returning to the same admission, “And I can’t get out.” By the outro, the private entertainment has exhausted itself: the curtain falls, the screen goes silent, and an empty chair remains. Even then, the imagined story keeps calling. Karotki built the recording around sampled bass guitar and bells, producing it on two vintage hardware samplers running from floppy disks. His intention was to keep the sound firmly within 1980s synthpop, with the equipment lending its own worn texture to the arrangement. He then mixed the track with Andrei Bobrovka, known for his work with Molchat Doma and Nürnberg, and completed the cover artwork himself. The self-filmed video extends Karotki’s affection for classic Depeche Mode imagery into stark black-and-white rural scenes. He sits blindfolded on a chair in an open field; elsewhere, he performs with a guitar or peers through a screen of leaves. Flocks of birds fold and turn across the sky, giving the opening lyric’s murmuration a visual counterpart. The field offers room in every direction, yet the blindfold makes that freedom inaccessible. Images of the chair picked out by light against darkness bring the song’s final sense of vacancy into view. Watch the video for Daydreaming below: Working with a hardware-only approach, Tomorrows Letters draws on New Romantic pop and minimal synth to examine isolation, compulsive creation, and the less hospitable corners of the self. On Up Against the Wall, Karotki cast self-judgment as a trial with no prospect of acquittal. Daydreaming approaches that inward confinement through the comforts that gradually become dependencies, extending his interest in the mind’s capacity to make captivity feel familiar. The single also includes a remix by Farforovyekoty, the side project of Nürnberg’s vocalist, which gives the song a more aggressive, post-punk treatment. Besides the original’s uneasy lullaby, it offers another route into Karotki’s fixation. The invitation is gentle enough; the difficulty comes when you try to leave. Listen to Daydreaming via Apple Music or Spotify below: The single is also available for purchase on Bandcamp. items.album: She 1 • Him 2 Share Video for Unsettling Synthpop Single “Obsessed”
items.artist: “I Know You Will Give In to Me”
items.excerpt: My sins are all forgiven. I might be desperate, but I won’t let you forget. I know you will give in to me. I am dead set. I am dead set. She 1 • Him 2 have built their latest single Obsessed around one of pop music’s most reliable bad ideas: somebody confusing romantic destiny with a complete inability to take no for an answer. The Cleveland duo of Evan Nave and Cassie Bishop bring years of Lestat and Shy Moon behind them, though Obsessed feels leaner and brighter than that résumé might suggest.
items.body: My sins are all forgiven. I might be desperate, but I won’t let you forget. I know you will give in to me. I am dead set. I am dead set. She 1 • Him 2 have built their latest single Obsessed around one of pop music’s most reliable bad ideas: somebody confusing romantic destiny with a complete inability to take no for an answer. The Cleveland duo of Evan Nave and Cassie Bishop bring years of Lestat and Shy Moon behind them, though Obsessed feels leaner and brighter than that résumé might suggest. The synths skip forward in sharp little patterns, Bishop keeps her vocal airy and cool, and underneath it all sits an electroclash streak that brings to mind the clipped attitude and wiry pop economy of Elastica fed through a rack of 80s electronics. There is plenty of Human League, Yazoo, Soft Cell, and Ladytron in the bloodstream, but the guitars give the track an extra shove. Producer Michael Seifert threads in parts with a distinctly Fixx-like character, adding just enough bite to keep the arrangement from becoming too polished for its own good. “This song has been amazing to put together,” says Nave. “An 80s vibe with a very modern spin. And our producer, Michael Seifert, dropped some very Fixx-like guitars on it. Love the dark lyrical tone versus the upbeat music dichotomy.” That contrast is where Obsessed starts getting funny in a slightly alarming way. The music suggests somebody having a marvelous time under bright club lights; the lyrics suggest that somebody has already memorized your commute. Bishop drew inspiration from the horror film Obsession and its character Nikki, played by Inde Navarrette. “I wrote the lyrics to this song based off the movie Obsession, which I loved and thought was a unique and fun idea for a horror movie,” says Bishop. “I wanted to capture some of the elements and mood of the film in this piece.” She certainly found the right emotional neighborhood. The character at the center of the song barrels through pleading, certainty, possession, and total romantic entitlement while treating every objection as a temporary inconvenience. Love becomes less a mutual arrangement than a hostile takeover conducted in excellent makeup. Bishop wisely keeps her delivery light. She never overplays the menace, and that restraint makes the character more convincing. The voice remains smooth, composed, almost sweet, even as the lyrics tighten their grip. It gives Obsessed the unnerving quality of someone smiling pleasantly while explaining why the two of you are obviously meant to spend eternity together. The electroclash edge helps, too. Those angular guitars and bright electronics give the song a brisk, fashionable nastiness, somewhere between synthpop precision and the kind of deadpan cool Elastica once made look effortless. Obsessed is catchy enough to dance to and unhinged enough to make you reconsider sharing your location. Romance, apparently, remains a dangerous hobby. The charming video channels that same bubbly sycophancy inside the studio, where eager autograph and selfie seekers chase the performers around, hoping for — and eventually fighting over — a moment with their idols. There is something wonderfully silly about the escalation, and visually it brings to mind Toni Basil’s Mickey, with its bright, performative enthusiasm and choreographed fan frenzy. The joke fits the song neatly: admiration is only one bad decision away from fixation. Watch the video for Obsessed below: Listen to Obsessed below and order the single here. items.body: The Future arrived Tuesday No one knew, however A girl packing her suitcase saying, “Maybe now or never” There is a bassline in Ganser’s Futuretripping that seems to know the economy is fake, the clocks are lying, and somebody somewhere is trying to sell you another subscription to tomorrow. Around it, Brian Cundiff’s guitars jab and veer while Alicia Gaines sings with the cool composure of someone watching the machinery malfunction exactly as expected. The result lands somewhere between Bikini Kill, The Breeders, and DEVO, all wired together by a song obsessed with time, delay, and the peculiar modern habit of waiting for permission to panic. Futuretripping is a wiry, nervy post-punk offering built from elastic bass, restless guitar, and the kind of lyrical absurdity that makes modern life sound only slightly more ridiculous than it already is. Somewhere between The Breeders, Bikini Kill, and DEVO, the song turns anxiety about time, media, and collective hesitation into something sharp enough to dance to. The track picks up the rhythmic intelligence that ran through Animal Hospital, the band’s third LP, while pushing the tension into a tighter frame. The bassline keeps the song in motion with a thick, spring-loaded bounce, while the guitar scratches and darts around it with nervous energy. Alicia Gaines sings with a dry, controlled delivery that gives the song’s stranger images room to land without forcing the joke. The lyrics revolve around a world trapped in endless anticipation. Screens insist that everything is going according to plan, people wait for the next signal, and tomorrow becomes something they can apparently borrow from a shady acquaintance with the right connections. Ganser turns that uncertainty into deadpan comedy, presenting the future as another dubious commodity sold to people who have already spent too much of the present waiting around. The image of someone selling umbrellas beneath a clear sky gets at the song’s humor perfectly. It is ridiculous, vaguely ominous, and just believable enough. “Ahead of going on the road with Bikini Kill, I was interested in the concept of cheating time, where one could go for just a little more of it,” says Gaines. “After coming back from Europe earlier this year, we found our personal senses of time were distorted as we were dropped back into life in Chicago, mixing the mundane with the fantastical. Reaching into tomorrow for a little more of today became an inside joke, now Futuretripping.” Cundiff frames that temporal confusion as something closer to collective agitation. “Everybody’s waiting for the sign to change,” he says. “People tend to wait around to be fed what they should react to these days, what to do, and I suppose there’s a bit of that restlessness in the music and lyrics as well. It’s an agitation that it’s not tomorrow while also wanting more time today, right now.” Gaines also directs the accompanying video, which leans into a loose ’90s montage aesthetic, cutting random footage against the band performing beneath a bright blue sky. The editing has the same sideways humor as the song, constantly shifting between ordinary images and mildly surreal interruptions. Ganser leave us with a world where everybody is waiting for the sign to change while the sign itself appears to have wandered off. Watch the video for Futuretripping below: Chicago’s Ganser have spent the years since their 2018 debut Odd Talk developing an increasingly restless conversation between post-punk, noise rock, and art-school absurdity. Just Look At That Sky followed in 2020, while the 2022 EP Nothing You Do Matters brought Liars’ Angus Andrew into the producer’s chair. Bassist and vocalist Alicia Gaines and drummer Brian Cundiff remain central to the band’s writing, balancing physical rhythms with dry humor and an eye for the contradictions of everyday life. Their third album, Animal Hospital, was released through Felte on August 29, 2025, with production shared by Ganser and Andrew. A deluxe edition followed on April 22, 2026, adding five alternate versions of songs from the record. Touring with IDLES, Mclusky, and Ted Leo has helped sharpen their live attack; this September, Ganser joined Bikini Kill for shows in Milwaukee, Chicago, Royal Oak, and Cleveland. Futuretripping, released September 10, extends that momentum with a new song written and arranged by Gaines and Cundiff. For future live announcements and ticket links, visit Ganser’s official shows page. Listen to Ganser’s Future Tripping below, and order the single here. items.body: With autumn extending its chilly tendrils and release season in full swing, I found myself in the welcome but somewhat overwhelming company of three album promo’s clamoring for review. Fortunately we have a perfect if seldom used format for this that may be dredged up from the blog’s murky depths when needed. Here we go...Brymir – What We Leave BehindIf you know Brymir, you know what they do. That may be one of my least inspired opening lines ever, but I stand by it. These Finnish purveyors of melodic death metal embellish the well-established style of Finnish melodeath with sweeping orchestral arrangements, mostly resulting in a predictable but no less exhilarating couple of absolute banging tracks on an album generally overshadowed by other acts. What We Leave Behind might claim to be Brymir's “most sinister album yet”, according to the promo, but I’m still getting my saccharine fix of high-octane full-blast-melody bangers and that’s what I want. I think Brymir and/or their label are largely aware of this, since they usually manage to drop these as advance singles. For your periodic fix of indelible, vanquishing albums akin to “Wings of Fire” and “Voices in the Sky”, look no further than “Tempestbound”, and especially the title track.For those curious as to what a darker Brymir might entail, I’ve found this plan largely successful. “True Darkness” and “Buried Legion” offer a more aggressive take on their established formula, and “The Roaring King” and “Broken Dawn” achieve varying success with a slower approach. While an Aether Realm like grandiosity permeates the tracks, they can be a tad indulgent and fatiguing towards the end of an album that already carries the weight of much bombast. While hilarious, unexpected, and surprisingly apt for their style, the closing cover of Scooter's “How Much is the Fish” (you’ll know it when you hear the melody) is a bit of a contradictory choice for an album that’s supposed to show their serious side. That being said, if you liked their previous album’s I’d bet you’ll like this one too. More Brymir being Brymir is hardly a bad thing, and I’m sure I’ll wake up in a few months with one of their earworms randomly crawling around in my brain.  What We Leave Behind by Brymir What We Leave Behind by Brymir Firtan – HeliosI’ve been following now-German sextet Firtan with intermittently bated breath since my first encounter with 2018s Okeanos. Firtan’s music is firmly rooted in icy black metal, but find sit’s most arresting foothold when the band’s progressive and symphonic leanings join the furious fray. While cuts like “Seegang” and “Uferlos” (2018), “Amor Fati’and “Peraht” (2022) and “Hrenga” (2024) showed glimpses of a ravenous yet poised and grandiose talent on each of their past three albums, Firtan have yet to write an album that sweeps me away as a whole. On their previous three releases, many excellent tracks or movements felt like sweeping vista’s being crammed into the corners of an overcrowded tableau. Arresting and immediately memorable, but ultimately groaning under the weight of overindulgence or less memorable surrounding compositions. Helios, while by no means a stark departure from their established sound, does show Firtan taking steps towards greater consistency and a more measured style of blackened metal. Abandoning some of the slavering hunger and much of the speedy outbursts present on previous albums, they opt for a more doom and death metal inspired soundscape, drawing parallels to particularly Schammasch. While this approach works well to keep songs more focused, it also exposes their sometimes unnecessary length,and makes the album sag under an entirely different but no less noticeable weight at times. Slowing down does allow both acoustic elements  and some of the more death/doom oriented riffing to shine. “Kalika’s Tongue”, “Solis Currus”, “Helios” and “The Hierophant” show the shining promise in Firtan’s new approach, and if they reintroduce some of the wilder aspects from earlier releases and intertwine them with the patience and focus on display on Helios, their next release may very well live up to the expectations that I’ve been quietly carrying around since I first heard that inimitable riff of “Seegang”all those years ago. Helios by Firtan Temic – CeibaIt’s been a while since I’ve written about an album so ingrained in heavy, modern prog (metal) as this one. Those roots come as no surprise when reading of the associated pedigree that comes with this relatively young and unheralded super-group. Featuring (ex or current) members of Devin Townsend, Mike Portnoy’s Shattered Fortress, the Neal Morse Band, Haken, Shining (Nor) and Maraton is a serious endorsement. Prog super-groups, however, are also notoriously prone to writing indulgent if not masturbatory escapades of soulless technicality. Fortunately, Temic manage to avoid this latter pitfall. While the occasional keyboard or guitar solo can test my patience, the album (at least for a prog metal album) is generally well paced and only features one 10-minute-plus song. In terms of influence, it’s mainly (older) Haken that springs to mind, as well as Leprous, Votum, Kingcrow and perhaps Caligula’s Horse. Somewhat ironically, the album’s less than polished vocal delivery might afford it most of its more obvious unique character. Had those rougher, accented edges not been present, I might have given up on the album before reaching its halfway point. That’s not to say it's bad by any means, I’ve just heard too many permutations of this particular style of prog to be easily impressed. Sticking around for the latter half of the album proves more interesting, with longer compositions less focused on generic heavy prog riffs and more of the charming melodicism and sweeping climaxes that elevate Temic above the sum of its well worn parts. “Casting Stone” and “See Myself” get the ball rolling, and momentum carries the album through to “Alone” and obligatory long and ambitious closer “As Long As We Last”, which drifts towards Southern Empire’s criminally underrated Civilisation in tone and mood (if not in song length). Ceiba is a good and occasionally great progressive metal album, just don’t expect to be blown away if you’re familiar with the style.  Ceiba by TEMIC

items.body: 2026.09.30 デビュー20周年を迎えるチェリストの新倉瞳さん。音楽人生と「今」が見えてくる50の質問前を前後編でお届けします！ 後編では、新倉さんの人となりに迫るべく、好きな食べ物から、オフの日の過ごし方、ストレス解消法まで質問しました。意外な一面も見えてくるかも……!? ONTOMO編集部 東京・神楽坂にある音楽之友社を拠点に、Webマガジン「ONTOMO」の企画・取材・編集をしています。「音楽っていいなぁ、を毎日に。」を掲げ、やさしく・ふかく・おもしろ... 詳しく見る 新倉瞳に50の質問！〈前編〉チェロを始めたきっかけは？ 演奏するときに大切にしていることは？ 好きな食べ物はラーメン!? 26. 朝型ですか？ 夜型ですか？ 新倉 夜型です。その日の前後の予定にもよりますが、時間が許すなら、ダラダラと夜を過ごしていたいタイプです。「低血圧」というのを言い訳にしているんですけど（笑）、本当に朝は弱いです。 基本的には時差ボケがあっても関係なく夜型ですね。ヨーロッパに行くと、最初はちょっと早起きになるんですよ。ちゃんと眠くなって。でも、だんだん慣れていくと、また夜が長くなっていきます。 新倉瞳（にいくら・ひとみ） 桐朋学園大学音楽学部を首席で卒業し、皇居桃華楽堂新人演奏会に出演して御前演奏を行う。その後スイスに渡り、バーゼル音楽院ソリストコース・教職課程の両修士課程を最高点で修了。これまでに毛利伯郎、堤剛、トーマス・デメンガ、マーティン・ツェラー（バロック・チェロ）の各氏に師事。国内外で数多くの賞を受賞し、2017年に第18回ホテルオークラ音楽賞、2020年度に第19回齋藤秀雄メモリアル基金賞チェロ部門を受賞。桐朋学園大学在学中にEMI Music Japanより『鳥の歌』でCDデビューし、同レーベルから3枚、アールアンフィニからは『11月の夜想曲～委嘱作品集』を含む4枚のソロアルバムをリリース。ほかにも多数のアルバムを発表している。 かつてカメラータ・チューリッヒのソロ首席チェリストとして活躍し、スイスを拠点にヨーロッパや中央アジア、日本でもソリストや室内楽奏者として幅広く活動する。近年はクレズマー音楽や民族音楽にも造詣を深め、音楽祭に招かれワークショップやレクチャーコンサートも行う。カザフスタンの民俗楽器ドンブラも演奏し、2025年にはカザフスタン国営放送で日本人として異例の紹介を受けた。 使用楽器は宗次コレクションより貸与のマッテオ・ゴフリラー（1710年製）。2026年にデビュー20周年を迎えた。 27. 犬派ですか？ 猫派ですか？ 新倉 今、我が家には猫がいるので、猫派です。でも、私、柴犬とかも大好きなんですよね。だから答えづらい（笑）。かわいいんですよね。 新倉さんの愛猫・紬ちゃん 28. 好きな食べ物は何ですか？ 新倉 イケメン好きなんです（笑）。演奏活動でいろいろな土地に伺うと、その土地その土地のイケメン（イケてる麺）探しを常にしております。 海外に長くいるときに一番恋しくなるのはラーメンですね。スイスにもラーメン屋さんは多いですし、最近は海外でも増えてきていますけど、やっぱり日本のラーメンは違います。一番好きなのは豚骨ラーメン。コテコテのものが好きです。 29. 苦手な食べ物はありますか？ 新倉 好き嫌いはないです。パクチーが苦手だったけど、あるとき、レモンとチーズがたっぷりのったパクチーサラダを食べたら、ものすごくおいしくて。それ以来、全然大丈夫になっちゃいました。 疲れていても愛猫が寄り添ってくれると癒される 30. 最近ハマっていることは何ですか？ 新倉 最近ハマっているのは、日本のお祭りです。おととし初めて青森ねぶた祭りに行ったとき、お囃子の音を聞いて、改めて日本のお祭り文化のすばらしさを感じたんです。去年はねぶた祭りに加えて、宮城の七夕祭りにも行きました。 東北では、山形の花笠まつりや盛岡さんさ踊り、福島のわらじまつりにも行ってみたいです。徳島の阿波踊りにも興味がありますし、旅先を選ぶときにも、お祭りがきっかけになることが増えました。夏の終わりには、各地で開催されるお祭りの情報をチェックするのも楽しみです。 31. 最近、一番笑ったことは何ですか？ 新倉 前編で12月3日に上演する「ベートーヴェンの小径」の舞台について、音楽と語りを交えた企画だとお話をしたら、休憩時間にMCの三井さんが「ベルリオーズみたいですね」とおっしゃって（笑）。「私、ベルリオーズだったんだ」みたいな感じで、爆笑しました。一番フレッシュな大爆笑です（笑）。 ベルリオーズは、私もなかなか演奏する機会が少ないので、ちょっと興味が出ました。 新倉瞳 × 南沢奈央「ベートーヴェンの小径」 32. 一番の癒やしは何ですか？ 新倉 やっぱり我が家の紬ですね。猫さまが尊いです。 この間も疲れて帰ったら、玄関に迎えに出てきてくれて。音でわかるみたいで、トントントントンって階段を下りてくるんです。鈴がついているので、リンリンリンリンと音がして。 ぼーっとしていても、私の前に来て、パサッと倒れて甘えてきてくれる。もう、一番の癒やしです。 紬ちゃんと戯れる新倉さん 寝つきがいいし午後まで寝ていることもできる！ 33. ストレス発散法を教えてください。 新倉 私、基本的に「おやすみ3秒」人間なんですよね。ストレスを感じているときって、体も疲れていることが多いですよね。いろんな人に気を使ったり、「何か考えなきゃいけない」と思ったりすると疲れると思うんですけど、寝ないともたないので（笑）、おいしいものを食べて、ぐっと寝る。 そうすると、次の日にまた頑張れる。ストレスに立ち向かえるんです。 34. オフの日はどのように過ごしていますか？ 新倉 放っておけば午後まで寝られる人なので、オフの日はよく寝ています（笑）。睡眠の質を上げるために、アロマスプレーを枕元にシュッとすることもあります。枕元でふわっと香るのは好きです。 35. 今、一番行ってみたい場所はどこですか？ 新倉 屋久島に行ってみたいです。海外にも、ブルガリアなど行きたいところはたくさんあるんですけど、まずは屋久島。国内では、音楽が伴って旅することがどうしても多いので、楽器なしで旅することへの憧れがあります。 36. お気に入りのアイテムや、いつも持ち歩いているものはありますか？ 新倉 あまり外でお化粧直しをしないんですけど、唇が乾燥すると嫌なので、リップクリームは常に持っています。 最近気に入っているのは、KATEの「明後日の水たまり」という名前がついたリップクリームです。保湿力が高くて、発色も自然にほんのり赤くなるところが気に入っています。 ベートーヴェンとコーヒーを飲みながら当時のチェリストの話を聞いてみたい 37. ご自身を動物にたとえるとしたら、何だと思いますか？ 新倉 これは、人に言われてから、すごくそうだなと思っているんですが、アザラシ！ 笑ったときの顔も似ているし、寝ているときの姿というか、ニコニコしてパタパタしている感じが、わりと自分にリンクするなと。 昔、南沢奈央ちゃんが私のコンサートに来てくださったときに、白寿ホールのバックステージで一緒に撮った写真があるんですけど、それがアザラシの写真と完全一致していて。水槽の中からアザラシがふっと笑っている写真と、私がふっと笑っている写真が同じ顔をしていて、「ああ、私はアザラシに似ているんだな」と（笑）。 アザラシに似ていると評判のショット。12月3日に開催される「ベートーヴェンの小径」でも共演する南沢奈央さんと 38. 家族や親しい友人からは、何と呼ばれていますか？ 新倉 「ひーちゃん」とか「ひいたん」とか。小学校の時代は「にいくらくら」と呼ばれていたこともあります。あとは「トミー」。アメリカに住んでいた頃、アメリカの方には「Hitomi」という名前がうまく発音されなくて、「トミー」になっちゃったみたいで。当時仲がよかったマイコちゃんも「マイケル」になって、「マイケル・アンド・トミー」だったんですよね（笑）。 39. 意外だと言われる一面は？ 新倉 ラーメンが好きとか、食べることが好きと言うと、意外と言われますね。クラシックの奏者って、どうしてもお上品な感じに見えるらしくて、そういった意味で「ラーメン」というワードが出てくると、意外みたいですね。 食べることが好きですし、食べるのもけっこう速くて。リハーサルの合間など時間に迫られたときに食べると、誰よりも遅く食べ始めて、誰よりも早く食べ終わっています。 40. 一緒にコーヒーを飲んでみたい歴史上の人物はいますか？ 新倉 いろいろな人と飲んでみたいんですけれども、今はやっぱりベートーヴェンです。 コーヒーは豆の数までこだわって淹れていたそうなので、きっとあまりきれいではなかったであろうベートーヴェンの書斎を訪ねて、火を入れるところから観察して、本当に豆を数えるのか見てみたいです（笑）。 それから、当時交流のあった素晴らしいチェリストの方々からインスピレーションを受けて曲を書いていたと思うので、その話も聞きたい。チェロ・ソナタを人生の長い期間にわたって書いているから、「どういう思いで書いたんですか？」ってインタビューしたいです。 関連記事：ベートーヴェンとコーヒー 民俗音楽に血が騒ぐ！ 41. 超能力を一つ持てるとしたら、どんな力がほしいですか？ 新倉 人の争いやいがみ合いって、たぶん誤解から生まれることが多いと思うんです。本当に悪い人っていなくて、生きていく過程でトゲトゲした気持ちが生まれてしまうんじゃないかなって。だから、そういう気持ちをピッと消せる超能力があったらいいなと思います。誰かが「今、トゲトゲしちゃってるんじゃないかな」と思ったら、ピッてやりたい（笑）。 でも、そういう思いから生まれる音楽もあるので、消せないものだとも思うんです。 あとは、単純にチェロがうまくなる超能力もほしいです（笑）。 42. 好きな映画を一つ挙げるとしたら？ 新倉 ジブリ作品は大好きです。一つ挙げるなら、『風の谷のナウシカ』かな。音楽もいいし、やっぱり自然や、人のいろいろな心が入っていて。あと、テトっていう肩に乗っているかわいいキャラクターも大好きです。ほかには『魔女の宅急便』も好きです。 43. これまでに影響を受けた本はありますか？ 新倉 『シーラという子』（トリイ・ヘイデン著）という本です。幼少期に虐待を受ける女の子の話で、私は幸いそういうことがなく育ってきたので、「ああ、こういう人もいるんだ」ということに、すごく衝撃を受けました。本を読むことで、自分の知らない人生を知ることができたり、まったく違う世界に入れたりするんだ、と感じられた一冊です。読書が好きになったきっかけの本でもあります。 44. 普段、どんな音楽を聴きますか？ 新倉 そのとき、たまたま出会った音楽を聴くことが多いんですが、突き詰めると、自分の血が騒ぐのは、やっぱり民俗音楽だと思います。クラシック音楽でも、民俗音楽に影響を受けているものに、ときめくことが多いかなと。 最近よく聴いていたのは、クリムゾンの「Moonchild」。ジャンルとしてはクラシックとはかなり離れていると思うんですけど、ちょっと民謡のような部分のあとに、即興的な部分が10分くらい続くような曲で、すごく気に入っています。 ベートーヴェンのイメージをアロマスプレーに 45. デビュー20周年を記念して、「天然回帰」とのコラボレーションによるアロマスプレーを発売されますね。なぜアロマスプレーだったのでしょうか？ 新倉 もともと香りに対して特別なものを感じていました。香りで思い出す記憶ってあるじゃないですか。 今回、マネージャーさんのつながりで、ソーシャルフレグランスブランドの天然回帰さんとコラボレーションすることになって。以前、香りを使わせていただいたときに、夜眠るときに枕元にシュッとしたり、朝出かけるときにフレッシュな香りを使ったりすると気分がいいと教えていただきました。自分にとって特別なときに、香りでリフレッシュできるのって素敵だなと思って。そこから、私の中では「朝と夜」がキーワードになりました。 46. 今回のアロマスプレーは、どのような香りをテーマにされたのでしょうか？ 新倉 今回はベートーヴェンの楽曲に合わせて、2つの香りを作りました。朝用は「田園」、夜用は「月光」をテーマにしています。 ベートーヴェンの楽曲を思い出してもらえるようなものを、12月の公演を聴きに来てくださった方に持ち帰っていただきたいと思ったんです。自分の癒やしになっているものと音楽を関連づけていただけたら嬉しいですね。 実際の香りは、天然回帰さんがベートーヴェンの背景などもすごく勉強してくださったうえで、交響曲第6番《田園》とピアノ・ソナタ第14番《月光》を聴いたときのイメージや気分に合うように何パターンか調香してくださって、その中から選びました。香りを嗅いでみて、「あ、これが月光だ」みたいな（笑）。そうやって、新倉瞳のベートーヴェンのイメージと香りがリンクしながら出来上がっていったんだと思います。 香りを選ぶ新倉さん 新倉さんプロデュースのアロマスプレーは、12月3日にサントリーホールブルーローズで開催される「ベートーヴェンの小径」で初めて販売されます！ 47. おすすめの使い方は？ 新倉 朝は、出かけるときにシュッとかけて、ふっと爽やかな気持ちになって、ドアを開ける。そんなタイミングで使っていただくのがおすすめです。夜は、眠る前に枕元にシュッとして、「ああ、今日もいい一日だったな」と、ちょっとしっとり受け止める感じで。あとは、リラックスしたいときには、いつでも自由に楽しんでいただけたらと思います。 ベートーヴェンの二面性を香りに。コラボレーションスプレーの香りが決まりました！ - 天然回帰 新倉瞳さんとつくる「人の持つ二面性のための香り」 聴いてくれる人と一緒に変化を恐れずに楽しんでいきたい 48. 今、一番やってみたいことは何ですか？ 新倉 そのときどきで「今、一番やってみたいこと」を叶えている感じなんです。毎年1回リサイタルをしているので、次のテーマについてもすでに資料を集め始めています。 やってみたいことは常に増えていくんですが、最近は日本の文化に改めて興味が湧いていて、着物に対する知識を増やしたいなと思っています。ひととおりきちんと着られるセットは持っているのですが、まだ知識が深くないので、着物のことをもっと知って、コレクションも増やしたいです。 49. 20周年を迎えた今だからこそ、これから挑戦してみたい音楽はありますか？ 新倉 ちゃんと取り組んでみたいのは、ジャズです。 これまでもジャズのような音楽を演奏したり、ジャズのすごいプレイヤーの方々に助けていただいて演奏したことはあるのですが、ちゃんと和音の勉強などもしないと、私の中では「ジャズをやっている」とは言えないかなと思っています。これからそういった勉強をしていきたいです。 50. これから新倉瞳さんの音楽を聴く方に、伝えたいことを一言お願いします。 新倉 私は興味の対象がどんどん移り変わっていくんですが、結局、それって点と点が線につながっていく、一つの過程だと思っています。そこに一緒に興味を持ってくださって、今の私を楽しみにしてくださっている方がいることは、とても光栄です。そういった変化を、私と一緒に楽しんでくだされば嬉しいです。 でも、その方々にもそれぞれの人生があるから、私の音楽を聴かないタイミングも出てくると思うんですよ。それでもいいと思っています。お互いに変化を恐れずに、一緒に楽しんでいけたら幸せだなと思います。 ポッドキャストの視聴はこちら 新倉瞳さんの出演情報 新倉瞳 × 南沢奈央 ベートーヴェンの小径 日時： 2026年12月3日（木）19：00開演 会場： サントリーホール ブルーローズ 曲目： 語りとともに綴るベートーヴェンの世界 ベートーヴェン／チェロ・ソナタ全曲 構成・脚本・演出： 新倉 瞳 出演： 新倉瞳（チェロ）、南沢奈央（語り）、横山瑠佳（ピアノ） スペシャルゲスト： 大萩 康司（ギター）、佐藤 芳明（アコーディオン）、大渕 愛子（フィドル）、渡辺 庸介（パーカッション） 詳しくはこちら

items.excerpt: 2026.09.30 9月29日、サントリーホール ブルーローズにて、第57回サントリー音楽賞を受賞した佐藤俊介（ヴァイオリン／指揮）と、第25回佐治敬三賞を受賞した「日野浩志郎新作音楽公演『Chronograffiti』」の贈賞式が行なわれた。 サントリー音楽賞は1969年の創設以来、毎年、その前年度においてわが国の洋楽文化の発展にもっとも顕著な功績のあった個人または団体を顕彰し、贈呈している。賞金は700万円。 贈賞理由には、「分断に歪み、混迷を深めるいまの時代において、芸術家にしかできないことをアクチュアルに示し続けている。楽しむだけではなく、思考を突き動かすためにこそ、音楽を。そうした佐藤のビジョンを照らし、クラシック音楽の未来の一翼を担うひとりとして、今後の歩みへの期待を示すもの」ということがあげられている。 ビーバー《ロザリオのソナタ》よりパッサカリアを演奏して喝采を浴びた後、贈賞式でスピーチを行なう佐藤俊介。 ヴァイオリニストであり、指揮者、室内楽奏者である佐藤俊介は、世界各地のピリオド楽器アンサンブルやシンフォニック・オーケストラを指揮し、ソリストとしても出演。2013
items.body: 2026.09.30 9月29日、サントリーホール ブルーローズにて、第57回サントリー音楽賞を受賞した佐藤俊介（ヴァイオリン／指揮）と、第25回佐治敬三賞を受賞した「日野浩志郎新作音楽公演『Chronograffiti』」の贈賞式が行なわれた。 サントリー音楽賞は1969年の創設以来、毎年、その前年度においてわが国の洋楽文化の発展にもっとも顕著な功績のあった個人または団体を顕彰し、贈呈している。賞金は700万円。 贈賞理由には、「分断に歪み、混迷を深めるいまの時代において、芸術家にしかできないことをアクチュアルに示し続けている。楽しむだけではなく、思考を突き動かすためにこそ、音楽を。そうした佐藤のビジョンを照らし、クラシック音楽の未来の一翼を担うひとりとして、今後の歩みへの期待を示すもの」ということがあげられている。 ビーバー《ロザリオのソナタ》よりパッサカリアを演奏して喝采を浴びた後、贈賞式でスピーチを行なう佐藤俊介。 ヴァイオリニストであり、指揮者、室内楽奏者である佐藤俊介は、世界各地のピリオド楽器アンサンブルやシンフォニック・オーケストラを指揮し、ソリストとしても出演。2013～23年オランダ・バッハ協会のコンサートマスターを、18年からは音楽監督を兼務し、録音したJ.S.バッハのカンタータや器楽作品の数々は、同協会のYouTubeで見ることができる。2011年からはコンチェルト・ケルンのソリスト、指揮者、コンサートマスターを務め、2013年からアムステルダム音楽院の教授としてヒストリカル・ヴァイオリンを教えている 贈賞式に登壇した佐藤は、「たいへん光栄であると同時に、身の引き締まる思い。ブルーローズは特別な思い入れがある場所で、26年前の2000年、当時16歳だった私は日本で初めてのコンサートを行なうことになり、その会場の1つがここだった。 4歳から19歳までずっとアメリカに住んでいて、当時は日本語の敬語がうまく使えず、アンコールの曲名を伝えるのに、お客様に向かってタメ口で話してしまった（笑）。そんなデビュー当時のとんちんかんな私でさえ、何かのスタート地点に立っているという意識はあったが、まさか26年後にサントリー音楽賞の受賞者として、再びこの同じステージに上がらせていただくとは思っていなかった。 この26年間、多くの方に出会い、ご指導いただき、私の未熟さや失敗を寛容に受け入れてくださり、私の音楽家としての価値を信じてくださった。困難や迷いに遭遇した時もあったが、これらの方々一人ひとりのおかげで、今の自分がここにいることを考えると、今回の賞を受賞したのは自分だけではないということを痛感する。 本日の贈賞式も、今の私にとって新たなスタート地点であるような気がする。これからどんな経験をし、どんな出会いが待っているか、楽しみでならない。これまで私を導いてくださった先生方、共演してくださった音楽家の皆様、演奏の場を作り支えてくださった皆様、そして何より演奏会場で音楽を共にしてくださった聴衆の皆様に、心より感謝申し上げる」と述べた。 最新アルバム『BEE1H0VEN~ベートーヴェン：ヴァイオリン・ソナタ全集』が新レコード・アカデミー賞第1回大賞に輝き、2027年4月からは、東京交響楽団のクリエイティブ・パートナーを3年間務めることになった佐藤。今年5月からは、自身が創設したロマン派以降の音楽を主な対象とする古楽オーケストラ「Past Forward Ensemble」の演奏活動もスタートした。 「強い信念で周囲の音楽家を巻き込みながら、卓越した行動力で新しい音楽の潮流を作っていく。日本の次世代を担う音楽家たちに大きな影響を与え、これからますます存在感を発揮していく」（サントリー音楽財団代表理事 堤剛氏）と讃えられる佐藤が、今後ヴァイオリニストとして、指揮者として、ますます多く日本の聴衆の前に姿を現してくれることを願ってやまない。

items.album: 【東京】TOKAS Project Vol.9「在ることの再演」

items.excerpt: トーキョーアーツアンドスペース本郷にて、国際的な交流を促進し、多文化的な視点で多様なテーマについて思考するプログラム「TOKAS Project」が開催されます。 9回目となる今回は、トーキョーアーツアンドスペース（TOKAS）とソウルとの交流20周年を記念して、過去にレジデンス・プログラムに参加した日韓のアーティストを中心に、知覚や存在の輪郭の揺らぎへの問いと応答をテーマに、5名のアーティストによる展覧会が行なわれます。 本展では、アーティストたちがそれぞれ異なる視点から観察した生の姿を、展示空間に再び立ち上げる行為（＝再演）をとおして、その瞬間の彼らの感覚や視点から新たな解釈を促し、現代における生の本質を見つめ直すことを試みます。 ＜参加アーティスト＞ ウン・ジェピル、キム・ドヒ、ク・ドンヒ、パク・ミンハ、三野新 関連イベント ■アーティスト・トーク ＊日英逐次通訳あり 日時｜2026/10/03（土）15:00〜17:00 会場｜トーキョーアーツアンドスペース本郷 出演｜ウン・ジェピル、キム・ドヒ、ク・ドンヒ、パク・ミンハ 参加費｜無料 ＊詳細はこちらをご覧ください。 ■パフォー

items.excerpt: 今年8月から渋谷のユーロスペースで始まり、現在は全国各地にその上映場所を移している「パフォーマンス・アート：身体と空間をめぐる映画祭」。合計4プログラム5作品のドキュメンタリーからなる特集上映ですが、東京在住の筆者はこの夏、予定の隙間を見つけては劇場に足を運び、なんとか全作コンプリート（それを可能にしてくれた長期間のプログラム編成に感謝）。そのいずれもが観に来てよかったとしみじみ思える作品たちでした。 夏の日差しがもはや懐かしい［筆者撮影］ 折角なら全作観ようと思えるこの「映画祭」のサイズ感も心地良く、作品同士の連関にはっとするだけでなく、そこで観たものが別の場所や次の季節でまた別のものに出会わせてくれる、というおまけのような循環も。例えばプログラムDの『ナム・ジュン・パイク 月は最古のTV』（アマンダ・キム監督、2023）を観た後にワタリウム美術館の「没後20年 ナムジュン・パイク｜じゅげむ展」（11月23日まで）を観ると、彼の作品のなかの音楽やパフォーマンスの部分に自然とフォーカスするようになったりと、また体験が変わります。あるいはピナ・バウシュとヴッパタール舞踊団の欧州ツアーを追
