items.album: 杉江あこ｜方丈記に学ぶ　–生きるを編み直す小さな建築–
items.tags: art sound art contemporary music improvisation
items.excerpt: 会期：2026/08/28～2027/01/11 会場：21_21 DESIGN SIGHT ギャラリー1＆2［東京都］ 公式サイト：https://www.2121designsight.jp/program/hojoki/ 人はそんなに小さな建築が好きなのか。確かに超高層ビルやマンションの林立、都心の再開発などが止まない現代社会だからこそ、その反動から自らの身の丈に合った建築を求めたくなるという心理はわからないでもない。近代建築の父であるル・コルビュジエも、地中海を望む南仏カップ・マルタンに休憩小屋を建て、晩年を過ごしたことで知られている。結局、大きな建築は国家繁栄や経済性などのためであり、対して小さな建築は個人のささやかな望みということなのだろう。 会場風景 21_21 DESIGN SIGHTギャラリー2 撮影：木奥恵三 本展は、鴨長明の名随筆『方丈記』に記された「方丈の庵」を起点に、現代における生き方への問いをテーマとした企画展である。方丈の庵とは一丈四方の住まいのことで、現代の面積に置き換えると約9㎡、四畳半程度の空間である。長明は晩年に都から離れ、山に方丈の庵を建てて隠遁
items.body: 会期：2026/08/28～2027/01/11 会場：21_21 DESIGN SIGHT ギャラリー1＆2［東京都］ 公式サイト：https://www.2121designsight.jp/program/hojoki/ 人はそんなに小さな建築が好きなのか。確かに超高層ビルやマンションの林立、都心の再開発などが止まない現代社会だからこそ、その反動から自らの身の丈に合った建築を求めたくなるという心理はわからないでもない。近代建築の父であるル・コルビュジエも、地中海を望む南仏カップ・マルタンに休憩小屋を建て、晩年を過ごしたことで知られている。結局、大きな建築は国家繁栄や経済性などのためであり、対して小さな建築は個人のささやかな望みということなのだろう。 会場風景 21_21 DESIGN SIGHTギャラリー2 撮影：木奥恵三 本展は、鴨長明の名随筆『方丈記』に記された「方丈の庵」を起点に、現代における生き方への問いをテーマとした企画展である。方丈の庵とは一丈四方の住まいのことで、現代の面積に置き換えると約9㎡、四畳半程度の空間である。長明は晩年に都から離れ、山に方丈の庵を建てて隠遁生活を送ったのだが、そこには厭世的な心情が大きく働いていた。隠遁生活は、心は自由でも、孤独と不便が付きものである。つまり暮らしの不自由さをある程度受け入れてでも、世俗から離れたい気持ちが強かったということだ。会場内には長明の方丈の庵の再現を試みた《非実在空間としての方丈の庵》をはじめ、参加作家によるさまざまな解釈の下での方丈の庵が建ち並んでおり、なかなか見応えがあった。中には靴を脱いで内部へ入れる作品もあり、体験型の楽しい内容となっていた。 会場風景 21_21 DESIGN SIGHTギャラリー1 《非実在空間としての方丈の庵》 撮影：木奥恵三 会場風景 21_21 DESIGN SIGHTギャラリー2 左：山口晃《螺庵》 右：2m26《living with》 撮影：木奥恵三 しかし、私自身、小さな建築に憧れるかどうかというと、今のところそうした気持ちはない。というのも、どうしても不便さが目に付いてしまうからだ。広すぎず、狭すぎず、ほどほどの面積で、雨風をしのぐだけでなく温度や湿度をちょうどよく保てて、清潔に快適に暮らしたいというのが希望である。都市から離れた山里で隠遁生活を送る勇気などまったくないのだ。たぶん多くの現代人が同じような考えなのでは……とここまで思案して、ふと浮かんだのはいわゆるミニマリストである。ミニマリストとは必要最低限の物だけで豊かな暮らしを送る人のことをいうが、つまり彼らこそ現代における『方丈記』の精神を体現しているのではないか。方丈の庵という住まいの狭小さばかりに目が向いていたが、自分にとって本当に必要な要素だけに削ぎ落とすという行為は、住まいの狭小さも物の少なさも同じなのでは……という考えに至り、本展のテーマがようやく腑に落ちたのである。 会場風景 21_21 DESIGN SIGHTサンクンコート 正田智樹＋竹中工務店＋veig《蓑庵 マウン庭》 撮影：木奥恵三 鑑賞日：2026/08/29（土）

items.body: Sometimes, the band is the standout performance. What’s up, everyone! Welcome back to yet another installment of the J-Music Exchange/Rate! Your monthly source of Japanese music album reviews brought to you by yours truly and my good friend and fellow Japanese music fan Al from Omunibasu. If you’ve been rocking with us for a while now, then you already know the deal, but if this is your first time here and you’re not entirely sure what the Exchange/Rate is all about, please give the following primer a quick readーThe Exchange/Rate is a tandem album review series conducted every month by yours truly alongside my good friend and fellow Japanese music fan Al (from Omunibasu). Each month we decide on a specific theme with which our reviews would revolve around. We then pick out albums from our respective libraries which we think best coincides with that theme. We will then give the album we chose to the other person and vice versa (exchange), after which we then listen to and subsequently review the album we were given (rate). This project has not only allowed us to explore music beyond our libraries, but it provides an opportunity for us to see our favorite albums from a different point of view. It is our hope that this series is able to do the same for you and that you either find a new artist to try out and/or we offer you a fresh take on one of *your* favorite albums Al and I take turns deciding on a theme for our reviews every month, and for September we’re handing the reins back over to him. And I gotta say, I thought he came up with a pretty interesting one this time around, as we’ll be talking about albums that we feel exemplify an excellent group effort. Now, what exactly do we mean by that? Well, I don’t necessarily think it’s as simple as picking out an album where everyone involved is just really good at what they do. Rather, we’re looking at releases where you can genuinely feel the importance of everyone’s contributions to the finished work. Where the drums, bass, guitars, vocals, keys, production, or whatever else might be involved all feel integral to what makes the album what it is, and where taking any one of those elements away would leave you with something noticeably different. Of course, how that group effort manifests can vary quite a bit from one album to another, which is also what makes this such a fun theme to explore. For my pick, I went ahead and gave Al Fooocus by Aooo, a release that I think demonstrates the concept particularly well with how each of its members gets an opportunity to bring their own musical identity into the fold while still working together as one cohesive unit. You can check out what Al thought of that over at the Omunibasu Substack! Al, meanwhile, decided to send me Mani Mani by CRCK/LCKS, an album made by a group of musicians who, as we’re about to find out, have quite the collective pedigree between them. And perhaps more importantly for today’s discussion, they might just have a thing or two to teach us about what happens when you put that much individual talent in the same room. Let’s get into it! ーー CRCK/LCKS (クラックラックス) is a five-piece Japanese band formed in 2015, consisting of vocalist/keyboardist Oda Tomomi, saxophonist and multi-instrumentalist Konishi Ryo, guitarist Inoue Mei, bassist Ochi Shunsuke, and drummer Ishikawa Shun. Comprised of musicians with backgrounds predominantly rooted in jazz, the group brings together their respective expertise to create a style that freely moves between jazz, pop, R&B, and other contemporary influences, with an emphasis on intricate ensemble work and experimentation. ＜Ｍａｎｉ Ｍａｎｉ (まにまに)＞(＊Spotify link to the full album) CDJapan Affiliate Link(s):Mani Mani / CRCK/LCKS ＜T ｒａｃｋｌｉｓｔ＞ ０１・あらわらわ/arawarawa０２・レンタル神様/rental kamisama０３・真空パック/shinkuu pack０４・Psycho Sky０５・T.I.C.０６・沖に出たら/oki ni detara０７・枝と嵐/eda to arashi０８・バラライカ/balalaika０９・つまらない毎日/tsumaranai mainichi１０・Tiny Mirror１１・7月27日１２・You say goodbye１３・manimani Ａｌ：Ever since I first discovered CRCK/LCKS a few years ago, I’ve always found them to be a pretty fascinating band. It’s possible that I didn’t fully grasp what they were all about at first, but their two Temporary albums were ones I’d always come back to randomly, just because of how avant-garde the songs were and their overall irregular take on pop music. One moment you could be hearing a groovy cacophony of guitar, bass, and even the saxophone going wild, and another moment can have you getting lost in an ethereal soundscape. They may be a group that I have an on-and-off listening relationship with, but their ability to come up with this nutty stuff never fails to catch my attention. And I do feel like that’s why I came to enjoy their most recent album, Manimani, a lot. I’ll admit that the thought process for this month’s theme was based on how much more perceptive I’ve become when I listen to music, with me often trying to mentally separate the instrumental and/or vocal performances in a song, in order to really appreciate everyone’s efforts individually (and thus, understanding how well it all gels together). And with a band like CRCK/LCKS, who seem to display so many different elements in their music, it’s hard not to take interest in the mesmerizing or pleasant oddities they’ve been known for. Especially considering how varied the song selection is on Manimani, as the band showcases a more rambunctious side in the opener’s ending sequence (“arawarawa”), the unbelievably calming jazzy nature of “edatoarashi”, or how the bouncy and weirdly hyper traits in song like “bararaika” made it a standout song during my initial go-through with the album… it’s a record that feels very familiar if you’re an existing fan of the band, yet their efforts still feel super fresh with how surprisingly varied it is, style-wise. Another reason why I might’ve picked this one was because it’s described to be a cool celebration of CRCK/LCKS’ existence as a group, and every single member is featured on its songwriting credits. And after finding that out, it made it clear how much of a collective effort this album was, with everyone being able to chip in with their own ideas. And honestly, it resulted in an even more of an enjoyable experience. ーー Now, I actually thought about doing this one a little bit differently than I normally do for Exchange/Rate album reviews. If you’re a longtime follower of this series and are thus quite familiar with how I structure my end of the reviews, you’ll know that I typically pick out, at minimum, four songs from the album to talk about. These aren’t necessarily always my four favorite tracks either. More often than not, I use them to formulate a framework for how I want to approach the record as a whole; what I find good or intriguing about it, what I think the artist is trying to accomplish, and ultimately what kind of music listening experience I believe the album has to offer. In spending some time with CRCK/LCKS’ Mani Mani, however, I very quickly realized that I can’t really go about doing that here. Or, perhaps more accurately, I don’t think I should. Part of my reasoning for that is ultimately going to be at the heart of my overall thoughts on the album, but I think a good place to start this discussion is by first looking at the individual parts that make up CRCK/LCKS. Because if we’re going to talk about Mani Mani, I think we first have to talk about the people who made it. The band is led by multi-instrumentalist and Berklee College of Music graduate Konishi Ryo, known primarily within Japanese jazz circles for his work on the saxophone. Joining him on keys and vocals is classically trained Oda Tomomi, with jazz guitarist Inoue Mei on guitar, Ochi Shunsuke on bass, and Tokyo University of the Arts graduate and credentialed percussionist Ishikawa Shun behind the drums. For your everyday overseas Japanese music fan, I don’t necessarily expect all of those names to immediately jump off the page. For those more entrenched in the Japanese jazz scene in particular, however, seeing these five musicians come together in service of one collaborative project might read as something closer to a supergroup. Across the five members are numerous accolades and accomplishments within the Japanese music world, with each having established themselves through their own work and collaborations with renowned musicians both within and outside of Japan. All of which is to say that nobody in CRCK/LCKS necessarily needs the band to prove what they’re capable of individually. Everyone involved is already exceptionally accomplished at what they do. Which, naturally, begs a much more interesting question. What happens when you put all five of them together? That’s ultimately where my interest in Mani Mani lies. With this much individual talent packed into one group, it would be incredibly easy to approach the album by pulling everything apart and pointing toward what each member contributes. But I also think doing so would miss what makes CRCK/LCKS so fascinating in the first place. The question I’m more interested in asking isn’t what each of these five musicians can do individually. It’s whether what they create together amounts to something greater than the sum of its parts. Given how skilled everyone in CRCK/LCKS is with their respective instruments, I think it would be perfectly natural to assume that there’d eventually be some sense of one member overpowering another. Put five musicians of this caliber together and surely someone is gonna end up taking over the room, right? Except, as you’ll hear even from the opening stretch with Arawarawa, and subsequently thereafter with songs like Rental kamisama and Shinkuu pack, that never really happens. Instead, there’s this remarkable cohesion to the way CRCK/LCKS perform together where nobody sounds as though they need to tone down their own musicality simply to accommodate the other virtuosos playing alongside them. Everyone is still very clearly doing what they do best, only somehow without any of it coming at the expense of somebody else. You can still hear and appreciate Ishikawa Shun’s impeccable drum work without it ever distracting from Oda Tomomi’s lovely singing. Likewise, Konishi Ryo can bring his saxophone into the arrangement without completely stealing the spotlight away from Inoue Mei and Ochi Shunsuke on guitar and bass respectively. Nobody necessarily has to retreat into the background for somebody else to shine. And I think that’s an important distinction to make when talking about Mani Mani. The impressive thing isn’t simply that five extremely talented musicians are able to play well together. You’d probably expect that much given everyone’s credentials. It’s that they can seemingly play to the full extent of their abilities at the same time and still sound like a band rather than five individually impressive performances happening on top of one another. Part of me wants to simply chalk that up to the members being incredibly compatible with one another. At the very least, you don’t get the impression listening to Mani Mani that anyone feels the need to constantly prove themselves or overshadow everybody else in the room. But I do want to pose another possibility as to why CRCK/LCKS work so well together, and that’s the fact that all five of them come from jazz backgrounds. Obviously, there’s already going to be some preexisting overlap there. Having five musicians who operate within the same general musical space naturally gives them a shared foundation to work from. What I’m more interested in, however, is jazz itself and how the characteristics of the genre might have helped provide CRCK/LCKS with that unifying thread. Jazz is, by nature, a remarkably loose and unrestricted style of music. One of its most defining characteristics is improvisation, which inherently asks musicians to be responsive not only to what they’re playing, but also to what’s happening around them at any given moment. A performance can shift depending on what somebody else decides to do, leaving everyone involved to react and find their place within it. There’s a certain volatility to jazz in that regard, but I also think that’s precisely what makes it so conducive to having this many different elements operating at once. And perhaps that’s part of why CRCK/LCKS never feel overcrowded despite how much musicianship is constantly on display throughout Mani Mani. These aren’t simply five talented musicians who happen to be playing alongside one another. They’re five musicians coming from a musical tradition that, at its core, places a tremendous amount of value on listening and responding to the people playing alongside you. So when Ishikawa changes something on the drums, or Konishi comes through with the saxophone, or Inoue and Ochi start working something between the guitar and bass, everyone else has the musical vocabulary to respond accordingly. Their individual contributions don’t have to be planned around as obstacles; they become opportunities for everybody else to build upon. In that sense, jazz isn’t merely one of the styles that informs CRCK/LCKS’ music. It might very well be the reason all of these moving parts fit together as naturally as they do. In that regard, I do view Mani Mani as something closer to one big jazz jam session between the members of CRCK/LCKS more than anything else, and this is again largely why I decided not to approach this Exchange/Rate the way I normally would. Rather than viewing the album as a collection of individual songs and picking apart specific moments contained within them, I think Mani Mani works better as a showcase of what these five musicians are capable of creating together. It’s less about waiting for any one member to step forward and give you that big standout performance, and more about listening to how everyone continuously interacts with and plays off one another as the album moves along. Though there’s another side to that too, which is that there honestly aren’t that many singular moments throughout Mani Mani that I find myself wanting to isolate in the first place. And I don’t necessarily mean that as a criticism. If anything, part of what made it so difficult for me to pick out four songs to talk about is that the individual tracks themselves don’t really stand out that much over everything else on the album. There are certainly songs I enjoy more than others, with You say goodbye being the one clear exception for me as a song that I absolutely adore and would probably call my favorite track off Mani Mani simply for how beautiful it is. But beyond that, I rarely find myself listening to the album and thinking about one song being the song. Instead, CRCK/LCKS just… play. They create, they experiment, they respond to one another, and then they move on to the next idea. There’s a free-flowing quality to Mani Mani that makes the boundaries between those individual tracks feel considerably less important than the experience of hearing the band perform across the album as a whole. In that sense, listening to Mani Mani reminds me a lot of sitting down at a jazz bar and taking in a live set. You might walk away remembering a particular melody or moment that caught your ear, but that’s not necessarily why you enjoyed yourself. Sometimes the pleasure comes simply from sitting there and watching a group of incredibly capable musicians do their thing, seeing where the music takes them and appreciating how naturally they’re able to find one another along the way. That’s more or less how I find myself listening to Mani Mani. And perhaps that’s the best explanation I can give as to why, for once, I don’t really want to pull the album apart into four songs and tell you what makes each one work. The thing I find most interesting about Mani Mani isn’t any singular moment contained within it. It’s CRCK/LCKS themselves. ＜Ｗｈａｔ Ｉ ｔｈｉｎｋ ｏｆ Ｍａｎｉ Ｍａｎｉ ＞ So, after all of that, I suppose we’re left with the question that I posed at the very beginning: is CRCK/LCKS as a collective greater than the sum of its parts? Well… yes and no. If we’re looking at Mani Mani purely as a showcase of what happens when you put five incredibly accomplished musicians together and let them create, then I do think the answer is a resounding yes. There’s a level of musical understanding between everyone involved that allows each member to perform at an incredibly high level without ever making the album feel like a competition for your attention. Nobody gets lost, but nobody has to overpower everybody else either. Instead, their respective talents continually feed into one another, and I think the jazz background shared between them goes a long way toward explaining why that interaction feels as natural as it does. At the same time, I do think there’s another side to that equation when we start looking at Mani Mani specifically as an album. Going back to my comparison of listening to the record as being akin to sitting through a live set at a jazz bar, there are naturally opportunities for the mind to meander between songs. And I did find myself doing that here. There were a couple of times listening through Mani Mani where I noticed my attention starting to drift, only for the band to pick things back up instrumentally and pull me right back in again. Curiously enough, I almost wonder if that’s somewhat intentional. There are a lot of starts and stops throughout Mani Mani, along with these little interstitial tracks scattered between the more fully realized songs, to the point where it can sometimes feel like you’re supposed to lose track of exactly where you are in the album. One song ends, another idea comes in, the band pauses, something else begins, and eventually you look down and realize you’re three tracks further along than you thought you were. In most cases, I would probably consider that a knock against an album. After all, you’d generally want the songs themselves to leave enough of an impression that you can distinguish one from another. And as I mentioned earlier, outside of something like You say goodbye, there aren’t really many tracks on Mani Mani that I personally came away viewing as these huge individual landmarks. But I’m also not entirely convinced that Mani Mani wants to be experienced that way. The more time I spent with it, the less I found myself approaching the album as thirteen separate tracks and the more I started treating it as one continuous performance. Sometimes you’re completely locked in on what CRCK/LCKS are doing. Other times you let the music play while your mind wanders elsewhere. Then Ishikawa comes crashing back in on the drums, Konishi’s saxophone cuts through, Oda catches your ear with a vocal line, or Inoue and Ochi find another groove together and suddenly you’re paying attention again. And honestly, there’s something kind of pleasant about that. It makes Mani Mani less of an album where I’m constantly waiting for the next song I like to come on, and more of one where I simply enjoy spending time in the presence of the musicians playing it. The individual tracks become less important than the ebb and flow of the performance itself, which I think explains why trying to pick four of them apart for this review never quite felt right to me. So, is the whole greater than the sum of its parts? From a purely musical standpoint, absolutely. CRCK/LCKS are five tremendously accomplished musicians individually, but what makes Mani Mani interesting isn’t simply getting to hear all five of them demonstrate what they’re capable of. It’s hearing what each of them becomes in response to the other four. As an album, though, I think that same collective quality comes with a tradeoff. Mani Mani can be so free-flowing that its songs occasionally lose some of their individual identity along the way. But perhaps that’s also the point. Sometimes you don’t go to a jazz bar because you’re waiting to hear one particular song. Sometimes you go because the band is playing. ＜Ｍｙ Ｒａｔｉｎｇ＞４ ｏｕｔ ｏｆ ５ ＆ ８ ｏｕｔ ｏｆ １０ Mani Mani is, in a lot of ways, both memorable and unremarkable And I realize those two things sound like they shouldn’t be able to coexist, but I think that’s ultimately the best way I can summarize my experience with the album. Outside of something like You say goodbye, I don’t necessarily see myself walking away from Mani Mani remembering a bunch of individual songs or singular moments that completely blew me away. What I will remember, however, is the experience of listening to CRCK/LCKS play together. Because even during the moments where my attention started to drift, I don’t think there was ever a point where I questioned the quality of the musicianship on display. If anything, hearing five musicians this accomplished play alongside one another with seemingly very little interest in individually taking over the spotlight made me appreciate the collective that much more. Perhaps that’s also what makes Mani Mani such a fitting album for this month’s theme. When everyone involved is already this talented individually, it’d be easy for the appeal to simply become the novelty of hearing all of them on the same record. Instead, the most impressive thing about CRCK/LCKS is how quickly you stop thinking about any one member at all. ーー What are your guys’ thoughts on CRCK/LCKS’ Mani Mani? Let us know down in the comments! Likewise, what albums come to mind for you when you think of an excellent group effort? Whether it’s a band where every member feels integral to the music or simply a group of musicians who bring out the best in one another, we’d love to hear your picks! Lastly, before I let you guys go, don’t forget to check out Al’s review of Fooocus by Aooo over at the Omunibasu Substack if you haven’t yet! Happy Listening!

items.album: John Coltrane 100: John Coltrane in Detroit, June 1966
items.excerpt: John Coltrane Memorial in Hamlet, N.C. Photographer unknown. By Stuart Broomer If I can write anything meaningful about the music of John Coltrane, it may be about the context in which I came to experience his work live, in 1966, after listening intently to his work for four years on record and writing reviews of some of it as well. One’s juvenilia is embarrassing almost by definition, but that’s my particular gateway here to a world in which Coltrane was playing live a few feet in front of me.
items.body: John Coltrane Memorial in Hamlet, N.C. Photographer unknown. By Stuart Broomer If I can write anything meaningful about the music of John Coltrane, it may be about the context in which I came to experience his work live, in 1966, after listening intently to his work for four years on record and writing reviews of some of it as well. One’s juvenilia is embarrassing almost by definition, but that’s my particular gateway here to a world in which Coltrane was playing live a few feet in front of me. 13 months later he passed away. I write this hopefully to communicate something of the challenging world in which Coltrane made his music, that ever more intense, more radically free music, as testimony to his courage and vision as a great artist, as large a person as one might be in that world. The John Coltrane Reference (Routledge, 2008) by Chris DeVito, Yasuhiro Fujioka, Wolf Schmaler and David Wild, edited by Lewis Porter (Routledge, 2008) is a monumental work of scholarship. After the introductions, there’s a Chronology of Coltrane’s life and career that runs to 357 large pages of fine print, followed by a Discography of 404 similarly sized pages in identical print, followed by 49 more pages of appendices, index, etc. Very near the Chronology’s conclusion, there’s an entry for the John Coltrane Quintet’s appearance at Detroit’s Drome Lounge from June 17-26, 1966. The personnel, then consistent, is identified as Coltrane, tenor and soprano saxophones; Pharoah Sanders, tenor saxophone; Alice Coltrane, piano; Jimmy Garrison, bass; Rasheid Ali, drums, Friday to Sunday, matinees on Sunday. Reviewed in Coda (“John Coltrane Quintet – Drome Bar—Detroit” by Stu Broomer, Aug-Sept., 1966, pp.32 - 33). The review is represented by just a few of its sentences, but I’ll restrict myself to the Reference editor’s choices and their punctuation as well. “This is probably the most moving working band in America (…) Tenor saxophonist Farrell “Pharoah” Sanders is now the most important soloist in the group. (…) When (Coltrane) first heard Albert Ayler in 1962, Coltrane told him he had heard himself playing like that in a dream once. (…). This band has recorded five times but nothing has been released. Perhaps Bob Thiele is hoping Coltrane will return to his old-time sanity. I for one hope he will not”. (Reprinted by permission of the author. All Rights Reserved). What I’m trying to get at here about John Coltrane is an essential drive for expression and liberation, for liberation from every constraint to discover what’s real or what’s at least possible. If my memories from 60 years ago mean anything, they’re about the value of revolt and the horror of the norm, the judgmental restriction of cultural norms, in some places becoming more restrictive than anything I might have felt 60 years ago (a festival of liberalism by comparison). As a result, I want the music more intense, more personal, more unpredictable and I’ll stand up for it anywhere. But it is not without ambiguities. As a teenager in the 1960s, I became obsessed with free jazz. It was a promise of freedom from restraint as well as constraint, an explosion of mixed emotions from great sorrow to ecstasy, in effect, perhaps, a promise too far. My absorption in jazz had begun in childhood with the 1957 TV special The Sound of Jazz and followed with the eventual LP. More television: I saw the Robert Herridge Presents episode with Miles Davis and John Coltrane in 1960 and loved it. My brief initial puzzlement and rapid-onset rapture with free jazz started when I picked up the September 1961 Metronome at the corner variety store. It included an epic essay on the jazz avantgarde by the then LeRoi Jones (I still have the essay somewhere — stapled together — the issue is gone). The writing was abstract, mannered and strange but also enchanting (I had already read a paperback of Kerouac’s Tristessa ), its subject an arcane revolution. By the time I had purchased Ornette! and Free Jazz a few months later, Metronome had ceased to exist. I had only Down Beat , a magazine at the time sufficiently reactionary to condemn John Coltrane and Eric Dolphy as anti-jazz in a cover story. A few years later, circa 1965, I started writing for Coda, then Canada’s only jazz magazine. If there’s a shock in that original account (in bowdlerized form), it’s likely the ranking of Sanders’ performance over Coltrane’s. Without digging for the original, I recall moments from that night when I was listening to the dense, tumultuous music and focussing on the brilliant screaming mayhem of the two saxophones, only to open my eyes and discover that John Coltrane was intently hitting a cowbell with a drumstick and Pharoah Sanders was the only person playing a saxophone. This isn’t a criticism of Coltrane. He was one of the greatest musicians who ever played jazz, but we all know now that he was seriously ill and still carrying a heavy musical load. Other memories: I already had certain knowledge that Jimmy Garrison’s solos, as memorably powerful as they were, depended heavily on the bass’s tuning in fourths, and the complex, droning solos dependent to a significant degree on the use of open strings (I was a bass player at the time). At one point in the evening, Coltrane spoke quietly to him (I was sitting at a piano-shaped stage, my ear within four feet of their mouths) specifying the key for one of his extended introductions. Garrison then looked upset, arguing for another key. I wasn’t surprised by the issue. I was surprised that it was happening about four years into Garrison’s tenure in the band. Another and crucial surprise goes to the heart of the history of free jazz. My party (myself and three others, young musicians from Toronto, three Caucasian, one Japanese) were, in effect, insiders (however “out” we might feel in the Drome). We arrived early, conveying Rashied to the venue since we were staying in the same place, the Detroit Artists Workshop. Arriving early, we found a strange mix of conviviality and formality. Standing just inside the foyer, Jimmy Garrison was shaking hands with patrons as they entered. Even to a bass player, Garrison’s right hand (the plucking one) came as a shock: it felt like a bundle of sticks. As popular, as great , as John Coltrane was, there was a fundamental divide in the audience about the shape his music was assuming, that was apparent from the time the music began (a shock perhaps influenced by the very music that Impulse was choosing to release). In essence there were two audiences. In the Drome it happened largely along racial lines, generally slightly older blacks on the one hand, and the white audience, many significantly younger, significantly suspended between hip and hippie. One audience looked disgruntled, offering spare, obligatory applause; the other clapped wildly with exclamatory shouts. Late in the evening, Coltrane broke into the opening phrase of his anthem, “My Favorite Things”, its bright coiling phrases instantly recognizable from the first note. It was amazing. With my back to the rest of the audience, I could actually feel the room lift, so strong was the shift in mood, comparable, for a brief instant, to the sun breaching a cloud cover. Within a couple of minutes, the sonic tumult had taken over again, and one could feel, even more intensely, the mood of the room dropping, to frustration and disappointment, perhaps, and most intensely, I felt, the abandonment, the sense of betrayal. In total, (expanding on Coltrane's grimly disappointed Black audience) the trip seemed at times to be about race but things would get much darker, or should I say lighter (toxic metaphors lurk in our tongue) -- I had gone there with three other young Toronto musicians with whom I played. I had an association with John Sinclair (then in jail on drug charges -- not sure how current John's name is, but his greatest moment of celebrity came when imprisoned during Woodstock: Abby Hoffman interrupted the beginning of the Who's performance with a comment to the effect that Woodstock didn't mean shit while John Sinclair was in jail; then Pete Townsend hit Hoffman with his guitar for trying to take over the Who's stage). In John’s absence, his partner Leni Sinclair was running the Workshop. I knew The Detroit Artists Workshop through shared performances between Detroit and Toronto, performances arranged by John Sinclair and the Toronto poet Victor Coleman of the Bohemian Embassy, a Toronto coffee house and performance space. Shared performances had included members of Detroit trumpeter Charles Moore’s MC5 with featured musicians that had included Marion Brown and Andrew Hill (through which I got to play bass with Andrew for a weekend among other playing associations). I had also published a poem and a record review in John's mimeo'd music journal Changes , which I think may have only gone to two (or maybe three) issues. The Workshop was the epicentre of radical culture in Detroit whether the issue was music, race, drugs, economics or language. Later it was the spawning ground of the MC5, of "Up Against the Wall Motherfucker" fame, who John Sinclair managed. He later was a founder of the White Panther Party, a Black Panther support group. When I met the members of [Ahmed] a few years ago in Guelph, talk turned to Detroit. Some members were thinking about visiting Detroit, and Pat Thomas and I found ourselves reminiscing about John, whose poetry Pat had accompanied during an Amsterdam performance. John's contract, Pat recalled, required a private pot smoking loft. A few days before our group arrived in Detroit, a young inter-racial couple from the Workshop had been violently attacked on the street by the sons of a former Mississippi sheriff whose property adjoined the Workshop at the rear. While we were staying there, the sheriff had invited the residents of the Workshop to a get together/ barbecue to make peace. None of the Workshop residents (naturally) wanted to go and Leni Sinclair asked our Toronto group (whom they were temporarily housing, four males sufficiently groomed to get across the border without close scrutiny) to go as their representatives. We accepted with a certain reluctance, though things (barbecue, blanched pleasantries) went civilly enough. An hour later, on the way out of Detroit, we stopped at an ice cream outlet before we hit the border. The sons and their wives and children were there as well. On neutral ground, none of us acknowledged the existence of the other. Charles Tyler, Stuart Broomer + Perry Robinson, 1966 ©2014 Bill Copeland AN AFTERWORD: 60 years on, I frequently listen to John Coltrane recordings, probably more than to any other historical jazz artist. I have the complete runs of the Prestige and Atlantic recordings and most of the Impulses on CD and the recordings with Monk and Miles Davis and isolated one-offs like Blue Train on Blue Note. My usual listening choices run the gamut from the Prestige and Atlantic recordings (especially Olé , the last of them, with Freddie Hubbard, Eric Dolphy and Art Davis added to the working quartet of McCoy Tyner, Reggie Workman and Elvin Jones). My listening range ends with one of my favorites, Meditations , with the “classic” quartet augmented by Rashied Ali and Pharoah Sanders. I hardly ever, if at all, listen to much that came later. Whether that’s because the actual experience of the last quintet live was enough – sufficiently intense -- to satisfy my need for that music, or that the music is so unstable or destabilizing that I don’t feel a need to hear it in its “frozen” form. The sole exception made among recordings of the last stage is Interstellar Space , the recording of four duets with Rashied Ali, recorded in February 1967, though it too is rarely played, singled out perhaps for the relative coherence of the music and the focus of its intensity. © Stuart Broomer, 2026 Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body:
Mrs. GREEN APPLE have released their sixth full-length studio album, POPS.

Out on 30 September via EMI Records / Universal Music Japan, the 16-track record marks a defining release in the Japanese trio's "Phase 3" and arrives as their first original full-length album in nearly three years.

With POPS, Motoki Ohmori, Hiloto Wakai, and Ryoka Fujisawa explore their own interpretation of what "mainstream" music can mean today. Rather than pursuing a single sound designed to reach everyone, the band move between genres, moods, and emotions, allowing each track to connect with listeners in different ways while retaining Mrs. GREEN APPLE's musical identity.

The album brings together previously released singles 'GOOD DAY', 'Wind and Town', 'Carrying Happiness', 'Summer Shadow', and 'lulu.', the opening theme for the second season of Frieren: Beyond Journey's End.

Also featured is 'Brand New', which Mrs. GREEN APPLE wrote and performed as the official Japanese theme song for Marvel Studios and Sony Pictures' Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

POPS arrives amid the band's continued growth outside Japan. Earlier this year, Mrs. GREEN APPLE ranked No. 13 on the IFPI Global Artist Chart, becoming the highest-charting Japanese artist on the list.

The release also follows the band's biggest stadium tour to date, ZENJIN MITO TO IM/MUTABLE, which drew 390,000 fans across six performances, including four shows at MUFG Stadium. Another 250,000 viewers tuned in to the finale through livestreams, screenings at more than 360 cinemas, karaoke viewing events across Japan, and international screenings in South Korea, Hong Kong, Taiwan, and Thailand.

With the album now out, Mrs. GREEN APPLE are heading back on the road for their first nationwide arena tour in approximately three years. The Mrs. GREEN APPLE Ringo Jam Tour 'SHADOWS' comprises 28 performances across 13 cities in Japan, beginning on 30 September at Anabuki Arena Kagawa.

items.body:
Singapore's homegrown acts could find themselves sharing the stage with some of alternative music's biggest names this December.

LAMC Presents has launched Big Night Out: Battle of the Stage, a contest for Singaporean artists to compete for the chance to open for Two Door Cinema Club, Wolf Alice, or Slowdive at their respective shows at Fort Canning Park. Each winning act will also receive a S$500 cash prize.

The competition is open to eligible Singaporean artists aged 18 and above, with three categories corresponding to each headliner. Entrants will have to submit a one-minute cover of one of the following songs:

Two Door Cinema Club: 'What You Know' or 'Undercover Martyn'

Wolf Alice: 'Don't Delete the Kisses' or 'Bloom Baby Bloom'

Slowdive: 'When the Sun Hits' or 'Dagger'

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by L.A.M.C. (@lamcpresents)

Entries must be posted on Instagram with @lamcpresents tagged and the relevant #BigNightOut_TDCC, #BigNightOut_WolfAlice, or #BigNightOut_Slowdive hashtag. Artists must also complete the submission form on the LAMC Presents website to be eligible.

Following the submission period, LAMC Presents will shortlist eligible entries for an online public vote, where audiences will vote based on each act's cover as well as a featured original song. The top three acts in each category will then be presented to the respective headliners, with Two Door Cinema Club, Wolf Alice, and Slowdive personally selecting their opening acts.

Submissions are open now and close on 13 October at 11:59 PM SGT. Online voting will run from 19 to 23 October, with the top three finalists announced on 26 October. The winning opening acts will be revealed at a later date.

The competition leads into three Big Night Out shows at Fort Canning Park. Two Door Cinema Club will bring their 15th Anniversary Tour to Singapore on 4 December, followed by Wolf Alice with ivri on 10 December, and Slowdive on 12 December.

Tickets for all three concerts are available via LAMC Presents.

items.body: Shell and Core takes its title from the unfinished concrete structures that have become fixtures of the Syrian landscape, and Tasgeelat Al-Husni تسجيلات الحُسني uses that image of arrested construction as a way of looking at lives left incomplete. Much of the record is assembled from things heard or observed in everyday life: bureaucratic rituals, checkpoints, cars, street conversations, scrap collectors and an uncle’s absurd political opinions. On “Spacetune” these details accumulate into a comic story that deliberately goes nowhere; “Existing” turns repetition and waiting into its subject, while the heavier “Grinder” pushes familiar material towards something more grotesque. The humour is important. Rather than presenting Syria exclusively through catastrophe, Tasgeelat Al-Husni draws on a local tradition of satire and everyday mockery in which absurdity is one means of living with circumstances that have themselves become absurd. The music operates in much the same way, refusing a clean division between local tradition and experimental electronics. The oud can introduce the relatively spacious “Existing”, sit behind electronic and guitar noise on “Spacetune”, or grind against doom-laden riffs on “Grinder”. Al-Husni explicitly rejects using the instrument as a nostalgic signifier of a disappearing culture; here it belongs to the present as naturally as synthesis, distortion or field recording. Progressive and heavy rock are equally embedded in the record’s vocabulary, particularly in its abrupt shifts between calm and physical weight. Lazar Mečanin’s production makes those contrasts unusually pronounced: passages of relative openness can suddenly thicken into distortion, low-frequency pressure and noise, giving the album the unstable logic of the environment it describes. One of the album’s most striking changes of register comes on “Perspective”, where the voice of Ukrainian opera singer Oksana Vakula introduces a radiant tone, briefly opening up the record’s otherwise rough and unstable sonic terrain. That makes the unfinished Massar Discovery Center on the cover more than an illustration. Along with Syria’s other abandoned concrete shells, it becomes an architectural counterpart to a record about interrupted trajectories. Yet Shell and Core avoids turning incompletion into a grand metaphor. What matters most is the peripheral and the discarded: things overheard, jokes, irritating routines, incongruous sounds and surreal encounters. The picture of Syria that emerges is at the same time damaged and precarious, but also mundane and funny, a place whose exposed structural bones are filled with everyday life. To help us better understand the production process for Shell and Core we reached out directly to Tasgeelat Al-Husni. Throughout عَ العَضم (Shell and Core), everyday Syrian life is depicted in a way that often feels almost surreal, allowing the ordinary and the mythical to coexist. The repeated “unknown” in “Spacetune”, the taxi driver nicknamed Azrael—the Angel of Death—blasting heavy dabke, the endless bureaucracy of “Existing”, the Ladas, and finally the litany of scrap collectors all feel like fragments of the same social landscape. There is also a distinctly sardonic humour running through the writing. Do you think of your lyrics as poetry, documentary montage, social commentary or simply another way of composing with sound? Most of the lyrics are rephrasing of something I have heard in Syria either in a conversation with friends or randomly on the street. I wrote down some of what I had heard and then integrated them with how I thought of each song. I am new to writing words, so I don’t know much, but I have tried writing a comical story with mild suspense that leads nowhere on “Spacetune,” describing recurrent scenes from daily life on “Existing,” and creating some surreal visual scenes on “Grinder.” The sardonic humor is essential to the environment where the album came from. It’s in the music we hear (such as the music of the Rahbani family), the TV we watch (such as Spotlight – بقعة ضوء), the books we read (such as Muhammad al-Maghut’s), so you would also hear it in your day-to-day life from your relatives, your college friends, the bus driver or even from a soldier on a checkpoint. Add to that the absurdity of people’s takes on the conflict, like that uncle on Spacetune, which naturally calls for mockery. Peugeot 504 – photo by Hussain Hussain The second track, “Existing”, opens with an oud before gradually expanding into a much broader electronic landscape. The instrument never feels nostalgic or symbolic of tradition; instead, it becomes another texture within the composition. Was it important for you to avoid treating the oud as a marker of cultural identity, allowing it instead to coexist naturally with electronics and noise? It was! I think such instruments are not supposed to sound like a distant cry from the past echoing in an empty space, or “a ghostly remnant from a lost culture”, like David Byrne once wrote. The oud, like any instrument, should be used to serve the song the way the song is meant to be. It definitely could be used in its classical character with takasim and as accompaniment for singing like on “Existing,” but it can also accompany heavy doom metal riffs to add a bloody drilling texture on “Grinder,” or do some finger picking behind synth and guitar noises like on Spacetune. If you listen to a based folk performance from the past, you hear the oud vital and integrated with the rest of the instruments, not sounding like an anomaly, and I think this is how it should be treated in any other (modern) context. Window – photo by Hussain Hussain Although the album is rooted in electroacoustic composition and experimental electronics, there are moments—particularly in the treatment of distortion, low-frequency weight and rhythmic pressure—that recall progressive rock, heavy rock and noise. Are those traditions part of your musical vocabulary, and how do they intersect with the experimental and electronic music you make today? These traditions strongly influence how we have approached this record and music making in general. The treatment of sound at this level was more Lazar’s part, so I have forwarded the question to him, and this is his response: “Those traditions have to be a part of our vocabulary given the fact it’s the music we grew up on – Floyd, Crimson, etc. These bands influenced us as players but they also influenced how we think about music. A song can exhibit cinematic properties and sometimes be even more immersive than a movie if done right. The record is really a landscape representing every-day life in Syria (if I understood it correctly myself hah), moments of beauty and calmness intertwined with unpredictable chaos mostly right next to each other, so in a way the music is interpreting life, and by using these acoustic and production techniques we are attempting to recreate the feelings one might have simply living there.” Random Structure – photo by Hussain Hussain How do you see your work in relation to other Syrian experimental musicians? Is there a shared aesthetic or set of concerns emerging from the scene, or do you feel that each artist is responding to the experiences of recent years in fundamentally different ways? I have learned a lot from contemporary Syrian and Arab artists — Tootard, Shabjdeed, Khaled Allaf, Lynn Adib, Al-Rahel Al-Kabir, Kulna Sawa, and many more — and that has encouraged me to work on my own stuff, sing about what I have heard or seen, and eventually release that. It is true that everyone is responding to their experiences in their own way; some express that in a desperate way, some in a cynical way, some tackle social issues, and some speak about personal experiences. Maybe what we have in common is our frustration and disgust with our situation now and in recent years, but who knows? What’s important to me is that many of our artists sound so fresh, so unique and so relevant, and I always look forward to hearing their new approaches and what they are talking about. The cover features the unfinished Massar Discovery Center (“Massar Rose”) in Damascus—a project that was meant to embody education, innovation and the future before construction stopped in 2014. Throughout the album, there is a recurring sense of lives shaped by interruption: bureaucratic waiting, checkpoints, abandoned trajectories and systems that never quite reach completion. Did you see the building as encapsulating that condition, or were you drawn to it for different reasons? Gardenia Towers – photo by Hussain Hussain Exactly, hence the name, ع العضم Shell and Core! The rest of the album art (partly prepared for a CD release) features some well-known incomplete buildings, such as the infamous 50-year-old Yalbugha Tower in the middle of the capital and the Gardenia Towers in Homs that became known among the public as the “Death Towers”, used by snipers during the war. Such giant incomplete, mostly ugly, structures are so common to see in Syria. They are ironically reflective of the life of Syrian individual that has become so crippled, it might never reach a sense of completion. Everyone who lost their home forever and had to live in a tent, everyone that lost their beloved ones, got detained for the stupidest reason, or had to serve in the army for 8 years or so, and also everyone who just had to live or grow up there during these awful times. To me, this building not only encapsulates these incomplete trajectories, but also resembles, with its bare bones (عضم) sticking out, how naked, exposed and fragile we are. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Achachay is what highland Ecuadorians say when the cold catches them, arraray when the heat does. Both words came into Andean Spanish from Quichua, and BRITTA builds “Achachay” on the pair: a love song about wanting someone enough to feel both. A requinto line, the small high-tuned guitar of Ecuadorian string music, runs over percussion drawn from the country’s Pacific coast and a trap low end. The alt-pop production leaves the guitar exposed and the beat holds a steady pressure under a vocal that stays at the point of anticipation. Born in Ambato in the central Ecuadorian Andes and based in Los Angeles in the US, Britta has been feeding Ecuadorian traditional forms into dance production for a while: on her single “NON3 (no te dejes avecilla)” she sampled her own voice singing an albazo, the fast triple-time song form of the Ecuadorian highlands, and built a house track around it. “Achachay” points that same working method at Latin alternative, with the Andean Spanish idioms running through the lyric carrying as much of the song’s identity as the requinto and the percussion do. Listen to “Achachay” HERE The post Daily Discovery: BRITTA – Achachay appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Much like tracing Charles Darwin's evolutionary chain, the jazz-rock movement, initiated by Miles Davis around 1969, saw a crucial intermediate stage through acts like Tony Williams' Lifetime and John McLaughlin's solo work (such as Extrapolation, also from 1969). Meanwhile, on the other side of the Atlantic, the Scottish trumpeter Ian Carr emerged with Nucleus, forming another pillar in the birth of fusion. Beyond sharing a stylistic current that was still taking shape, these groups were united by a spirit of great freedom, both in composition and performance, a quality that would diminish in later bands more constrained by the established rules of the genre.It is against this backdrop that Nucleus's debut album stands as an essential starting point for understanding the "Big Bang" of jazz-rock, a movement that would go on to influence generations of musicians far beyond its own borders, right up to the present day. When trumpeter Ian Carr teamed up with guitarist Chris Spedding, who had played on Jack Bruce's early albums, and keyboardist/saxophonist Karl Jenkins (who would later join Soft Machine), the group's creative core was already more than 50% established; Brian Smith (tenor and baritone sax), Jeff Clyne (double bass and electric bass), and John Marshall (drums) rounded out the rest of the lineup.A flamenco-esque vibe ushers in 1916, and on Elastic Rock, the title track serves as the key to understanding, or rather, hearing, what their musical approach was all about. It is a sound driven by prominent drums and guitar work that, while seemingly improvised, wanders freely, all set against the backdrop of a modern-sounding electric piano, the very instrument Herbie Hancock had resisted adopting in the 1960s until Miles Davis finally convinced him.At this stage, the innovation and revolution lay in funk, specifically, the inherent groove felt rather than merely heard between the drum section and the electric piano, all within a jazz context that was becoming increasingly psychedelic. The definitive genres would emerge years later with bands like Return to Forever, Mahavishnu Orchestra, Weather Report, and Herbie Hancock's Headhunters. "Striation" features Eastern-style melodies played on the double bass (bowed like a cello), while "Taranaki" is a jazz piece with ethnic roots; the driving pace of "Twisted Track", featuring Ian Carr on muted trumpet and Chris Spedding on guitar, truly broke the mold, and the oboe on "Crude Blues, Pt. 1" reminds me of Andy Mackay from Roxy Music.In "1916, The Battle of Boogaloo," we can hear the seeds of Soft Machine's future sound; and then there is "Torrid Zone", a very important track for me, where the bass and electric piano play their respective parts, and then, over the trumpet solo, the guitar begins to break up the melody, interfering with it and introducing a separate meter. That controlled, calculated chaos was as infectious and innovative then as it remains today. Once modern... forever modern. Like Coltrane, if the comparison holds.As the muted trumpet and electric piano are left alone in "Stonescape", and later joined by the drums, the atmosphere takes on a space-like quality, foreshadowing what is to come. With the otherworldly mood created by the oboe, and as the guitar and double bass accelerate and cut in once more, these musicians, along with so many others, were laying the groundwork for a new kind of jazz: one that was open and hungry for fresh influences, destined to grow ever larger, provided it retained that spirit of inquiry, its most valuable asset, which prevents it from becoming rigid over time.

Yes their main influence is classical music, but theywouldn't name have named their kids Ludwig, Johan Sebastian or Wolfgang Amadeus. They might havethought of Edgar, Karlheinz or Gabriel, though. BTW, it's not just about modern classical , as thereare hints of jazz dispersed throughout the duration of their first works. Noteworthy, TGD was firstreleased as vinyl-only, waiting some three years to finally release it in the user-friendly formatcalled CD.Indeed, while relatively dissonant, SS is not extreme Avant Prog like Guapo would be, but they'renot very careful about your sanity beyond your eardrums. Their Grand Design is still relativelyaccessible, if you like atmospheric improvisation, almost cinematic, gloomy ambiances with also PostRock moments. This instrumental quintet will be remarkably stable throughout their career, focusingon the violin and piano as lead instruments, but backed up by a guitar. There are some lovelymoments, but also plenty of tense passages, not necessarily providing a release outlet for thenervous accumulation.TBH, not my cup or tea, but it's definitely worth their Bandcamp detour at least once, even if itwill never be an essential piece of work. Add another half-star, though !!!

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The use of synthesizers and the Mellotron, combined with an abrasive, dense hard rock sound, defined Black Bonzo's debut as progressive hard rock; vocalist Magnus Lindgren, with his very clean voice, and keyboardist Nicklas Ahlund, capable of playing everything from rock 'n' roll to classical organ passages, evoke the more daring side of Deep Purple, while on the title track, "Lady of the Light," they also create an almost cinematic, eerie atmosphere."Brave Young Soldier" also features psychedelia, rhythmic shifts, and dissonances that greatly enrich the track; once again, Magnus Lindgren demonstrates his own distinct personality and style, avoiding the path of other singers in the genre. Guitar and organ combine for a brilliant riff at the end, blending a medieval past with rock music evocative of spells and stone forests."Fantasy World" evoked a different atmosphere, reminiscent of Wishbone Ash; "Freedom," on the other hand, could easily have appeared on Queen's debut album. The melody ultimately took center stage, a gothic, operatic tune that kept evolving. While this didn't necessarily contribute to the album's cohesion, the diversity added emotional depth, featuring the Mellotron from "Sirens" and, above all, the drumming, which, combined with the acoustic guitar, recalled King Crimson's debut.On one hand, there is the clenched-teeth rock and tight sound of "Jailbait," and the dark, ominous lyricism of "Leave Your Burdens", complete with Black Sabbath-style riffs reminiscent of their bluesier moments, while the hypnotic conclusion of "Where the River Meets the Sea" serves as the perfect finale. It clearly defines an artistic vision that was at once velvet and steel, possessing scales and gills to dive through the ocean, yet also lungs to scream and fill with air in order to fly.

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — *Limite Acque Sicure* by *Limite Acque Sicure*?a surprising title and surname, a sort of metaphor with multiple possible levels of meaning: the cartographic contours of the Mediterranean Sea in the Middle Ages? A body of water of a certain depth, not to be exceeded? The knowledge of our inner selves (or that of others), beyond which it may be dangerous to venture? The need to push past our own limits in order to grow? Or simply the name of a red wine from Abruzzo? Please refer to the very interesting lyrics on this album for a hint of an answer (be sure to have an Italian translation tool on hand if you don't speak the language). Musically speaking, you don't need to be an expert on Banco's music to understand that *Limite Acque Sicure*, hailing from Ferrara and formed in 2005 by singer Andrea Chendi and keyboardist Antonello Giovannelli as just one of many tribute bands, is a true devotee of the golden age of the Nocenzi brothers' band?a fact confirmed by the inclusion on this self-titled album of the iconic "Il Giardino Del Mago" (Banco 1972), in a dazzling live version.Between the introductory "Sogno D'Oriente" (12:48)?with its oriental sounds, as its name suggests, reminiscent of the famous "Kashmir"?and the short "Ti Salver� " (2:11)?placed at the other end, in the style and spirit of Banco's "Traccia II" (that album again) Certain tracks on *Limite Acque Sicure* stand out more. These are the ones where the band most clearly demonstrates that it has something personal to convey to us. "Terra Straniera" (7:53), with its majestic, enthusiastic, and determined finale, is closer in style to *Prowlers* than to *Banco*; "Il Respiro Dell'Anima" (8:25), with its more lively rhythm, ambitious structure, and shimmering arrangements that leave plenty of room for highly effective guitar and Moog solos. And above all, the epic "Fiamme Intorno " (10:48), with a darker main theme (though carried by a deceptively light rhythm), as if weighed down by a relentless exploration of humanity's spiritual wanderings, then giving way to a second, more open and luminous section, full of hope, whose coda?and this is quite unexpected?features a few drum beats dedicated to? Neil Peart. On a more contemporary note, the music of Limite Acque Sicure evokes memories of Museo Rosenbach, Campo Di Marte, Il Rovescio Della Medaglia, Alphataurus, and Apoteosi, all those meteor-like bands that shone for the duration of a single album (often released in 1973) before disappearing for a long time?or forever. "Limite Acque Sicure" seems to be a tribute to the RPI of the past, yet one that looks toward the future. In other words, it is less a relic of a glorious past than a promise of what the RPI may have in store.

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — Reale Accademia Di Musica is a italien band from Rome, best known among us for its self-titled debut album released in 1972, an Italian progressive rock sound similar to that of PFM from the same era, though lacking the Milanese band's charisma. The rest of their discography, led by composer Adriano Monteduro under the acronym RAM, is of much less interest to us? until their 2018 revival spearheaded by Pericle Sponzilli, the band's original guitarist, who enlisted the talents of virtuoso keyboardist Fabio Liberatori (a prolific composer of Italian film scores) and Erika Savastani, a young singer with a powerful voice, to release *Angeli Mutanti* that year?an interesting, if not essential, fusion of modern Italian pop and flamboyant, timeless Italian progressive rock.*Lame Di Luce* is in the same vein, while at times drawing closer to the Italian neo-prog of the '90s (Leviathan, Mad Crayon?) as on the magnificent "Ascesa al Fuji," one of those gems that seems to smile at us and make life so sweet as it comes alive with vibrant colors. Fifty years later, the pastoral feel of the debut album is very much present on "Onde di Sabbia," and a few other echoes of the RPI masters charm us effortlessly (Le Orme on "Due Pietre Preziose Birmane" or Banco on the jazzy "Si Parler�"). This band excels at writing melodies that are out of the ordinary while remaining accessible to a wide audience, as heard on the irresistible "Lame di Luce," which seems to be to Italian song what the Moody Blues' music was to English prog: sophisticated pop without being ostentatious, capable of sounding harmonious even to the most delicate angels in heaven. The final quarter-hour of *Lame di Luce* may seem a bit weaker. "Una Ferita da Disinfettare" is a well-crafted symphonic prog track, but it will primarily catch our attention for a brief, unexpected quote from the famous guitar solo in "Firth of Fifth." "Ore Lente" could pass for a simple, dynamic song with a catchy chorus, and "Incontri" for a nostalgic Pink Floyd-style ballad that's a bit too slow?were it not for the cinematic influence of Fabio Liberatori, which enriches the mood and atmosphere of both tracks.Ultimately, the best moments carry the album and overshadow the few, quite excusable weaknesses, ensuring that our favorable opinion remains. *Lame di Luce* is a pleasant surprise and deserves our full attention. All it needs are a few more instrumental developments to make it an excellent modern RPI album worthy of its illustrious predecessors, among whom *Reale Accademia Di Musica* was counted in the early '70s.

items.body: Review by DimitrisTheHead — There is something about those late '60s/early '70s English albums, in contrast to the American ones, that make them sound epic. Is it the atmosphere? Is it the lyrics? Is it the keys? Is it something else? Maybe it is all these things combined. Now this record, has all that trademark elements of that era, it's bluesy, it's heavy, it's dark in some moments and happy on other moments, it's progy. "Repent Walpurgis" is an amazing instrumental and one of my favorites from that era. Matthew Fisher on the hammond, give me that same feeling, Jon Lord (Deep Purple) or Ken Hensley (Uriah Heep) give me when I'm listening to their records. Yes lads, it is that good.Procol Harum, as a typical British band, decided to leave "A whiter shade of pale" off of the UK vinyl release and put it just on the North America release, plus they left some amazing songs as bonus tracks. (Just listen "Homburg"!!!)A must listen for the fans of that era.

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — SS's second album certainly starts in a WTF, but if Elements of Architecture stretches their TGD debut by a mile, and go the extra-distance to play on the dissonance frontier, but never crossing it. BTW, they must have a fascination about construction design, since their next three releases will mention it on the record sleeves. On the sonic front, it seems that Kim's bass guitar is playing a more prominent role than previously - especially on the title track. In a general way, Kim seems to be the head honcho, handling design & mixing/production, even, if the album is released again on the violinist Dancing Butterfly label. In some moments, via the guitarist, King Crimson is not far away.Definitely a harder grasp on what SS tried to do in this Avant-Post-Prog creation, but if all tracks were more in the mould of Floating Debris, then then they might've gotten that fourth star. .

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — Third album in three years after taking 18 years to create their first one, Architecture might sound/read like a logical successor to their previous one, but there is quite a sonic progression here;eve,n if SS' collective paws are plainly recognizable. Indeed, we've taken a steep turn away from Avant-Prog, but I"m not sure this is due to the new arrival Katie's saxophone on three tracks, because it doesn't really change the overall soundscapes, even if the energy reach a different level and intensity - for the better, I might add. But indeed, the general sonic direction of this album tells us that we are at a corner of the band's career.The dissonance element present in their first two albums has almost disappeared, and this helps the accessibility o�f their music. Relatively absent from their first two album, there is a sense of drama permeating most of the tracks, endearing us to their musical escapes and extravaganzas. Emotional melodies over tight rhythms. BTW, it was their first album directly sold in CD, and for both formats, SS took the carte to make an attractive sleeve with a transparent protecting plastic sleeve. TBH, I really don't know why the band will change its name and record label (I guess the departure of their violinist played a big role), after the release of their best-yet album . But there will be two undeniable links: the Architecture link (purposely misspelled) and the same type of line-up (new violinist) and a now-permanent sax player replacing the too-discreet guitarist. but that's for their next album. In the meantime, their third is definitely the one I preferred at the time.

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — Obviously, the band's name change meant trouble had arisen in the original Superstring quintet. Arkitekture's new name (voluntarily misspelled) is a clear link to SS' previous two albums, thus claiming its legacy despite two new members and a la record label change. Indeed, the change of violinist (the departing one was also their old record label founder) and replacement of the guitarist by a full-time sax player are notable difference, but in terms of sonic, we're in the direct line of SS' Architecture.But if they claim SS' legacy, their fourth album is quite a step forward in the direction taken with the predecessor, with loads of emotions, dramatics, frantic escapes and grandiose passages Three of the five tracks are divided in multi-sections (5, 4 & 5) and the changes of climates are vertigo-inducing and chills-down-the-spine are guaranteed if played LOUD. Their cute double female front-woman attacks add even more charm to their dark, moody, intense, dramatic music. Belgian expat Johan Ahn explodes with his washes and tsunamis of keys, such as organ, electric piano, piano, Mellotron and diverse synthesizers.Another sign of changes, for the first time, the CD was released a couple of years before its vinyl brother.Clearly one of 2022's top releases, as far as my eardrums and neurons are concerned (AFAME&NAC ;-))))). K-Prog at its best ;-)))).

items.body: Review by Warthur — Bakerloo's sole album reveals them as a truly diverse progressive group of the early prog era. They've clearly emerged from the same blues rock primordial soup formented by the Yardbirds and Bluesbreakers and Cream and which saw peers like Jetbro Tull and Black Sabbath emerge. Bakerloo actually shared a manager with Sabbath, but it's Tull who you'll be reminded of most - in particular, the sound of their earliest days, before Mick Abrahams left. There's no flute, but plenty of harmonica - and the power trip work in enough influences from jazz and classical music to suggest a group just as broad in influences as Tull, though perhaps with more influence from the calmer, more meditative side of psychedelia creeping in at points.It's no surprise that they fell by the wayside at the end - this was a crowded scene, after all, and it was all too easy for groups to get lost in the shuffle, and with Tull already evolving away from their early blues influences and Black Sabbath turning the blues into doom metal their peers were moving to distinguish themselves, so you can see why Bakerloo were in danger of being eclipsed. In retrospect, it's a gem of its particular scene - it's just that the scene in question was on the cusp of being overtaken by other strands of prog and blues-derived rock.

items.body: Review by Hector Enrique — Recorded simultaneously with its hostile and murky counterpart, "Deliverance", during the summer of 2002, the gentler and more melancholic "Damnation" - Opeth's seventh album - didn't see the light of day until April 2003, due to their record label's decision to separate the two releases for commercial reasons. An album unexpectedly devoid of Mikael �kerfeldt's guttural vocals, the brutal riffs and abrasive textures that had defined the Swedish band, and their usual monolithic instrumental displays, the result of �kerfeldt's deliberate intention to immerse himself in the smoother, more experimental side of 1970s progressive rock, accompanied for this purpose by the fantastic Steven Wilson, whose decisive work as co-producer and musician brings a sensibility and sonic aesthetic that resonate with those of his band, Porcupine Tree.While it's true that in their earlier work Opeth included acoustic and refreshing sections amid their stormy arrangements, on "Damnation" they take it a step further by devoting its just over forty-three minutes to dreamy melodies set in an introspective and tense atmosphere that flows unhurriedly over the misty, ethereal soundscapes woven by Wilson's Mellotrons and Peter Lindgren's clean, serene guitars. Tracks like the hypnotic "Windowpane," with its magnificent jazz-inspired solo, or the psychedelic "In My Time of Need," "Death Whispered a Lullaby," and "Closure" evoke the most dreamlike and hazy side of genre icons such as King Crimson, the pre-"The Dark Side of the Moon" Pink Floyd, and the Gabriel-era Genesis.And staying true to that evocative, immersive vibe, the instrumental "Ending Credits," with its long guitar bends reminiscent of Camel's Andy Latimer, and the impeccable backing -as throughout the album- from the standout Mart�n M�ndez on bass and Martin Lopez on percussion, along with the trance-like and unchanging "Weakness," featuring a whispering, spectral �kerfeldt, ultimately round out "Damnation": the beginning of Opeth's stylistic transition and one of the most controversial phases of their career.3.5/4 stars

items.body: Review by alainPP — An evolving, melodic, synth-driven sound; the track evokes human degradation in the face of AI."Tears Of The Muse" kicks off as a dark, mid-tempo rock track featuring 80s-style keyboards?somewhere between rock, prog, and dark wave. A thunderous beat reminiscent of Genesis and Gabriel gives way to a sharp riff and vocals that trade lines with a vocoder. "EKO" features a hook redolent of Saga?think sugary new-millennium prog-metal with Martin stepping in for Damian. A dash of Arena, a touch of Lalu?it works perfectly for this groovy track with its driving bassline. "I Am The One" features piano accompanying Simon's metronomic drumming. It has a rich, proggy sound?like Toto?complemented by a heavy riff and a solo from Joop. There's a groovy, jazzy, Yes-style break leading into a warm choral finale. "Mayacama" is an instrumental that channels Toto and Saga?I can't help but hear the resemblance. A guitar groove underpins the melody, building into a progressive crescendo with the keyboards following suit. A piano break and a synth-led ballad section precede Joop showing off his dexterity. "Prince With The Swift Warning" features rolling pads and vocal harmonies that add complexity, navigating between rock, pop, and ballad styles. It includes a tense break with a sharp guitar solo, an infectious rhythm, and a second solo that is delicate, bluesy, and proggy."Learning To Fly" features airy vocals and echoes of Saga?or even Marillion. It's an accessible track that surprises with its evolution, while a dark organ keeps the listener on edge. The guitar solo is pure prog, leading into a riff where Martin shows off his impressive vocal range, backed by Simon. The finale soars as Joop and then Vivien drive the track to a spine-tingling climax. "A Drop Of Water" is an acoustic guitar interlude featuring a brilliant, ear-piercing arpeggio?a nod to Steve Howe of Yes. "Fhloston Paradise"?named after the station in *The Fifth Element*?blends hard-hitting rock and vocoder with the energetic, percussive groove characteristic of Joop, reminiscent of Iron Maiden. It features a Yes-style coda, confirming Vivien's admiration for the band. "Cordal Weaves" is a unique track with ethereal, searching notes and a stereo soundscape that creates a distinctly progressive atmosphere. It offers a funky, simmering moment: Martin rallies the energy, Joop lays into the rhythm, and Simon unleashes a barrage of drums. The finale features soaring vocals and a guitar full of melancholic longing. "Midnight Ink" serves as a piano-bar-style closer, driven by a poignant, whispered croon. Melancholic strings lend the track a solemn tone?the perfect way to wrap up the album.A melting pot of mainstream rock in the vein of Saga, Yes, and Toto, created above all for the sheer joy of it. It offers a softer take on prog metal and an intense jazz-prog vibe that feels like a journey in a time capsule.

items.body: Review by sgtpepper — After a long-term hiatus (last good album released in 1981), Collegium Musicum returned at least to the stage in 1997 with the original members of which Freso remained in a particular good shape. The choice of tracks performed was good as it didn't only feature the first two albums but reached later into their career. I am personally a bigger fan of their 1971-1975 period rather than their first eponymous album.The guest Andrej Seban provides elastic guitar while Hajek hasn't lost his edge on the drums.I'm not very content with Varga though because I find his playing somehow sloppy - as if he couldn't hit all the right keys, or not always on time. This suspicion raised with me in the beginning of the first track but hasn't evaporated later. Or is it just the not keyboard sound which does not allow for careful key distinction?In any case, this was the first official live album with their classic songs, however the double live album from 2010 could be more appealing.
