items.body: Metanoia, Yulianna Avdeeva’s new album for Pentatone, focuses on the transformation of Liszt’s style between his Weimar and late periods. Liszt had already shown an experimental curiosity with structure and form in the Sonata in B minor—a work presented here alongside later pieces such as the Bagatelle sans tonalité and Nuages gris. Metanoia Amazon Presto Apple Given the many versions available, Avdeeva’s B minor sonata is impressive. Some renditions are either entirely too heavy or too light, but hers strikes a sensible balance of power, speed, and musicality. There are admittedly some moments where velocity comes at the expense of clarity, but the furious and urgent spirit is aptly captured. Avdeeva shows firm command in the first section (track 1). The octave passages are bold and brash, while the runs remain light, agile, and effortless. I did find the lead-up to the second theme somewhat rushed: the Grandioso (track 2) is rousing but needs more breadth for us to fully appreciate the arrival of the D major section—something Argerich’s 1971 recording does so well. The more tender moments of the section, however, are exquisitely rendered with translucent passagework. Fortunately, Avdeeva does not rush the Andante (track 3). Its blend of nostalgia, reverie, and introspection offers a much-needed respite from the frenetic parts of the sonata and leaves enough space for the return of drama in the finale. The fugue (track 4), meticulous in its rhythm and articulation, gives a powerful drive back to the recapitulation but never leaves us with any sense of uncomfortable volatility. The late works begin with La lugubre gondola II (track 5), whose origins are as dark as the music. In 1882, Liszt is said to have had an eerie vision that his son-in-law Richard Wagner would die and that his body would be carried on a black gondola. The vision came true a few months later, in early 1883. Avdeeva reflects the grim nature of this realization as she highlights the starkness of the sparse textures and the austerity, foreboding, and finality of the monophony. The work is as much an homage to Wagner as it is a premonition, and the second half is where we hear more elements of tonality and lyricism. R.W. – Venezia (track 9), the companion work to La lugubre gondola, was written after Wagner’s death. While just as somber and still minimalistic, the piece lies largely in the lower register. Avdeeva gives the left-hand octave ostinato plenty of depth but also a necessary sense of severity. The brighter Bagatelle sans tonalité (track 6) recalls the showmanship of earlier works, though the bravado now takes the form of a more elegant virtuosity. The unmistakable element of caprice is well evoked. Yulianna Avdeeva. Photo © Kevin Kinzley. Nuages gris (track 7), like La lugubre gondola, has sinister undertones amid its minimalism. Avdeeva still finds a way to create some breathtaking tone colors; the final two mysterious chords are a good example, offering a fleeting sense of whimsy quite different from the ominous mood that pervades most of the piece. The Hungarian Rhapsody No. 17 (track 10), written just a few years before Liszt’s death, diverges considerably in character from the earlier rhapsodies, Nos. 1–15. The flamboyant, fiery, and playful profile gives way to more ominous undertones and an atonal base. Avdeeva brings out a threatening and even aggressive nature: accents and dissonances carry a stinging sharpness, and the octave passages at the end are adamant and tumultuous. Unstern! – Sinistre (track 11) is perhaps the most jarring of the late pieces, owing to its harsh atonality and even harsher textures. The accents and chords here are abrasive (as they should be), yet never become too strident on the ears. Unlike some of the other works, whose endings offer some form of catharsis, the latter sections here only prolong the doubt and disquiet, a distinction Avdeeva makes clear. The juxtaposition of works from different eras is well judged. In one sitting, the heavy mood of the late works may become a bit overbearing, but this only goes to show the effectiveness of Avdeeva’s interpretations. All in all, a series of excellent performances that should find a place on the shelf of any Liszt enthusiast. items.body: London duo Placebo release the single “Helen Keller” on 28 September 2026, the same day their 30th Anniversary Tour opened in Porto. The song reworks the piano melody of “H.K. Farewell,” the hidden instrumental from the band’s self-titled 1996 debut album, into a new rock track. “Helen Keller” was recorded in London and produced by Placebo together with Adam Noble, who also mixed it. Placebo ‘Helen Keller’ Brian Molko described the song as “a new rock song inspired by the piano melody from ‘H.K. Farewell'” and said it is named after one of his favourite people from history. The single is out now on streaming platforms. The 30th Anniversary Tour opened at the Super Bock Arena in Porto on 28 September and continues in Lisbon, with the setlist drawing on Placebo’s first two albums, “Placebo” (1996) and “Without You I’m Nothing” (1998), including songs the band has not performed regularly in over two decades. Placebo has confirmed that “Helen Keller” will be played live during the tour. UK and Ireland dates follow in late November and early December, including Nottingham, Glasgow and London, with a Latin American leg set for February-March 2027 covering Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Peru, Colombia and Mexico. About Placebo Placebo formed in London in 1994 after vocalist-guitarist Brian Molko and bassist-guitarist Stefan Olsdal met at South Kensington tube station. The pair first performed together as Ashtray Heart before adopting the name Placebo. The band released its self-titled debut album in 1996 through Elevator Music, followed by “Without You I’m Nothing” (1998), “Black Market Music” (2000), “Sleeping with Ghosts” (2003), “Meds” (2006), “Battle for the Sun” (2009), “Loud Like Love” (2013) and “Never Let Me Go” (2022). Matt Lunn has drummed with the band since 2015. On 11 April 2026 Placebo announced “RE:CREATED,” a reworking of the 1996 debut album produced from its original master tapes, led by the single “Nancy Boy (Re:created Version).” “Helen Keller,” released 28 September 2026 as the band’s 30th Anniversary Tour opened in Porto, extends that anniversary chronology with a new song built from a 1996-era melody.

items.body: Dark synthwave producer Das Mörtal releases the two-track single “DRAIN ME” on Lisbon Lux Records on 30 September 2026. The single pairs the original version with a remix by synthwave producer Dan Terminus, and precedes Das Mörtal’s mini-album “DECVY I,” out 29 October 2026. Das Mörtal, the project of Montreal-based producer Cristóbal Cortes, describes “DRAIN ME” as “a track about the feeling of running in circles in the health care system while being drained from the multiple tests one person might go through.” The track opens with a cinematic, sweeping tone before shifting into a fast-paced, techno-driven rhythm section with an arpeggiated synth pluck, washed-out vocals and a half-time breakdown before its final chorus. Dan Terminus, grouped alongside Perturbator, Carpenter Brut and GosT as one of what press materials call the “Four Horsemen of Synthwave,” reworks “DRAIN ME” with chopped and manipulated vocals, punchy percussion and an occasional violin line over booming basslines that combine acoustic and synthesised elements. “DRAIN ME” follows the double single “Parasite & Ghost,” which Das Mörtal released on Lisbon Lux Records on 4 June 2026, also ahead of “DECVY I.” An official teaser for “DRAIN ME” is available on YouTube, and the single is available to pre-save via ffm.to/drainmee. About Das Mörtal Das Mörtal is the project of Cristóbal Cortes, an electronic music producer and DJ based in Montreal whose work began in Berlin, drawing on artists including Steve Moore and Aphex Twin. Das Mörtal’s sound blends techno, occult electro and Italo disco into a dark, nostalgic style informed by German techno as well as horror and science-fiction soundtracks. Das Mörtal has released material including the double single “Parasite & Ghost” (2026), the “Bury the Sorrow” and “Hotline Miami II” EPs, and the “Miami Beach Witches” album, among other releases on Bandcamp. The project has performed close to 100 shows since 2015, including more than 70 dates across the United States and Europe, at festivals such as Osheaga, Transmusicales de Rennes, FME and MEG Festival, and on tour with Vitalic, Perturbator and Carpenter Brut. “DRAIN ME” is Das Mörtal’s second single of 2026 on Lisbon Lux Records, after “Parasite & Ghost” in June.

items.body: Norwegian gothic industrial metal act Gothminister release the album “We Are All Demons” on 16 October 2026 via Elevator Records, distributed through The Orchard. The 11-track record is the project’s ninth studio album. Frontman Bjørn Alexander Brem recorded, produced, mixed and mastered “We Are All Demons” entirely himself, the first time he has handled the full process alone. Musically, the album combines gothic industrial metal with EDM elements, synthesizers, industrial guitars, theatrical vocals, female duets and choral passages. Lyrically, it addresses inner darkness and the parts of the self normally kept beneath the surface. Tracklist: Darkest Side of Earth We Are All Demons Nightmare King The Dark The Spell Welcome to Hell Salsa My Revenge Darkness Is My Throne Fearless There’s a Crown for All “We Are All Demons” follows the single “My Revenge,” released from the album on 31 July 2026. The album is available for pre-order via The Orchard’s smart link. A digipak CD edition is also listed through Napalm Records’ webshop. Gothminister has confirmed the following live dates around the release: Tour dates for Gothminister’s ‘We Are All Demons’ release 16 October 2026: Fiskepiren, Stavanger, Norway 19 November 2026: Parkteatret, Oslo, Norway 20-21 November 2026: Hellsinki Industrial Festival, Helsinki, Finland More dates are expected to be announced. About Gothminister Gothminister was formed in Oslo, Norway, in 1999 by Bjørn Alexander Brem, who handles lead vocals, programming and instruments. Guitarist Glenn Nilsen is the project’s other current member. The band’s studio discography includes “Gothic Electronic Anthems” (2003), “Empire of Dark Salvation” (2005), “Happiness in Darkness” (2008), “Anima Inferna” (2011), “Utopia” (2013), “The Other Side” (2017), “Pandemonium” (2022) and “Pandemonium II: The Battle of the Underworlds” (2024). Gothminister was also a candidate in Norway’s 2024 Eurovision Song Contest selection, Melodi Grand Prix. “We Are All Demons” follows “Pandemonium II: The Battle of the Underworlds” from 2024 and arrives 16 October 2026 via Elevator Records.

items.body: New Order released their fourth studio album, “Brotherhood,” through Factory Records on 29 September 1986. The Manchester band split the record’s two sides between guitar-driven post-punk and synth-pop electronics. “Brotherhood” turns 40 this year. New Order recorded “Brotherhood” during 1986 at Jam Studios in London, Windmill Lane Studios in Dublin and Amazon Studios in Liverpool, with Michael Johnson engineering and the band credited as its own producer. The sleeve, designed by Peter Saville, photographed a sheet of titanium-zinc alloy. The album opens with a rock-facing first side – “Paradise,” “Weirdo,” “As It Is When It Was,” “Broken Promise” and “Way of Life” – before turning electronic on side two with “Bizarre Love Triangle,” “All Day Long,” “Angel Dust” and “Every Little Counts.” “Bizarre Love Triangle” became a top 20 hit in Australia and New Zealand and remains the album’s only single. “Brotherhood” streams on Spotify. About New Order New Order formed in Manchester in 1980, after singer Ian Curtis’s death ended Joy Division, when surviving members Bernard Sumner, Peter Hook and Stephen Morris continued as a trio and were joined that October by keyboardist Gillian Gilbert. The band’s debut single, “Ceremony,” a song written in Joy Division’s final weeks, appeared in January 1981, and the debut album “Movement” followed on Factory Records that November. “Power, Corruption & Lies” (1983) pushed the band further into synthesizers and sequencers, and its non-album single “Blue Monday” became the best-selling 12-inch single in UK chart history. “Low-Life” (1985) refined that mix of guitars and electronics on tracks including “The Perfect Kiss” and “Sub-culture.” “Brotherhood” arrived on 29 September 1986, dividing its rock and dance instincts across two album sides. New Order’s early singles, including those surrounding “Brotherhood,” were gathered the following year on the compilation “Substance” (1987), and the band reached UK number one with “Technique” in 1989. New Order also co-owned Manchester’s Haçienda nightclub with Factory Records, a venture whose costs contributed to the label’s 1992 collapse alongside labelmates Happy Mondays. The band moved to London Records for “Republic” (1993), split in 1993, reunited in 1998, and released “Get Ready” in 2001. Peter Hook left in 2007 following disputes with the rest of the band, and New Order continued as a quartet, releasing “Music Complete” in 2015 and the “Be a Rebel” single and remix EP in 2020 and 2021. In 2026, Joy Division and New Order were announced as joint inductees into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, with the ceremony set for November. “Brotherhood,” the record that opened New Order’s run of transatlantic hits, turns 40 this year.

Delgado described the story behind the cover: “I was trying to embody the spirit of not exactly a dom/sub relationship, but more like a master/servant one. This story isn’t romantic in nature, but still has that sweet feeling that the characters do take care of each other.” About The Phantom Eyes The Phantom Eyes is the Seattle-based recording project of Bex Delgado, mixes darkwave and dark electronic music with post-punk elements. Delgado describes the project’s focus as horror, isolation and existential dread. The cover of DEVO’s “Puppet Boy,” released in May 2026, is one of the project’s singles; its video, filmed by Tori Kellogg and released 25 September 2026, is the most recent visual release under the project’s name.

items.body: This new release from the Belgian act Hybryds is a remarkable record. The title leaves little to the imagination, focusing—as the work of many artists across various disciplines has so often done—on the seven deadly sins. What makes this release particularly intriguing, however, is that four of the tracks date back to 2002, originally appearing on the “Lust”-EP released by Spectre. After all these years, the original singer, Miss Poly-Ester, got back in touch with Sandy Nijs and asked him to complete the album. So Sandy returned to the music, and the lost tracks were finally completed with the singer’s vocals. In total, we are treated to eleven tracks. Alongside the songs addressing the seven deadly sins, there are extras such as an intro and two live tracks dating from 2003. Hybryds has continued to surprise me in recent years. The project remains true to its trademark Ritualistic style, yet everything sounds more modern. This record stands out in particular for its slow, infectious, Trip-Hop-like rhythms. At times, I get the impression of hearing an Industrial version of Tricky—and that is very much intended as a huge compliment. After all, Hybryds naturally retains that familiar industrial DNA. The atmosphere remains dark, mysterious, and unsettling, evoking the feeling of stepping into a forbidden place where a certain decadence gradually sweeps you away. This impression is further reinforced by the artistic and highly explicit booklet accompanying the album, allowing Sandy Nijs to indulge his interest in and inspiration from fetish culture through a series of photographs that remain closely connected to the central theme. It is the kind of booklet that algorithms would rapidly detect and block instantly. Fortunately, there are still artists daring enough to go there—artists for whom it isn’t simply about nudity, provocation, or shock value. The music is far too good for that. I wouldn’t claim that Hybryds have reinvented themselves, but in recent years they have clearly been riding a new wave of inspiration, and this record is a fine example of where that has taken them. The older live tracks don’t exactly add much value, but the rest of the album is simply magnificent. As far as I’m concerned, it’s one of the best albums I’ve discovered this year. It would be a true sin to let this particular gem pass you by… (Ratring:9). Listen to “Envy”: Envy by Hybryds About Hybryds Hybryds is a Belgian project centered on Sandy Nys, active since the mid-1980s and known for ritual, mythical and industrial electronic work rooted in the cassette-era Belgian underground. Nys’ career began with the 1986 cassette “Mythical Music From The 21st Century,” followed by releases including “Music For Rituals” (1992) and “The Ritual Of The Rave” (1995). In the 1990s Hybryds became a duo with Leen Smets (Yasnaïa); from 2000 Nys continued the project solo before German vocalist Madeline joined, with multi-instrumentalist Peter De Koning later expanding the lineup. On 3RioArt / Zoharum, Hybryds has released “Mythopia” (2022), “Mythopia, The Sequel” (2024), “In The Wake Of The Witch” (2025), “Fire And Ice, Flesh And Bones Part 1 & 2” (2026) and “Desert Of White Salt” (2026). “7even Deadly Sins” follows on the same labels, reworking four tracks that originally appeared on the 2002 “Lust” EP on Spectre with new vocals by Madeline and Katherina.

items.body: Ductape Faded Flowers Swiss Dark Nights Turkish duo Ductape have been gathering a following on the basis of a steady stream of singles and albums, in a very of the moment sound. More than anything, the duo of Çağla Güleray and Furkan Güleray have found a style that sits between the gloomy darkwave of She Past Away and the more light fast-moving quirky post-punk that we’ve come to associate with Molchat Doma and their ilk, with a touch of modern electro-darkwave for taste. And while their latest LP Faded Flowers is certainly very au courant in terms of the songwriting and performances, there’s also no denying that the band have a talent for it. Listening to cuts like “Figures” or “Gölgesiz” should give a good idea of Ductape at their most straightforward; there’s a strong propulsive bassline backed by stiff kicks and gated snares, plenty of tremelo’d guitar lines and the charismatic vocals of Güleray, who imbues her low moans and whoas with plenty of muscle. It’s a sound the band never stray too far from, but keep fairly fluid, adding in some synth leads (as on the zippy “Delilik”) or touches of other styles (the italo-infused intro of “Burn”) to taste. And while the record does have a certain sameyness to it, it’s fast-moving and has enough switch-ups to keep things moving, such as placing the occasional combo-breaker like the oompah-cabaret stylings of “Velvet Dawn” into the middle of the album. That said, the band’s bag of tricks has its limits, and multiple listens will show some of their weaker tendencies. A big one would be their general production sensibility: the bass and guitar sounds don’t vary much, their drum programming leans on eighties drum machine toms for fills to the point of distraction, and Güleray, for her confidence and power always sits in the same place in the mix, always up front, never varying in dynamics or range. To that point, these songs are often short of an actually memorable hook, usually relying on simple repeated keyboard licks or a simple refrain to fill the role. The fact is that even on multiple listens songs will tend to melt into one another, with only a few really standing out by virtue of having a vastly different tempo or arrangement. “Sad Gravity” is perhaps the most interesting song simply by virtue of using some more fully-fleshed out electronics and touches of spanish guitar. You can see why folks would enjoy a record like Faded Flowers, it’s got a sound with proven appeal, performed expertly and with enough verve to wallpaper its musical shortcomings. Having it on is never unpleasant, and it’ll no doubt have folks dancing at your local goth club, but there’s simply not enough substance here to rise above perfectly fine. Ductape are a band that probably have a really good record in them, and it’ll be interesting to see how they get there from here. Buy it. items.body: Tear a piece of this and shove it hard into your mouth A lilylicker sounds like a particularly devoted suck-up, someone whose admiration has become a full-time occupation. Put the word beside Oscar Wilde’s fascination with actresses Lillie Langtry and Sarah Bernhardt, and a whole society of worshippers comes into view: flowers, flattery, beautiful women placed upon pedestals. Wilde was a cunning linguist, of course, though Patriarchy have a few suggestions about putting that talent to more practical use. The lily remains a lovely flower, though its innocence becomes somewhat harder to maintain once somebody starts licking it. The Los Angeles snuff-pop duo of Actually Huizenga and AJ English, otherwise known as The Drummer, premieres the video for Lilylicker, taken from their new EP, Appendices. Written and produced by Huizenga and English, the song takes its initial inspiration from Wilde’s devotion to those celebrated performers, then puts the woman receiving all that attention in charge of the proceedings. A menacing bass synth and a blunt kick drum set the terms, leaving Actually’s near-whispered vocal close enough to feel conspiratorial. Her poetic purr slips between the beats before the track opens into a metallic industrial-techno rhythm, bringing the hard physicality of ’90s industrial into contact with contemporary darkwave. The bass keeps its grip while crushed guitars tear through the chorus, making the move from intimate persuasion to open command feel deliciously abrupt. The words play a similar game. Wanting to be liked becomes wanting to be licked; affection, appetite, and obedience get tangled in the same exchange. Actually moves from seeking approval to prescribing exactly how it should be delivered, with an impatience that gives the song its humor. For all the literary ancestry, the central proposition is straightforward: admiration should have practical applications. Directed by Patriarchy and shot by Hazel Hill McCarthy, the video makes that business of putting people on pedestals unusually literal. Figures revolve on small platforms against an almost uninterrupted black background, their costumes and gestures exposed by direct light. Actually appears in a white gown holding lilies, in a pale pink dress draped with chains, and in a metallic corset with enormous gold wings and a guitar. English handles a skull while wearing little white wings; their young son appears in family tableaux and as a cherub perched on a classical column. The arrangements suggest devotional statues brought to life by people with their own ideas about sainthood. There is an affectionate absurdity to these living ornaments. The solemn poses give way to movement, expressions change, and the family portrait keeps interrupting the fantasy of immaculate statuary. Against all that black space, the slightest human detail becomes conspicuous. Even the insects have supporting roles. The setting came about through necessity. According to the band, the owner of their original studio location objected to the proposed content and the presence of their son, who was also appearing in the video. With the shoot abruptly displaced, the crew relocated to the Angeles woods and rethought the production outdoors. Huizenga subsequently edited the footage “happily alone and for many hours,” describing editing as “one of my secret pleasures.” “I decided not to retouch anything either. So all razor bumps, dark circles, cellulite, and sock lines are fully visible if you wish to judge me physically… I had a baby, so kill me! The boys are perfect though. A lot of the things that went ‘wrong’ ultimately added to the beauty of it, like having to shoot outside, where moths kept flying in front of our lenses, drawn in by the bright lights” For Huizenga, leaving those imperfections intact also connects to Patriarchy’s larger, apocalyptic view of power: “Patriarchy has never been about perfection, it’s about realizing we are the last remnants of human existence before AI enslaves us all; that’s why the project is called Patriarchy after all, patriarchy is the final human ruling order. Our next masters wont be women or men or human in any form, so we need to embrace our chaos and imperfections while we can.” Watch the video for Lilylicker below: Released in the wilting days of this past Summer, Appendices brings together five songs developed across different periods of the band’s life, reaching back to The Unself sessions and forward through the aftermath of 2025’s Manual For Dying. These recordings have survived abandoned versions, rewrites, and changes substantial enough to turn industrial tracks into orchestral ballads and minimal synth into metal. Alongside Lilylicker, the EP includes Bite Marks, Servile, Ode (to an Apprehensive Tyrant), and Hate Fuck, with additional production and mixing contributions across the record from Ben Chisolm and Matia Simovich. Huizenga’s reading supplies another connection between these otherwise unruly songs. Wilde, Marchesa Luisa Casati, Emperor Tiberius, and the Manson family furnish starting points for examinations of sexuality, submission, obsession, and violence. Across three full-length albums, a live record, and numerous remixes, Patriarchy have pursued those interests through industrial electronics, synth-pop, metal, and performance art. Appendices also documents Huizenga and English becoming an increasingly self-contained production team, with Lilylicker pointing toward the club without surrendering their taste for theatrical excess. That appetite for the personal and the unruly carries into Actually’s Sex and the Pity, Huizenga’s new podcast and livestream concept, whose pilot is announced for this Friday at 10 p.m. Pacific. Pitched as Elvira meeting Gore Vidal, it promises secret guests, fireside conversation, and previously untold stories from Patriarchy’s tours and beyond, forming a living journal for a future film project. “I can only really seem to recount these hilarious stories properly when I’m talking one-on-one with a cute gay at a party; so I’m gonna try to recreate that free-form energy for the podcast.” Listen to Lilylicker below and order the Appendices EP here. items.body: Does anyone read these intros? Doesn't matter; much like the blog itself, I am writing them for myself. As time goes on, I like coming back to Editors' Picks in general more and more; again, for myself. It has become clear over the past, oh let's say eight years, that what people crave more than anything is curation, voices that will help make sense of the noise. As everybody likes to point out, the blog is dead. But is it? Is not the function of the blog, and of posts like this on it, to help cut through the insanely massive number of albums out there and give you the few we think were exceptional?And you listen to us because you know us, you know our taste. And you can be 200, 500, 1,000 people. Probably not more. I mean, the blog does a lot more traffic but honest to god people who read these words? I'll take 200 any day of the week because, guess what, I also need help to cut through the noise, through the pressure of finding your audience in the accursed year of our absent lord 2026. Guess what (again)! That's you. Good job. Let's listen to some absolutely sick music together, shall we?-Eden KupermintzPhoebe Bridgers - Lost WeekendI was introduced to Phoebe Bridgers’ brilliant debut Stranger In the Alps the week after it released back in 2017, winding down for bed and looking for some new music to listen to. After listening to it, staring into the void in awe of how incredible it was, I sent it to the Heavy Blog editors and a true love affair was born. Since then, her profile has risen exponentially. I saw her live in Denver in a small, intimate venue and now she’s playing major festivals and selling out stadiums. She’s got herself a high profile boyfriend, an also great sophomore album, and plenty of cultural influence under her belt since then. That being the current situation, hype for her third record Lost Weekend was incredibly high across the music criticism spectrum. Does it hold up under the weight of those expectations? The short answer is hell yes it does. Lost Weekend feels like a culmination of sorts, blending her newfound penchant for sonic experimentation and CinemaScope stadium bangers with heartfelt acoustic crooning in a manner that is both strange and perfectly in keeping with her aesthetic. Tracks like “Lost Boys” present arena-ready vibes that match well with the expectation she established in Punisher, but there’s plenty of old school softness to be had for fans of her first album. “Kill Me,” “The Governor’s Waltz,” and the absolutely gorgeous “As Above” feel like even more fleshed out versions of tracks from Alps, with the latter in the running for the single best song she’s ever written. There’s a very personal bent to her songwriting as well, almost to an uncomfortable extent. It’s her most heart-wrenching album by a pretty wide stretch, which makes her already intimate style feel all the more palpable. Her sonic experimentation is both refreshing and a bit inconsistent, and the portion of her songwriting growth that probably needs the most work. I could absolutely do without the strange interlude “Never Going Back!” but her principal strength is adding new bells and whistles to songs that exist within her more traditional structure. Album opener “The Outside” is a much better example of the highs she’s capable of reaching in this regard, with the juxtaposition of her robotic auto-tuned vocals mixed with her clean, fragile clean vocals as an exposition on grief works incredibly well, and I’d love to see her follow this path more steadily as her career continues. While Alps will always be closest to my heart when it comes to her discography, Lost Weekend comes awfully close to eclipsing it in many ways. It’s a special album that has several genuinely gorgeous and potentially career-defining tracks that are among the best of her career, and I have been enamored with it since it dropped. There’s a high likelihood that this ends up as a high-end lister for me in December, and I can easily recommend it to folks who’ve enjoyed her output thus far and anyone who’s into the sad girl wave of the 2020s. Brilliant stuff.  Lost Weekend by Phoebe Bridgers -Jonathan AdamsMastodon - Marrow DeepKnowing when to walk away from a band is an important skill to master, not only because it saves you from wasting your time on music you don't like but also because it keeps a chance alive that you'll ever return to said band. If you just keep forcing yourself to give their music a try, you'll develop resentment. This will keep you from enjoying any future release, even if quality rebounds at some point. Luckily, I am well versed in this skill, honed by years of listening to bands I once loved grow stale. Therefore, on the rare occasion that they do end up figuring things out and going back to making great music, my ears are fresh and I can enjoy these better releases, unburdened by resentment.I deployed this skill on Mastodon years ago. Don't get me wrong, Emperor of Sand is fine, even good, and Hushed and Grim had some great ideas hiding within its monstrously long runtime. But yeah, to state the obvious, they're no Blood Mountain or Crack the Skye or...you get it. And that's exactly the point, who wants to read me write that sentence release after release? Certainly not me! So I let bygones be bygones and didn't much listen to new Mastodon releases beyond a single or two. Until Marrow Deep where, suddenly, my ears were able to pick up on the fact that Mastodon is fucking BACK baby! It's not that the sound is so different to Emperor of Sand or H&G. Rather, the balance is back. The album feels tight, essential, devoid of fat, heavy hitting in its insistence to not choose between groovy stoner metal and more progressive sounds.Which is the whole fucking point of Mastodon, right? The whole idea is that they invented, or helped popularize really, progressive stoner metal, that they were masters of walking the tight beam between big, rocking riffs, and winding, complex compositions. Even if you loved the last two releases, you can't really argue with me when I say that was mostly gone in favor of the Big Riff. Which, if you love Big Riff, is great but it's not why I listened to Mastodon, thanks very much. And so, Marrow Deep returns Mastodon to exactly that - why I listen to them. It's definitely not the early releases and it never will be and I don't want it to be. I just want to hear Mastodon make good, interesting music and now, they have again! Marrow Deep by Mastodon -EKKilling Of A Sacred Deer - Encephalic AngelsWhile the old-school deathcore revival sound has grown a lot of momentum in recent years, many bands seem more focused on trying to replicate what was done before rather than trying to make something that's actually fresh and original. Even that Thus Spoke Zarathustra album from last year that was well executed and widely acclaimed was arguably too much of a homage, with several riffs nearly copy-pasted from As Blood Runs Black. This year in particular hasn’t offered a lot to get excited about for us fair-weather deathcore fans. That is, up until the latest album from Killing of a Sacred Deer, Encephalic Angels. Put simply, they understood the assignment. It feels influenced by that “myspace scene” without worshipping it, combining this with the strengths of modern bands in the genre, death metal itself, and dashes of mathcore. This is easily the strongest deathcore record of 2026, and one those apprehensive of the genre might just want to give a shot. It’s impossible to avoid talking about production with deathcore discourse, so let's start there. Encephalic Angels bring some of the noisy roughness from the roots of the genre, while keeping enough of a punchy sharpness and booming low end to convey that sense of heaviness that modern fans have grown accustomed to. The snare still sounds like one of those big red bouncy gym balls, but it’s not drowning out a Line 6 Spider. This combined with plenty of variation across their tracks allows for a reasonably dynamic listening experience. It has the riffage and violent frenetic energy of Through the Eyes of the Dead, combined with the earth-shaking heaviness of modern groups like Brand of Sacrifice. It’s not shocking to learn that this band shares members with Alberta mathcore group Abrupt Decay, as the technicality and time-signatures get appropriately spastic and unpredictable, avoiding that feeling of overstaying it’s welcome that deathcore albums can sometimes fall into. There’s a certain unhinged viciousness. Things feel uncalculated, untethered, just unfolding chaotically in front of you. Yet they’re not afraid to bask in the vile. Tracks like “Cognitive Reconfiguration” capture this really menacing, suffocating atmosphere in its relentlessness. A lot of that has to do with their aptitude for writing death metal, and the way that leeches into this release is a big factor in its quality.The vocals here do less of the heavy lifting compared to most deathcore, but still serve a prominent role and fulfill that in stride. They’re not training for the deathcore vocal olympics, and in a more death metal fashion, are fit in to serve the instrumentation, and the songwriting itself. They range from moments of higher-pitched, almost Knocked Loose like wailing which are much more digestible in the short doses here, to more typical lower deathcore gutturals. Killing of a Sacred Deer has shown steady growth since their formation two years ago, and now with three releases in that short span have truly cemented themselves at the forefront of a genre that has been desperate for some fresh faces. Encephalic Angels by Killing Of A Sacred Deer -Trent BosFurther ListeningPapangu - CelestialMost works of music get better with time but that's doubly (or even triply!) true for progressive music. Papangu's Celestial has so much going on in it, like all of their releases, that I have been spending the last few weeks unravelling it slowly in my head, like a good glass of scotch. I think I have about 40% of it figured out and I can't wait to spend even more time getting that number up. Celestial by Papangu -EKWarforged - The Grove | AlmanacAfter several line-up changes, this is not quite the same band who brought us the blackened tech death of their debut EP or the progressive death metal brilliance of their 2019 LP. What it is, is a surprisingly unique take at progressive deathcore, showing refreshing incorporations of post-metal into a dissonant atmosphere-driven release with a continuously murky and haunted aura. The Grove | Almanac by Warforged -TBDorena - KvarIf you need to take a break from dissonant brutality, I can’t recommend a better new release than the comeback album from Sweden’s Dorena. Their first in 13-years, Kvar is the perfect “running through flowers” album of late summer. Stocked full of gorgeous instrumental post-rock melodies and cinematic build-ups, it encapsulates everything that I come back to this genre for: the full spectrum of the human-experience sinking in from your ears to your heart. items.album: 【東京】建築展覧会 2026「the lives of ephemeral form──建築の不確かな生を記録する」
items.tags: art sound art contemporary music improvisation
items.excerpt: 東京・建築博物館にて、日本建築学会140周年企画として、建築展覧会「the lives of ephemeral form──建築の不確かな生を記録する」が開催されます。 本展は、建築そのものだけでなく、それを記録してきたフィルムやVHS、写真、図面などもまた、媒体の劣化や再生環境の消失によって失われうる存在であることに着目しています。2か年にわたって「記録する行為」について出展者と共に向き合うプログラムとなっており、その第1期として、出展者とキュレーターによる展示、映像上映、トーク、ガイド、公開作業が行なわれます。 ＜出展者＞ 青山道乃（長谷川逸子・建築計画工房）、印牧岳彦（神奈川大学特別助教）、高野ユリカ、塩崎太伸＋小林佐絵子（アトリエコ）、篠田優（明治大学助教）、Book Shop Boys ＜キュレーター＞ 桂川大（STUDIO 大／おどり場代表）、稲垣晴夏（records from nowhere共同主宰／東京藝術大学教育研究助手） フォーラム ■Talk Program TALK 01「建てる、住まう、映すこと」｜2026/10/02（金）20:00〜21:30 ゲスト：鈴

items.album: 山﨑健太｜東京演劇アンサンブル『魔法老女ポストキュア』
items.tags: art sound art contemporary music improvisation
items.excerpt: 会期：2026/07/24〜2026/07/27 会場：吉祥寺シアター［東京都］ 作：西尾佳織 演出：小森明子 公式サイト：http://www.tee.co.jp/wordpress_3/?p=3577 親／子であるとはどういうことか。鳥公園の西尾佳織が初めて外部に書き下ろし台本を提供した東京演劇アンサンブル『魔法老女ポストキュア』（演出：小森明子）は、そんな問いと向き合う作品だった。ひとまずはそう言うことができるだろう。 ある日、高校生のマヤ（林亜里子）は目が覚めると老女になっていた。どうやらマヤの意識は母・サナ（洪美玉）の母、つまりはマヤの祖母・カエデ（志賀澤子）の体に宿っているらしい。目の前には高校生姿のサナ。突然現われた妖精・マルル（奈須弘子）によれば、マヤは魔法老女ポストキュアとなり、何らかの理由で崩壊しつつあるサナの記憶の世界にいるのだという。サナが救われれば元の世界に戻れるのでは？ と言われたマヤは、魔法老女の先輩・ミズホ（真野季節）とともにサナを救うために彼女の同級生として高校に潜り込みサナをサポートしようとするのだが──。 ［撮影：松浦範子］ 物語の前半はサナの学校
items.body: 会期：2026/07/24〜2026/07/27 会場：吉祥寺シアター［東京都］ 作：西尾佳織 演出：小森明子 公式サイト：http://www.tee.co.jp/wordpress_3/?p=3577 親／子であるとはどういうことか。鳥公園の西尾佳織が初めて外部に書き下ろし台本を提供した東京演劇アンサンブル『魔法老女ポストキュア』（演出：小森明子）は、そんな問いと向き合う作品だった。ひとまずはそう言うことができるだろう。 ある日、高校生のマヤ（林亜里子）は目が覚めると老女になっていた。どうやらマヤの意識は母・サナ（洪美玉）の母、つまりはマヤの祖母・カエデ（志賀澤子）の体に宿っているらしい。目の前には高校生姿のサナ。突然現われた妖精・マルル（奈須弘子）によれば、マヤは魔法老女ポストキュアとなり、何らかの理由で崩壊しつつあるサナの記憶の世界にいるのだという。サナが救われれば元の世界に戻れるのでは？ と言われたマヤは、魔法老女の先輩・ミズホ（真野季節）とともにサナを救うために彼女の同級生として高校に潜り込みサナをサポートしようとするのだが──。 ［撮影：松浦範子］ 物語の前半はサナの学校生活を中心に進んでいく。マヤはそのなかで母であるサナの高校時代の姿を目の当たりにし、そしてサナが母・カエデとの間に確執を抱えていたのを知ることになる。それは子としての、ひとりの人間としての母の姿を知ることでもあるだろう。一方、サナの学校生活はポストキュアのサポートのおかげで円滑に進むが、それでもマヤは元の世界に戻ることができない。それどころかやがて、ブルセラと援交の話をきっかけにサヤと友人のアキ（原口久美子）、そしてヤヨイ（町田聡子）との仲がぎくしゃくしはじめてしまう。しかも、そんなときに限って魔法は効果を発揮しない。そう、魔法は何でもできるわけではない。「魔法は、その人の願いと、それを助けたいと思ったポストキュアの願いが重なったときに発動する」ものなのであり、救われたいと思っていない人間を救うことはできないのだ。 これは魔法のみならず現実における真理でもあり得る。例えば親と子。両者の思いはときに絶望的にすれ違う。だからこそカエデとサナの間には大きな溝が生まれてしまった。サナとマヤとの間にも同じように、しかし違ったかたちで溝が生まれてしまっている。 ［撮影：松浦範子］ ［撮影：松浦範子］ 後半で明かされるのは、実は現実のマヤが事故で生死の境を彷徨っており、そのことがサナを苦しめているということだ。学校に通えなくなり、引きこもっていたマヤは、サナとの口論の末に家を飛び出し、そして事故に遭ってしまったのだった。カエデはそんなサナを苦しみから救うためにマヤを生の側へと引き戻そうとしていたのだが、それを知ったマヤはサナの側から見た一方的な物語を押し付けるなとカエデを拒絶する。「弱者のつもりで、正義のつもりで、わたしの声は聞こうともしない」というマヤの言葉は痛烈だ。そしてマヤの側から見た物語が語られる。 では、マヤの願いとは何か。改めて問われた彼女は「お母さんと他人になりたい」と答える。それに対して「家族なんてもともと他人じゃない」と応じるカエデ。マヤは「考えたことなかった、家族が他人なんて」と驚くが、やがて「わたしはわたしの人生を生きたい。から、お母さんにも、自分の人生を生きてほしい」と改めて願いを告げる。その願い自体は「魔法で人の心を変えてはいけない」というルールに抵触するからと却下されてしまうものの、代わりにサナを海外旅行に送り出すというささやかな願いを叶えるかたちで、親子それぞれの生の時間が実現して物語は幕を閉じる。 ［撮影：松浦範子］ ［撮影：松浦範子］ 拍子抜けとも思える結末である。マヤが抱えていた問題も、それを母親であるサナとの関係に限定したとしても、一時的に緩和されたに過ぎないように思える。だが、そのようにあるしかないのだ。家族もまた他人なのだという気づきがあったことはもちろん重要である。しかしそれを知識として知ることと実感をもって理解することとはまた別の話であり、さらに関係を変えていくには相応の時間がかかる。だから、いずれにせよそこはマヤにとってはスタート地点に過ぎない。 この結末においてもうひとつ重要なことは、魔法が問題を完全に解決することはなく、問題解決に向けたきっかけとしてしか機能していないということだろう。誰かを救いたいという願いがその誰か自身の救われたいという願いと一致し、そして救いが与えられることは、ほとんど奇跡のようなことであり、だからこそそれは魔法と呼ばれるのだ。 整理しきれていない部分もあるように感じられるものの（たとえば一個人としての母を知っていく前半と、母もまた他人であるという真理に辿り着く後半とはもう少し有機的に接続できたのではないだろうか）、西尾は鳥公園での創作とはまったく違った台本を書き上げ、自身の新たな可能性を開いて見せた。本作における救いをめぐるテーマは西尾作品としては第62回岸田國士戯曲賞最終候補作となった『ヨブ呼んでるよ』（2017）とも通底するが、それを魔法というかたちで取り出してみせた点にこの作品のユニークさとある種の逆説がある。外部への台本提供は、西尾が継続して取り組んできている問題系に新たな角度から光を当てるよい機会にもなったのではないだろうか。 ［撮影：松浦範子］ 観賞日：2026/08/10（月） 関連リンク 『ヨブ呼んでるよ -Hey God, Job’s calling you!-』（2023）舞台映像：https://youtu.be/DFus-knNKi8?si=nDE1FTpDNz3qVGIT

items.body: 展覧会カタログ、アートやデザインにまつわる近刊書籍をアートスケープ編集部が紹介します。 図録「ぬけみち展 かわす・つくる・ともにいる─生きるための回路」 企画・編集：高橋由佳（アーツ前橋） 寄稿：阿部航太、高野ユリカ、SIDE CORE、坂本舞ニルセン、鈴木哲生、ドットアーキテクツ、三野新、山本卓卓、青田麻未、川勝真一、川上幸之介、水野大二郎 発行：BNN 発行日：2026年08月06日 サイズ：A5判、128ページ 2026年7月4日からアーツ前橋で開催される「ぬけみち展」の公式図録。「ぬけみち」とは、不安や閉塞感が覆う現代に対して、実践者たちが「この場所・この社会」をわずかにひらく文化実践のこと。…本図録では、展示作家たちによるテキスト、および研究者による論考・対話を掲載。 ［発行元ウェブサイトより］ 隈研吾 場所の建築 著者：隈研吾（序文／グレース・ラ） 訳者：井原恵子 発行：グラフィック社 発行日：2026年08月10日 サイズ：A4変形、352ページ 世界的建築家・隈研吾による2011年から2024年までの主要40プロジェクトをまとめた最新作品集。 国立競技場、角川武蔵野ミュージアム、オドゥンパザル現代美術館、UCCA陶美術館、中橋など、国内外の公共建築、文化施設、美術館、都市空間を横断的に取り上げ、建築が単なる構造物ではなく、人の行動や交流、記憶を生み出す「場所」となる過程を示す。 ［発行元ウェブサイトより］ 増補 記憶のエチカ──戦争・哲学・アウシュヴィッツ 著者：高橋哲哉 発行：岩波書店 発行日：2026年08月18日 サイズ：A6判、390ページ 「出来事の衝撃にさらされることなしに、歴史一般を論じることは空しい。出来事から出発し、出来事をめぐって哲学することをわたしは夢見ている」──証言不可能性、「忘却の政治」、〈アウシュヴィッツ〉という、物語りを拒む凄惨な出来事。「忘却への罠」がもたらす幾重ものアポリアをくぐり抜けながら、記憶の倫理を探る。 ［発行元ウェブサイトより］   元学芸員の美大教員が教える美術鑑賞の楽しみ方 著者：ちいさな美術館の学芸員 発行：イースト・プレス 発行日：2026年08月26日 サイズ：四六判、248ページ 「そもそも美術って何？」という素朴な疑問から、作家や名品の鑑賞のコツまで、知っていれば鑑賞が楽しくなるポイントを紹介！ この本を読んで見方がわかれば、美術館にもっと行きたくなる！ 元美術館の学芸員で現在は美大の教員になった著者が教える、美術がわからない人のための鑑賞入門！ ［発行元ウェブサイトより］   日本デザイン文化史──モダニズム・大衆化・日本らしさ 著者：井上雅人 発行：河出書房新社 発行日：2026年08月27日 サイズ：新書判、320ページ 幕末・明治維新、消費社会黎明期、第二次大戦前後、高度成長期、バブル……デザインを社会の中での運動と捉え、モダン・大衆的・日本的の三つの視点から、日本近代の文化や生活の変化、社会の変質を描く。 ［発行元ウェブサイトより］   近代日本陶芸史──ゲテモノからニセモノ、そして現代アートへ 著者：藤原貞朗 発行：講談社 発行日：2026年09月10日 サイズ：四六判、288ページ いまや「日本人だけが知らない現代アート」と世界で賞される日本陶芸は、実は昭和元年から現代アートであり続けてきた。 柳宗悦は「下手もの」に内なる美を見出し、 民藝派を批判する魯山人は古陶を「コッピー」し、 加藤唐九郎は「永仁の壺」というシミュラクルで人々を幻惑した。 さらに「前衛陶芸」「オブジェ焼き」「モダニズム陶芸」を経て、桃山以来の磁場をもつ「茶碗」をもポストモダン化するほどの、表現が渦巻き爆発するカオスが現出している。 フォルムの美を追究し日本・近代を内破する陶芸家たちの百年史。 ［発行元ウェブサイトより］ キュレーション主義──いかにしてキュレーションはアートから世界までを席巻したのか 著者：デイヴィッド・バルザー 訳者：牧尾晴喜 発行：草思社 発行日：2026年09月11日 サイズ：四六判、272ページ 美術作品からSNSまで、キュレーションはどのように誕生し、私たちの世界を支配するに至ったのか。キュレーションの過去から未来までを占う、刺激的な一冊！ ［発行元ウェブサイトより］   解築学──解体から始まる建築と構成材の循環デザイン 編著：松村秀一、輿石直幸、権藤智之 ほか 発行：学芸出版社 発行日：2026年09月25日 サイズ：A5判、300ページ 建物ストック時代を迎え、現代の建築行為はまず解体から始まる。ないから建てるという近代建築学から、解体された既存建物の循環に挑む新建築学=解築学への転換である。改修・解体技術、マテリアルの性能評価や循環デザイン、都市制度、建設経済を再整理し循環型社会における建築の新たな学問領域を15の先進事例と共に示す ［発行元ウェブサイトより］

items.body: 富山県美術館の前身である富山県立近代美術館は、1981年の開館から2016年の閉館まで35年にわたり、展覧会のポスターを永井一正氏に依頼してきました。その数は約250点にものぼります。永井氏は、自主制作である「LIFE」シリーズにも、いつしか同館の英称を添えるようになりました。こうした同館との関わりから永井氏の仕事をたどる追悼展示（2026年4～7月開催）を、担当した学芸員の内藤和音さんが振り返ります。（artscape編集部）   永井一正氏の訃報を受けて 2026年2月23日、永井一正氏が逝去された。1929年生まれ、終生現役でグラフィックデザインの世界の第一線を走り続けた伝説的なデザイナーだった。 それからおよそ2カ月後の本年4月から7月にかけて「デザインコレクション展I ポスター・ライフ 追悼 永井一正 富山県立近代美術館・富山県美術館への仕事から」と題した小さな展示を、当館デザイン・コレクション展（常設展）の2026年度第一期のテーマとして開催した。 富山県美術館開館から4年目の年に入職した私は、永井氏にはお会いしたことはおろか、声を聞いたことさえなかった。当館で永井氏のことをよく知る、旧・富山県立近代美術館（以下、富山近美）時代より勤務し、仕事をご一緒した職員は皆、敬意を込めて「永井先生」と呼ぶ。そう呼ぶのは、永井先生が富山近美が開館した1981年から閉館した2016年までのおよそ35年にわたり、自身の作風を前面に打ち出した展覧会ビジュアルの数々を制作してくださったことを大きな誇りとしているからだろう。本記事でも敬意を込めて、永井先生と呼びたい。 来年、当館は富山近美が移転新築し、富山県美術館となってから10周年を迎える。この機会に何かのイベントとして永井先生を再びお招きすることができると良いねと、そんな世間話をしていた矢先の訃報だった。訃報が飛び込んできたとき、私は、2026年4月初旬から始まるデザイン・コレクション展の担当者として、同時期の企画展に関連したテーマのもとにポスターと椅子のコレクションをセレクトしようと、展示作品の検討を進めていた。訃報に接したとき、強い使命感が胸に生じた。誰かに言われたわけでもなかったと思うが、このとき以外にいつ永井先生を取り上げるべきときがあるだろうか、そんな思いだった。 1980年代の富山県立近代美術館開館から、2010年代の閉館までのほぼすべてのポスターを一人のグラフィックデザイナーが担ったこと自体が稀有だが、そのグラフィックにおいても旧富山県立近代美術館の展覧会ポスターのシリーズは一線を画する特徴がある。一般的に展覧会のポスターには、展覧会名と作品画像、作家の肖像写真などを大きくレイアウトすることが基本的な画面構成だと思われる。だが、永井先生のポスターは、幾何学的な図形と色の組み合わせや、後の「LIFE」シリーズに見られるような生き物の姿が目をひくデザインなど、展覧会の告知という美術館をクライアントとするポスターの第一の目的に加え、一人のデザイナー、永井一正の自由な表現がなされる場でもあったのだ。 そうした類稀なポスター群や関連資料を有する当館だからこそ可能な展示があり、なおかつ、（僭越ながら）制作当時を知らない世代ゆえにできる構成に挑んでみたいと思った。 展示室入口側には、1981年の開館のポスターと2016年の閉館記念展のポスターを並べて展示した 記録映像に見る、制作の現場と信念 展示では、1966年のワルシャワ国際ポスタービエンナーレで日本人としてはじめて金賞を受賞したポスターや、札幌オリンピックのシンボルマークをはじめとする「クライアントワークのポスター」、そして「富山県立近代美術館の展覧会ポスター」、転換点とされるポスターシリーズ「JAPAN」、ライフワークとなったポスターシリーズ「LIFE」の4つの章で構成した。 このほか、富山近美時代に制作された、インタビューを中心とするドキュメント映像が5本ある。最も古い映像は、1984年に当館のポスターを制作する様子を取材したもので、永井先生が原案となるラフを描き、それをもとに烏口や写真植字の手法で文字を切り貼りして版下原稿を作る模様が映像に残されていた。一言でデザインするといっても、アシスタントの方々や各工程の職人たちの手の技を結集させ、長い時間をかけて紙の上にグラフィックデザインが組み上げられていた。 この頃の永井先生のポスターは、幾何学的に組み合わされた直線や、鮮やかな原色のグラデーションが目を引く。まるで初期のコンピュータが描いた3次元空間のような構成による作風だった。すべての工程を液晶画面の中で完結できる今となっては、たやすく思えるような作業でも、想像も及ばぬほどの緻密な手作業の組み合わせによって制作されていた。 ドキュメント映像より。版下を制作するスタッフとラフスケッチを前に打ち合わせする永井先生 ドキュメント映像より。版下を制作する様子 2014年に富山近美で開催された個展「永井一正 POSTER LIFE 1957-2014」展に併せて制作されたドキュメント映像では、長く富山近美の展覧会ポスターを担うことになった理由や、意識していたことを語っている。 「（富山県立近代美術館初代館長の小川正隆氏は）一人のデザイナーに長く展覧会のグラフィックデザインを担わせることで、美術館の（当時はデザイン・ポリシーと呼んでいた）ブランディングとしてイメージを確立したいという思いがあったのだと思う。そう言われるからには、特徴づけるため、僕の個性を100パーセント出した。グループ展ならむしろ僕のイメージでやる方がいいだろうし、個展であっても僕の一貫したデザイン・ポリシーが被さって一体となりながら、作家の特質をより強調していくという方法をとった」 展覧会はその時々に美術館の顔として大々的に広報が展開される。その顔とも呼べるポスターを、永井先生は信念をもって、あえて情報伝達のためのグラフィックデザインに留まらないポスターを制作し続けた。富山近美の展覧会ポスターは、いわゆるクライアントワークだが、自身の世界観を前面に出すことが許された、クリエイターにとっては理想的な仕事のようにも感じられる。反面、展覧会の企画や作品、作家の名のもつ訴求力に頼らずに、自分の力量のみによって観る者の関心を惹きつけなければならず、とても重い責任を引き受けることでもあった。 インタビュー映像の中の永井先生は、静かで淡々とした語り口ながらも、その言葉には、自らのグラフィックデザインへの自信と、重責への覚悟がにじんでいた。 2014年に開催された「永井一正 POSTER LIFE 1957-2014」展のインタビュー映像より 「JAPAN」から「LIFE」へ———生き物たちの眼差し 1987年の、亀倉雄策氏、福田繁雄氏、田中一光氏との富山近美での展覧会「4-G.D ポスターとマーク」をきっかけに制作された「JAPAN」シリーズ以降、永井先生の作風はそれまでとは大きく変化を遂げ、真っすぐにこちらを見つめる目をもった生き物の姿が現われ始める。そうした生き物は、富山近美のポスターでも、子どもたちの作品の展覧会や、現代美術のグループ展、個展「永井一正展」（1990）にも登場した。 「永井一正展」ポスター（1990） 2000年代に入ると、人の手の痕跡を感じる細かな線と色面のグラデーションにより、クマやゾウ、時には虫のような生き物が見られるようになる。この頃、永井先生は銅版画の技法に興味を寄せ、ポスターの中でも盛んに自作の銅版画をグラフィックに取り入れていた。 デザインや印刷の工程でコンピュータが担う部分が拡大し、かつての版下から写植、印刷へと分業された職人技の連携が過去のものとなりつつあったこの時代に、あえて印刷技術の基本とも言える版画に立ち返ることで生まれた作品には、人間のコントロールの及ばぬ掠れや滲みに、生き物の生命の強さが感じられ、何よりコンピュータによるグラフィックからは生まれない新鮮さがあった。 少しさかのぼり、ライフワークとなる「LIFE」シリーズの制作が始まる。当初は、銅版画により描かれた、野生味を感じる鋭い眼差しをもったチーターや鳥のような生き物と、画面の片隅に小さく「LIFE」の4文字が記されていた。このポスターはクライアントワークではなく、永井先生の自主制作作品である。「LIFE」は生命、生涯、生活のように多義的だが、生きとし生けるものに普遍的に当てはまる言葉をテーマとして、その尊さに気づかせ、讃えるようなポスターのシリーズである。 いつしか、「LIFE」シリーズには画面内に富山近美の英称「Toyama Prefectural Museum of Modern Art」と加えられるようになった。これは、当館から依頼して加わったわけではない。生前、永井先生の口から直接にこの文字列が加えられた理由は語られず、当時を知る職員に聞いても、残された映像からもこの経緯は正確にはわからない。いわば、富山近美への継続的な贈り物と言ってよいかもしれない。 仮説を立てるならば、35年にわたって年に4〜5本という頻度で当館の展覧会のポスターを手がけてきた永井先生は、仮想のクライアントとして当館を意識し、館名を含め画面構成を考えたのではないだろうか。そうしたことから、本展のタイトルに「富山県立近代美術館・富山県美術館への仕事から」という副題を添えた。展示室では最も長い壁に選りすぐった「LIFE」シリーズのポスターを並べた。展示作業が終わり、「LIFE」が並ぶ光景を見たとき、画面の中の生き物たちがこちらに向ける視線が自分に向けて集まってくるようで、内心、動物的な怯えさえ感じた。同時に、このポスターのタイトルは「LIFE」のほかに考えられないと確信した。 展示室内の横長の壁面には「LIFE」シリーズを展示。3枚1組で制作されることが多いが、本展では選りすぐった14点を展示した 永井先生が創り出した美術館の顔とともに 本展では、富山近美のポスターを軸に、4つの章に分けて41点展示した。生涯で制作したポスターを時系列に並べ、作者の視点や興味の移り変わり、制作手段の技術的な変化を見られる構成を目指したが、概ねその目論見は果たされたように思う。 展示室の端には、過去のインタビューなどから抜粋した映像を放映するモニターを設置した。その向かいには、当館の椅子のコレクションを展示するエリアがあり、その中に、永井先生が好んで仕事場あるいは自宅に置いていたアルネ・ヤコブセンのエッグ・チェアを展示した。画面の向こうでは、そのエッグ・チェアに腰掛けた40年前の永井先生が当時の日本のポスターの特徴を語っていた。 永井先生の穏やかな声が展示室を漂う。一つの美術館で一人のデザイナーが、それぞれ異なる性格をもつ、展覧会の顔とも言えるポスターを、およそ250点手がけた。やがて、ポスターの中に力強い眼差しの生き物を描き、デザイナーが生涯を終えるまで、このシリーズは毎年制作し続けられた。 同じ展示室内の20世紀の名作椅子を展示する一角。映像の中で永井先生が同時代の日本人のデザイナーとして名前をあげた剣持勇や倉俣史朗の椅子も並んだ 永井先生は、富山県立近代美術館が富山県美術館に生まれ変わる際、新しい美術館のロゴマークを手がけた。これが当館のための最後の仕事だった。これからも当館は永井先生の創り出した顔とともに歩んでゆく。 限られた資料、限られた時間の中で構成した小さな展示が、拙く、ささやかな構成ながらも、かつてこの美術館と永井先生がグラフィックデザインを通じて行った新しい試みを改めて伝える機会となり、これまでのご縁に報いる場となったならば幸いである。 「デザインコレクション展I ポスター・ライフ――追悼 永井一正 富山県立近代美術館・富山県美術館への仕事から」 会期：2026年04月09日（木）～2026年07月14日（火） 会場：富山県美術館 3階 展示室5（富山県富山市木場町3-20） 公式サイト：https://tad-toyama.jp/exhibition-event/20418 ※記事内に登場するドキュメント映像は、富山県美術館内の映像コーナーで視聴可能

items.album: John Coltrane 100: Exploring the Archives
items.excerpt: John Coltrane - One Down, One Up: Live At the Half Note (recorded 1965, released 2005), My Favorite Things: Coltrane At Newport (recorded 1963 and 1965, released 2007), Offering: Live At Temple University (recorded 1966, released 2014), A Love Supreme: Live In Seattle (recorded 1965, released 2021), Evenings At the Village Gate: John Coltrane with Eric Dolphy (recorded 1961, released 2023) By Lee Rice Epstein 1965 was remarkably transformative year in Coltrane’s history. Thankfully, through its
items.body: John Coltrane - One Down, One Up: Live At the Half Note (recorded 1965, released 2005), My Favorite Things: Coltrane At Newport (recorded 1963 and 1965, released 2007), Offering: Live At Temple University (recorded 1966, released 2014), A Love Supreme: Live In Seattle (recorded 1965, released 2021), Evenings At the Village Gate: John Coltrane with Eric Dolphy (recorded 1961, released 2023) By Lee Rice Epstein 1965 was remarkably transformative year in Coltrane’s history. Thankfully, through its ongoing archival releases, Impulse Records has continued to fill in the picture of how, as an artist, he continually pushed himself and his band, deeply and passionately giving his all at all times. One Down, One Up takes us right to March 26, 1965, where Coltrane, McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison, and Elvin Jones play an astonishingly high-wire, high-energy “One Down, One Up” that runs nearly 30 minutes. The electricity crackling between players says exactly why Coltrane still matters, why he’s still adored, and why countless players of all kinds continue to study and revere him. The set’s recapitulation on the Newport stage months later (the second half of My Favorite Things: Coltrane At Newport ), more clearly shows how the group was thinking about and working through their headiest ideas. That the Newport set was released with a 1963 performance featuring Roy Haynes in the drummer seat gives some additional dimensions to the quartet’s changes over time. Tyner and Jones moved on by the next year, while Garrison held down the Alice Coltrane, Rashied Ali, and Pharoah Sanders group. Reportedly, he didn’t play with them in the fall of 1966, when Coltrane led a phenomenal set at Temple University. Offering has been alternately reviled and lauded, cited by some as a polished but unnecessary bootleg for completists only. But, if one just takes a step back and considers Offering happening the same season as Albert Ayler’s seminal European tour—with the quintet of Ayler, Donald Ayler, Michel Samson, Bill Folwell, and Beaver Harris—and if one wants to get really interested in sympathetic wavelengths, you hear Coltrane singing reportedly for the first time ever during “Leo” on November 11, 1966, while Ayler was recorded doing the same on a performance of Sanders’s “Japan” the previous night, November 10, 1966. That Ayler later screamed during his memorial performance for Coltrane would be too on the nose if someone manufactured it. The two shared both intellectual and spiritual bonds, a beautiful thing we’re scarcely able to know of or understand even partly. As the saying goes, it would have been enough to get these first three albums, but the 2020s has produced two seemingly impossible sessions: a live recording of “A Love Supreme,” also from 1965, and an unissued session with Eric Dolphy from 1961, featuring “Greensleeves” and “Africa.” What, truly can be said about Coltrane and Dolphy that doesn’t lead to a mountain of what-if or if-only hypotheticals? The hour-plus set is fiery and rich with ideas in motion. If someone told me this was 1963 or ’64, I wouldn’t doubt it. By ’61, both Coltrane and Dolphy were already well out in front of many contemporaries, and the mutual support demonstrated during their brief time together is beautifully realized here. On A Love Supreme (fascinatingly, recorded a couple days after Live In Seattle), Coltrane leads a kind of crossover group, with Tyner, Garrison, and Jones as the core quartet, joined on the tour by Sanders and Donald Garrett on bass, with Carlos Ward jumping in on sax at Coltrane’s invitation. Both Coltrane and Sanders add percussion along with Jones’s drumming, and if Offering represents some kind of approaching end point in Coltrane’s art, the Seattle performance of “A Love Supreme” leads in the same direction, ever forward. items.tags: 映画／映像 intoxicate 2026 August 映画／映像 # 映画 映画／映像 ペドロ・コスタ

items.body: Label: Burning Ambulance Records, 2026 Personnel - Wadada Leo Smith: trumpet; Sylvie Courvoisier: piano (#1,3); Marcus Gilmore: drums (#1,3); Bobby Naughton: vibraphone (#2-5); Lamar Smith: electric guitar (#2,3,5); Bill Laswell: electric bass (#3,4); Melvin Gibbs: electric bass (#3,4); Mauro Refosco: percussion (#2,3,5); Brian Jawara Gray: percussion (#2,3,5); Pheeroan akLaff: drums (#2-5). Trumpeter and composer Wadada Leo Smith assembled various ensembles for his new album, Constellations and Hemispheres , rooted in harmonic intensity, open structures, and modal depth. The project was sparked by quantum physics, parallel universes, and shifting dimensions, in a no-nonsense approach that explores timbre and atmosphere with serious intentions and exceptional versatility. The album kicks off in trio format, with Smith joining forces with the quick-witted pianist Sylvie Courvoisier and adaptable drummer Marcus Gilmore on “ Dark Energy ”. Cymbal activity is paired with sparse piano texture, while Smith's declamations extend from sharply piercing to dolefully lugubrious. This mournful reflection swells and intensifies via Courvoisier's phenomenal work, expanding and contracting by way of intricately coiling patterns that work as a perfect foil for Smith's obscure idioms. Gilmore is granted a brief unaccompanied passage. " Lake Tanganyika " emerged from a sextet session with trumpet, vibraphone, guitar, percussion, and drums. Ancient, water-surrounded landscapes are evoked via the emotionally powerful lyricism brought by Smith over Bobby Naughton's gossamer vibes and Pheeroan AkLaff's gloriously relentless drum flow. The seasoned drummer also gets our attention on the closer, " Meditation on Love ", a cosmic, open-ended manifesto of peace and hope. Smith traces a spiritual and artistic connection with the Rastafari—associated with the reggae music of Jamaica—but I'm unable to spot that influence here. Yet the music is able to knife through the speakers like a lightning bolt. " Dark Matters, Particles of Light, Mirror of the Unseen " is a full-length workout clocking in at 22 minutes. Powerful and moody, the piece is bookended by the same trio that had shaped the opening track, expanding in its middle part into an octet featuring two distinguished electric bassists, Bill Laswell and Melvin Gibbs, who contribute to the dismal, apocalyptic scenario with authority. A lighter, tactile percussive quality appears by the end, relieving the pressure. The two bassists are also prominent on " Deep Canyons on Mars ", diffusing ominous vibes through gravelly distorted sounds. The heavy, nightmarish tones are pacified when vibraphone and trumpet step forward, yet obscurity still lives here when the bass returns with wah-wah bluesy sounds drowned in electronics. Though the result of multiple sessions, Constellations and Hemispheres feels like a unified experiment—mostly stripped down of gloss but still with haunting and transcendent moments to reflect upon. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Dark Energy ► 02 - Lake Tanganyika ► 03 - Dark Matters, Particles of Light, Mirror of the Unseen

items.body:
Sleeping With Sirens are making their way back to Asia.

Presented by PULP Live World, the American post-hardcore band will bring the An Ending In Itself Tour Asia 2027 to three cities in the region next April, with stops in Singapore, Kuala Lumpur, and Manila.

The upcoming shows will bring together favourites from the band's catalogue and material from their latest and eighth studio album, An Ending In Itself.

Produced by Will Yip, An Ending In Itself explores hardship, resilience, and the search for meaning in uncertain times. The record marks the latest chapter for a band whose songs have soundtracked the lives of alternative music fans across generations.

Fans can expect to hear from a catalogue that includes 'If You Can’t Hang', 'Kick Me', 'Apathetic', 'If I’m James Dean, You’re Audrey Hepburn', and 'Roger Rabbit'.

The band's current lineup comprises Kellin Quinn, Justin Hills, Nick Martin, Matty Best, and Tony Pizzuti. Pizzuti, who had been touring with Sleeping With Sirens since 2022, is now officially part of the lineup.

A post shared by PULP Live World (@pulpliveworld)

items.body: Ambient label Hibernate have relaunched, returning from a lengthy hiatus – pulling out of their own musical hibernation – well rested, and awakening to a new era despite the steady, soporific state of their new output. Anthéne’s Colour Fields bends and slowly stirs, its head ruffling the pillow and its ambient body grazing the sheets with the first tentative signs of movement after a deep sleep. Its eyes begin to open, and the synths begin to drink in the light. As soon as those lidded shutters are pulled up, the music floats on legs it doesn’t own, levitating in its warm, self-fulfilling light. Colour Fields is a rural form of ambient music, evocative of wide-open plains and swaying oaks drunk on the promises of summer. The music lives in and is a part of an endless field, existing in the fabric of every blade of grass, in a budding lavender bush and a late-to-wake patch of bluebells, oversleeping like a hungover teenager who forgot to set the alarm. The ambient is jettisoned, spreading outwards like a sprinkling of dandelion seeds. The music is as delicate as a wing – one touch, and it would crinkle and crease. In terms of length, Colour Fields is a short release, but it’s perfect as it is, and there should be no time scale when it comes to music. After all, a longer album doesn’t necessarily mean a better album, does it? That train of thought can ruin a musician, who is then forced into lengthening (and subsequently weakening) the album: that kind of obesity and excess is rife in a culture that can’t get enough. Less is always more, and as soon as you start pandering to the thoughts of others, the music ceases to be your own. Hibernate’s new season also includes a new album from Mind Over MIDI. Tussmørke’s quivering, grey-skinned synth reminds one of early science-fiction, while the more pronounced use of electronics adds a good deal of mystery to the music, complete with a dome-shaped flying saucer and all the clichés that accompany such an image. Something has landed in this quiet field, and the cows don’t like it. But the landing isn’t an obvious craft, less an iconic image embedded in popular culture and more like something that stealthily creeps around in the undergrowth. A snaking synth seems to exude a strange form of radiation, capable of incinerating an entire harvest of crops with a mutated form of vitamin D. Water-like melodies run alongside the gentle tweets of birdsong. The melodies themselves seem to hover, lying low over the treescape. Its skin-tearing temperatures quietly and methodically decimate, but the surrounding atmosphere is a stormy sky, a colour close to malignant lead, and as lethal as a speeding bullet. Beats are suppressed, draping low over the background like a metallic curtain. The music’s picked up like a radio wave, but it’s hard to tune out of its frequency once it arrives. You feel it in the pit of your stomach, a steady trickle of indistinct rain or a treble-thin rustling which not only nestles into the mix but invades it, recurring throughout the album along with a skidding synth and the sound of trampling. Those hurried footsteps litter the album – the owner of those worn shoes is running from something, chased through a mile-long cornfield. With its recurring themes and lightless copses, it’s not exactly dark ambient… but it has been exiled. www.hibernate.bandcamp.com

items.body: Franny is listening to a program on wolves. I say to her, Would you like to be a wolf? She answers haughtily, How stupid, you can’t be one wolf, you’re always eight or nine, six or seven. Not six or seven wolves all by yourself all at once, but one wolf among others, with five or six others. Percussionist and composer Sarah Hennies’ new album “Everything Else” is comprised of two 20-minute tracks. ‘Falsetto’ is a piece performed using a variety of different hand-held bells sourced from thrift stores and flea markets, with layer upon layer of slightly different rhythms and timbres interacting acoustically to the extent that they are constantly merging and separating, making it difficult to distinguish them or tell how many there are. They become like a crowd or a pack, as the above quote from Deleuze and Guattari’s A Thousand Plateaus indicates: both one and more-than-one, uncanny and unpredictable in its/their indeterminacy and multiplicity. The piece’s sudden stop implies an endless ringing continuation just out of earshot. Second piece ‘Everything Else’ introduces the clicking, ripping, and scrunching of what sounds like a frustrated or distracted typewriter operator. Lurching, unsteady tones emanate in a scattered fashion from an accordion or some other bellows instrument, along with peeps from a similarly unstable duck whistle. Apart from the gradual introduction of instruments, the piece changes very little in overall effect, and again ends in an arbitrary manner that suggests the possibility of perpetual continuation. There’s a sense of dry absurdity and irreverence here, yet it’s difficult to write this off as simply a joke piece, as it shares a certain uncanny multiplicity with the first track. Better to say that humour doesn’t necessarily indicate shallowness, nor does profundity necessarily require seriousness. What ties the two pieces together, above and beyond an uncanny multiplicity, is the sense in which they are both always exceeding and overspilling their own context. ‘Falsetto’ is technically ‘just’ a bunch of different bells clinking, and yet the sensory experience of the piece is so much richer and more intense than this description would suggest. Likewise, ‘Everything Else’ goes nowhere yet is in constant Brownian motion, its momentum all the more relentless for having no overall direction. There’s something very captivating about all this excess, a psychoacoustic absorption in resonances and not-quite-repetitions. This overspill seizes and charms the ear, making beguiling music out of unlikely sounds.   "Everything Else" (NRR37) by Sarah Hennies   Sarah Hennies No Rent Image: ‘Mexican Wolf Pack’ by Eric Kilby on Flickr, Creative Commons Attribution-Sharealike 2.0 Generic licence.

items.body: Opening with a melody that would go down easily in a town like Twin Peaks or Wayward Pines, the nightmarish lullaby of Heat & Entropy lights the fuse that sets the rest of the record on fire. The bass does more than shiver; it shudders, close to its breaking point. The music almost rips itself apart, but, as is always the case, a fragile ecosystem must take root if the music is to survive, progress and prosper. Somehow, the major knots and sharp twists find a way to coexist. Underpinned by an abrasive layer of static, the electronic melodies are planted like inorganic seeds that spread and then ripen when the time is right. Ever-shifting tones constantly move, and they bring with them a dragging, heavy substance. Heat & Entropy contorts itself, the multiple sequences twisting and turning like a nest of snakes, the melodies so flexible they could resemble the boneless bodies of a hundred pythons, their undulating motion rising and then consistently falling. And it’s got plenty of venom in its bite. Heat & Entropy is a heavily electronic album. It’s a hard-hitter, pulling punch after punch and never missing a trick. Obscured melodies glint like ‘Phantom Lights’ seen across the sunset-soaked waters. Like looking out at French cottages from the cliffs of Dover, the lights are there, and they’re very real. The music is always striving to get somewhere, always building and building until the stress of it all takes its toll and it collapses. Heat & Entropy is on the verge of overloading, fierier than the deserts of Mars. ‘The Kraken’ is another monster of a track, as is ‘Surface Tension’. They nestle in a dark place. Melodies light up and then slowly fade out, and a gravelly feminine voice glitches in and out of the music. Constantly adapting to its new, added layers and intricate synths, the music builds and builds upon mountains of sand, on foundations that crumble away to nothing but dust. An electric guitar’s melodies are left to burn in the background, dissolving into red embers that can only pop and crackle for a very brief time. The wicked, orange sparks that rise out of the fire are the only providers of light. The safety of the piano gives way to the creaking, unhealthy dissonance of the strings, which grinds against the other elements (‘Corpseways’). Heat & Entropy’s swampy electronic tones are always active. Resembling the video game Doom in its disturbing intensity, the music doesn’t let up, emitting the light of a black sun. www.badabingrecords.com

items.body:
After the OĽUN album I reviewed enthusiastically a while back, here’s the next project, again motivated and led by violinist/fiddler/composer Ján Kružliak Jr., continuing the rapprochement, indeed embrace, between Slovakia’s traditional music and its classical music. This time it reconnects the works of classical composers who were inspired by and drew on village musics with those traditional sources and styles.
Three ensembles are involved: the Spectrum Quartett led by Kru�liak with two violins, viola and cello; Nogaband, the traditional-style quartet of fiddles, contra (chording viola) and bass that’s led by fiddler and singer Michal Noga; and the female vocal group Ulijanky, plus guest singer Simona Hulejov�.
The majority of the tracks are interpretations of works by Slovak composer Eugen Suchon (1908-1993), with others from fellow-Slovaks Ilja Zeljenka (1932-2007) and Alexander Moyzes (1906-1984), and Hungarian B�la Bart�k (1881-1945) who did a lot of his very detailed collecting of folk music in Slovakia.
In each case the sources - musicians and locations in villages across Slovakia - are credited in the notes, and these arrangements and performances reconnect with the energy and traditional vocal sound of those sources.
In no way is this an orchestra-smoothed thing; this is gutsy, brilliantly played and sung music with all the spirit, skill and technique of traditional music, from players and singers who deeply understand and inhabit it. It’s a glorious piece of work, music to luxuriate in. There’s too much richness to begin to detail, but here’s a dip into a few moments to give the flavor. The tracks all have very long titles detailing their sources, so for brevity’s sake I’ll just give track numbers.

items.body: Karine Polwart has proved herself to be an exceptional talent as a singer and songwriter for many years, all the way back to her time with Malinky (the song �Thaney� was a revelation). As a solo artist she�s grown and continually expanded her horizons, coming now to Windblown , a project that began life seven years ago, when Polwart, along with sound designer and composer Pippa Murphy, was artist in residence at Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh. The album, with its stage show and book, tells the story of the garden�s oldest specimen, a Sabal palm tree ( Sabal bermudana ), which was gently felled in 2021, and contained a surprise nobody had expected. The tree is the starting point. From there, imagination runs free. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan It�s an album of voice and piano (the outstanding, sympathetic Dave Milligan), and, for all its global outlook on connections, one that�s very rooted in Scotland. You can hear it on the opening track, �Hear The Rigging/Last In Line,� where the melody becomes a slow, aching lament that would sound completely natural on the pipes. The stripped-down sound gives the songs both crafted stateliness and real intimacy. Each one is an exhalation, a memory, a celebration and exploration, with recurring phrases in the words and music acting as touchstones � or even hooks; they certainly stick in the mind. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan In many ways, this is a modest album, with piano, voice and light, judicious soundscaping. It won�t overpower with noise. Yet at the same time, it�s epic, a look at history, at the flow and grandeur of nature, and the things we all carry within us. The music, and especially Polwart�s warm, compassionate voice, envelop the listener, and makes them a participant, not an observer, but a part of the journey and the history. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan The irony arrives at the end, when the venerable old tree is down, and seeds are examined. What people for two hundred years had believed to be a Sabal bermudana turns out to be something different, a Sabal mexicana � and one of the small plants fill grow where it�s forerunner once stood. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan Like music, plants keep to a different time � and this album/book/show give the tree the requiem it deserves, as well as hope for the future. Find the artist online. Sara Serpa - Encounters and Collisions (Review) Karine Polwart- Laws of Motion (Review) Live in the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh, 2025

items.body: Sudan Dudan is a Norwegian duo, Marit Karlberg and Anders Erik R�ine, who have released four albums over the last twenty years. On M�rke refrenger , their fifth, they are joined by Hans Hulb�kmo and Magnus Skavhaug Nergaard, contributing instrumentally and with the production. There are eight songs on the album with accompaniment principally led by acoustic guitar, augmented by fiddles, langeleik, lyre, jaws harp and more. The opening track, �Gard og grind� (�Fence and gate�) is a fine introduction to what is to come: finger-picked acoustic guitar, fiddle, bass and snare-drum played with brushes leading into the harmonized vocal, together creating an alluring sound drawing the listener in. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The mood of the album, reflected in its title which translates as �Dark Refrains,� is not always dark, but most of the material, including the title track, certainly has a reflective quality. According to the press release �the lyrics smoulder with unease about the present and the future, while looking back to the myths and riddles of the past. They speak of the earth, the sun, the moon, stars and planets, of lost brothers, quarrelling sisters, loss and grief, of the power of imagination, and of the answers to the simplest and most difficult riddles.� The lyrics of all the songs, in Norwegian, are included in the sleeve notes and while a hasty online translation can aid with some understanding, the full meanings tend to remain cryptic, but there is a sense that words and music complement each other. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan For all its dark moodiness, M�rke refrenger does have its lighter moments. �Bagatelle� recalls and reinvents the melody of a well-known French song, adding some off-kilter harmonies, while �Rulleball� is more characteristically Norwegian, employing a vocal style known as tralling in which words are replaced by a vocalization of the melody, originally used to accompany dances when no instrument was available. No translation necessary there. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The final track �Skriften p� veggen� (�the writing on the wall�) features, for the only time on the album, electric guitar. The sound is deep and twangy, shades of Duane Eddy or a David Lynch soundtrack and it works very well. All in all a fine, imaginatively conceived and beautifully produced record, available as a download or vinyl. Find the artists online. items.body:
Though this recording documents the work of thirteen of Belgium's most innovative ensembles, the real star is the Park Abbey located just outside Leuven and founded in 1129. Built and maintained for the purpose of quiet meditation, the abbey hosted the musicians who used the quiet surroundings to prepare and record their unique musical imaginings. The result is a mostly instrumental collection that mines the riches of Belgian folk and world music traditions, including Romani scales,
La Pump
rhythms, and accordion-based
bal-musette
flavors.
For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. They have rendered a warm sound using the natural reverb of ancient stone provided by the project�s silent partner.
